"What do I do?" said Oryn.

"You keep the stone. Somebody must be standing at the place where we began, so that we know it when we come round to it from the other side. And I should like one of us to be outside the whole time, with the mule, where an Arbiter is an Arbiter."

The healer nodded. She had expected nothing else, Cael thought, and she took up her post beside the grey stone with the rein in her hand, as she would have stood at the head of a bench.

They set off northward, with the ring on their right hands and the ruts some forty yards away on their left.

It went slowly at first. Lira walked with her arms a little out from her sides and a look of deep concentration, like a person carrying a bowl filled to the brim; twice in the first cord she said "Out," sharply, and stepped to her right. Karis felt her way along beside her. At the cord's end she stopped, and shuffled a hand's breadth inward, and a hand's breadth out, and stood still.

"Here."

Brom came up, and drove the hooked point of the bill into the turf, and levered out a square of it as big as a plate. He laid it grass downward. It showed black on the frost.

"One," said Cael, and wrote it.

At the second station Karis did a new thing. She turned round and looked back along the cord to the first turf, and beyond it to the stone; and then she waved Seln forward along that same line, until he stood a full cord ahead of her with a peeled wand held upright.

"That is where the next mark would fall if the line ran straight," she said. "It won't. Watch."

They walked the third cord. Lira kept to her stride inside, and Karis to the line, and when the cord came tight Karis was standing well to the right of Seln's wand. She had her short cord out already, and she laid it on the grass from the wand to her own boots and read the knot.

"Six feet and a half. Inward. Write that beside the three."

He wrote it.

It was the third line of a new table, and it was of another kind from the sixty-three that he had written on a mountain. There a cord and a clock had shown what anybody could check. Here the only instruments were two people's Arbiters, going out and coming back; he had none to offer, and so he held the pencil for the people who had, and it surprised him a little that he did not grudge it.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

It was Brom who found the iron.

He had come up to cut the third turf, and he set the bill's point where Karis's heels had been and leaned on the haft; and there was a sound that did not belong on that hillside, steel on iron, a short dull clink. Brom took the bill away as if it had burnt him.

"There's a thing in the ground," he said.

It stood a boot's width from the place where she had stopped, and the grass had hidden it. When Brom parted the stems with the side of his hand they all saw it: a square bar of iron, as thick as two fingers, driven straight down into the turf so that a hand's length of it stood clear. It was brown with rust and flaking, and its head had been beaten a little flat, and spread at the edges, by something heavy.

Lira had come out across the line to look, and she crouched and tipped her head.

"There's a mark on it. On this side. And figures."

The mark was stamped into the iron, a thumb's breadth below the head, and Cael knew it before the rust let him see the whole of its shape. He had seen it painted over a hearth in a wool-factors' counting room, and cut in a lintel at the last station on a western road; it was printed in the corner of the sheet that lay rolled in the middle box, back at the turn of the ruts. Under it somebody had punched two numerals.

"Thirty-one," said Karis.

She had gone very still, with the cord's end in her fist.

"That's the registry's stamp," said Lira. "That's theirs. What's it doing in a field two days past a fence that isn't on their map?"

Seln had come back down the line with his wand, and he stood over the stake and looked at it without bending. His mild face told Cael nothing whatever, and by now Cael knew that for a kind of news.

Something in Cael had turned toward the thing as well. Anchor asked now, more quietly than it had ever asked, as one craftsman takes note of another's work. There. It was not a question. Here was a point that somebody else had fixed, and told to stay, and it had stayed.

He put that down, and looked at what was left.

He had laid two things side by side at a wash four days ago, and had refused to rule a line between them for want of a third. A query had come down to a registry from somewhere above it, asking which way certain people had gone. A paper had come over a river with a hundred marks, in the hand of somebody who had learned to write at a ruled desk. And here, on the edge of a place where a carter would not put a wheel, was a bar of iron with a registry's stamp on its neck.

That made three. He could rule the line now, and it would be straight. What he could not do was say which way along it he was looking.

"Don't touch it," said Karis. Her voice shook a little, and then steadied. "Nobody is to pull at it, or clean it. I have three stations and I want sixty. It has stood there a good while without us and it will stand until we come round." She turned her back on it with a visible effort. "Brom. Cut the turf a foot short, and I'll allow for the foot."

"You're leaving it," said Lira.

"I am finishing a count. If I stop at every wonder on this hillside we shall be here at dusk with half a shape, and I had rather have a whole one."

They went on. Cael walked the fourth cord with his head turned back over his shoulder. The bar stood in the grass where they had left it, brown and small, beside a square of black turf; and he thought that it was a strange thing to have crossed a Line, and a mountain, and ninety-six days of road, and to be met at the far end of all of it by two numerals that somebody at a counter had signed for.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

By the tenth station she no longer needed the wand.

"It is in my wrist," she said. She was standing with the cord's end held out before her, and as Cael watched she swung it to the right, without looking down, and stopped. "There. Lira?"

"In," said Lira, a stride beyond her.

He laid the short cord down all the same, since a wrist is not an instrument, and wrote what the knot said. He had written that figure nine times already.

They went round the north side with the ruts beside them. He could see where the carts had gone, forty yards off, keeping the same distance from the line the whole way, as exactly as if the carters had had a cord of their own; and he supposed that in a sense they had. A man who walked in front of a mule here for twenty-two years, with a Path in him, would have learned to the yard where he ceased to be comfortable.

From the north the ring looked different. The eleven uprights had closed up and overlapped, and between two of the tallest he had his first clear sight of what lay among them. It was a floor, grey and pale and perfectly level, raised a little above the grass like the top of a low table; and the morning light lay on it without a shadow.

The ruts came back to their old line on the eastern side, and went away from them over the next swell. Seln was waiting there, a cord ahead, and he was down on one knee.

"Here," he said, when they came up. "And there, and beyond that tussock. I should like all of you to see it before it is trodden."

There were paths in the grass, and Cael would not have found them. They were no wider than his two hands, and the stems had not been broken, only pressed aside, low down, by something that went under them rather than through. Three of them crossed the line within twenty yards of one another. Where the nearest ran over a patch of bare ground there was a print in the frost-softened earth, as broad as a palm, with no mark of a claw.

"Going in?" said Lira, very low. "Or coming out?"

"Both. That one is this morning's, and it points inward. This is older, and it goes out. They use these as a hold uses its gate." Seln had not risen. "I cannot give you a number from a path. I can say that it is not one animal, or two. And I can say that I have gone the whole of the north side and not found a single run. They come and go by the east."

"He told us they lived in them," said Brom.

"He did. I had hoped that he was repeating something." Seln stood, and dusted his knee. "I have seen no animal. I should like that entered exactly. I have seen where they walk."

Cael looked at the print, which was the breadth of the ones beside a white stone in a valley, and of the ones on a gravel bar; and then he looked at the sun, which was a third of the way up the sky.

"We go in at noon," he said. "Not before; it's the hour they've never once been seen abroad, on a stretch or at a ford. And we're out again and on the west side of that stone with the sun two hands above the hills. Whatever isn't done by then isn't done."

"Two hands," said Seln. "I shall hold you to it."

They took the south side at a better pace, since by now each of them had the work by heart. Lira drifted out twice more and said so. Brom's turfs lay behind them in a long curve, black on the pale grass; and when Cael looked back along them from the fiftieth, he could see the curve closing on itself like a hoop.

From the south he had the whole of it in one view, for the first and only time. The grey stone was away on his left hand, with a small brown mule beside it. Beyond it the ruts swung out round the north in their wide curve. The floor lay in the middle of everything, with its eleven broken stones, and on the far side, where no turf had been cut, there was the low place in the grass where Seln had knelt.

Nothing moved in the whole of it but themselves. It looked like the plainest piece of country in the world, and five people had just walked the edge of it with their Arbiters going out and coming back at every stumble.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The last cord fell short.

They had come up from the south, with the grey stone in plain sight ahead and a square brown figure standing beside it with a mule. Karis reached the end of the sixty-second cord, and stopped, and found the line, and Brom cut his turf; and the stone was still some way off.

She coiled the cord over her shoulder, and walked the rest on the line, in her own short steps, counting under her breath, until she set her last foot down against the stone itself.

"Sixty-two cords and twenty strides," said Karis.

She stood there with her eyes shut, and her lips moved for some time. Cael knew what she was doing, since she had the length of that cord in feet, to the knot, in a notebook that nobody else had read, and had paced her own stride twice against his in the dark. He would have given a good deal to check the sum; he had only her figures for the half of it, and so he waited.

"One thousand three hundred and seventy-four yards, and a piece."

"Round a field," said Brom.

"Round a field, and home to the stone that it started from." She opened her eyes. "I have one offset written sixty-two times in his hand. There is only one shape that will do that."

She turned her head and looked across the grass to the east, where eleven broken stones stood about a pale floor.

"From any mark on it to the middle is ten cords. I can work that without a table. Ten cords from this stone, on the old line of the road, and one would be standing in the centre of those."

Then she said one thing more, without any weight.

"A circle is a made shape."

It lay in the air a breath. Lira was looking at the stones, and Brom had the bill over his shoulder and was counting his turfs. Oryn, who had stood at that stone since first light, was watching five people come toward her along a line that she could not see. Nobody took the words up, and Karis did not seem to look for anyone to do so. She had entered a property of the figure, and she bent to tie the cord.

Cael heard it. He put it with the three other things, a little apart from them, since it was of another kind.

Seln had already started back along the black marks toward the third.

Cael went after him, and they stood over the iron together. In the full light it was plainer than it had been: the square bar, and the spread head, and the stamp. Seln crouched now, without laying a finger on it, and looked at the rust, where it had lifted in leaves, and at the turf round the bar's foot, which had grown up close against the metal on every side.

"Five years in the weather. A cold term either side."

"You can tell that from rust?"

"From rust, and from the grass. It has had time to forget that anything was done to it." He tilted his head to bring the stamp into the light. "I have seen iron of this pattern given out across a counter, and signed for. A man answers for what he takes."

"Thirty-one."

"I do not know what the number counts, and I shall not guess." Seln rose. He looked from the stake to the ring, and back along the line of turfs to the stone, as he would have looked over a room that somebody had left in a hurry. "It stands a boot's width from where she stopped. She found that place with her feet, this morning, knowing nothing. Whoever drove this found the same place to the same boot's width."

"With a cord," said Cael.

"With a cord, or a chain. That is what I should like you to carry away." He nodded at the iron. "You drive them where you've measured to. Not where you've measured from."

Cael looked at it. A stake marked the far end of a measure; somebody had stood at another place, with the other end of a line in his hand, and had paid it out until it reached exactly here.

He looked along the only line there was. It ran from the stake's foot, across two hundred yards and more of pale grass, to the middle of eleven stones.

Chapter 29 — A Stride Inside

[Measured, watchful narration; hold the quiet ground's pressure beneath the ordinary work]

They held the trials at the stone, at noon, and Karis set the order.

"Smallest first," she said. She had ruled a fresh leaf into five rows and given it to Cael, with the pencil. "A one-armed man has told us that nothing can be declared in there, and five of us felt our Arbiters go, and I believe both. I believed in a ledge as well. There are prints in the grass on the far side of this field, and I am not going to learn that he was mistaken by having Lira crack the sky open a quarter of a mile from whatever left them."

"I'd not crack it on purpose," said Lira.

"You did not crack it on purpose the last time. That is rather my point." Karis looked round at them. "So I go first, with one point, unlit. If it sets, I shall know it, and nobody else will, and we stop there and think. If mine does not, then Brom. Then Seln. You are last of the four, and you go only if the three of us have had nothing."

"And outside the line nobody tries anything," said Seln. "It is a road. I should like that kept."

"Nobody tries anything outside. We know what we are outside."

The sun stood as high as it would go at that time of year, pale and small, and their shadows lay short on the frosted grass. They had gathered on the western side of the grey stone, with the turn of the ruts at their backs and the ring two hundred yards and more in front. Oryn had the mule by the cheek-strap a few yards behind the rest, and her free hand tucked into her armpit for warmth; she had watched the whole of the morning from that stone without a word.

Cael looked at the leaf that he had been given. There were five rows on it, each headed with a letter, and his own was not among them. That was as it should be, since he had been handed the pencil for the very reason that there was nothing of his to enter. He had kept the count at a great many trials of other people, and had thought himself used to the seat.

Karis stepped over.

Cael saw her shoulders tighten as her foot came down, and ease again; she had done this nine times in the dark, she had told them at first light, and it plainly did not grow pleasanter. She stood a stride inside the line, with her back to the ring, and her eyes went slowly along the slope in front of her from left to right, as he had seen them go over a district floor before a bout.

"I can see them," she said. "Every place. I could put sixteen down on that bank and tell you where each would sit, to the hand. That is not altered in the least."

"That's only knowing how," said Brom.

"It is knowing how, and it is still here; I want it written that it is still here." Her right hand had come up. "Now I am going to set the first, eleven paces off, by that tuft with the frost on it."

The hand dipped, the small exact dip of a person dotting a page.

Nothing happened that he could see, and that proved nothing, for a set point gave no light; so he watched her face instead, and it had the look of somebody who has put a foot down for a stair in the dark and found the floor.

"No," said Karis. She tried it a second time, and a third, quickly. "No. It has not set. A lecturer would say that the declaration did not render. And that is not the whole of it. When I am empty and try to set one, I feel myself reach into the purse and close my fingers on nothing. Here I am not even reaching. I am three parts full, and I can't find the hand to reach with."

"Does it hurt?" said Oryn, from behind the stone.

"Not in the least."

"Does it tire you? Trying."

Karis thought about that with real care.

"It costs nothing. There's nothing to spend."

She stepped back over. He saw the colour come into her face as the foot came down, and her eyes go, for an instant, to something at the edge of her sight that nobody else could see.

"Back," she said. "First row. Write it as I gave it: every place seen; none set; no cost."

He wrote it, and looked at it a breath longer than a line needed. He had sat in a whitewashed room for the better part of a year while that small exact person laid points on a wall for him to study, and he carried one of them still, the fifth of his nine; and he had not known until this noon that there was a place anywhere where her hand could make that dip and have nothing come of it.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Brom went over with his sleeves rolled.

He had done that on purpose, Cael thought, so that all of them should be able to see his forearms: the left with its pale dry seam from the heel of the hand to the middle, and the right, which had never had a mark on it. He stood a stride inside and held them out a little before him, with the palms down.

For forty-three days he had refused that Path, and Cael had watched him do it on a ferry, and in a wash, and under a cart on a crust of rock. He had seen the grey start at those wrists whenever a load came on suddenly, and each time he had seen Brom put it down again, like a man pressing a lid onto a pot; it had been the hardest kind of work, and it had been done every hour.

Now, for the first time since a river, Brom told it to come.

"Skin."

He said it aloud, in his ordinary voice, as he might have called a dog that was lying a yard off.

They waited, and the big brown wrists stayed the colour of wrists. He turned them over to look at the insides, and turned them back.

"Well," said Brom.

He did not seem distressed; he stood there with his arms out, frowning a little, like a person who has walked into his own kitchen and found a chair moved.

"What's it like?" said Lira. "You said a door, yesterday. Closing behind you."

"It's that. The door's shut, and I'm on the wrong side of it from where I keep the thing." He let his arms fall. "It's queer. I've not used it since the ford, and I'd have told you I'd got used to going without. But I always knew where it was. I could feel it in the next room, as you can feel a fire through a wall. There's no next room."

He looked about him, and his eye fell on the middle box, which sat on the grass just outside the line where he had put it down. He leaned across the stone and took it by its two beckets, and lifted it over, and stood holding it against his chest.

"Same," he said, after a moment.

"The same what?" said Karis.

"Weight. I wanted to know whether a hundredweight was a hundredweight in here, with nothing behind me." He set it down inside the line, quite gently. "It is. So that's what I've got. Write that."

"I am to write that a box weighs the same."

"It's the only thing I've tried that worked."

Cael wrote it. He wrote Skin called aloud; none, and under it, since the row was Brom's, lifted a hundredweight; no difference; and it seemed to him that of the two findings the second was the one that Brom would take home.

Seln had been standing at the end of the row with his hands behind him.

"I shall be brief," he said. "I have very little to show."

He stepped across, and for a breath he only stood, with his eyes half shut. Cael knew what he was reaching for, since he carried a piece of the same thing himself, sealed, and had felt it lift in him at every dusk for two years.

"There is nothing to lift," said Seln. "I looked for it as one feels for a banister. It is not that it resists. It is not there to be asked."

"Then you're only a man in a coat," said Lira. "Like the rest of us."

"I have been only a man in a coat for a great deal of my working life. Will you all look at the mule for a count of three, and then look back?"

It was an odd request, and they did it. The mule was regarding a tussock; Cael counted three, and turned his head, and the place where Seln had stood was empty.

There was the grass, and the short noon shadows, and a stride beyond the stone a patch of bent stems where two boots had been. Lira made a small sound. She had the best eyes of the five, and Cael saw them go the whole length of the slope and come back with nothing.

"Four yards to your right," said a mild voice. "And down."

He was crouched low against a tussock of the pale grass, side on to them, with his face turned down into the crook of his arm and his hands drawn up into his sleeves. He had put himself to the south of them, where the low sun came from behind him into their eyes. There was no Path in it, and no trick that a child could not have understood once it was shown; and it had still taken five people, all of them looking for him, the better part of a breath to find a man in a dark coat on an open hillside at noon.

He stood up and brushed the frost from his knee.

"I've a knife and fifteen years. It was never most of what I do."

"That isn't a trial of anything," said Karis. But she was looking at the bent grass, and at where he had got to, and her pencil hand had twitched. "I suppose that it is a trial of you. Third row. Path sought; none. Practitioner not found for a count of two."

"A count of three," said Seln, coming back over the stone. "I should not like the record to flatter you."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Lira went last of the four, and she did not make a joke of it.

She sat down on the grass outside the line and took off the great boot, and unwound the whole of a spare shirt, and stood up on her own taped foot with the frost under it. She was to run on nothing for a fortnight yet, and nobody reminded her of it; this was one stride, and she had plainly weighed it against a healer's month before she touched the lace.

"I want all of it," she said. "Not a lean. I'm going to ask for the whole thing, the way I'd ask on a card with a panel watching, and I'm going to ask along the line, that way, north. So if the old man's wrong I come down in grass and not on top of one of you."

"And if he is wrong," said Karis, very quietly, "it will be heard at Thornwater."

"I know what it'll be. I heard it come back off a mountain." Lira's face was pale. "It went off by itself, that morning. I never told it to. I've got to walk into a place with dogs in it on this foot, and I'd like to know, before I do, whether it can."

There was no arguing with that. Cael had the ruling, and he gave it with a nod, and she stepped over the stone and turned to face north, with the ring on her right hand.

He did not watch her go. If a one-armed man had been wrong for thirty years, the answer to it would come out of the grass on the eastern side, a quarter of a mile off, where three runs crossed a line; and somebody had to have his eyes there when the air broke. He fixed them on that place and kept them on it.

So it was his own feet that told him. Wind stood up in them to go with hers, harder than it had leaned in three months, and he put it down; and in the same instant the grass behind his shoulder hissed.

He waited for the crack, and for whatever a far hillside would send back, and the air lay as it had lain all morning, cold and still. Nothing stirred on the eastern grass.

He turned his head. She was a yard and a half along the line from the place where she had planted herself, with the left foot forward and the right drawn up beside it, looking down at the pair of them on the frost.

"That was a step," she said.

She said it to her feet. Then she looked round at the row of them, and her eyes were very wide.

"I asked for all of it. I went up onto my toes and let the whole of both legs go, the way I'd go on a card, and I didn't stop it. I've stopped it every day for three months, just there, with my heels off the ground. I never touched it this time. Brom saw; he'd have seen if I'd held any back."

"She went like a hare off its form," said Brom. "For a yard."

For an instant Cael thought that she was going to weep, and then he saw that it was not that at all.

"It's in me. It's not in the air."

She turned it over, standing there.

"I'd always thought of it as mine. They told me at Fenmark that it was a thing I did, and I believed them, and I was proud of doing it well. And every piece of the doing's still here. I can feel it. I could do that step again exactly." She set her right foot forward on its whole sole, and drew it back. "There's just nothing out there to take hold of."

"Come out," said Oryn. "You've a bare foot on frost."

Lira stepped back over the grey stone, and stopped dead on the near side with her breath caught.

"Oh," she said.

"Back?" said Karis.

"Back." She had her hand flat against her own breastbone. "I felt it at the stone last night, but I wasn't looking then. I was looking this time."

"What is it like? I want it in your words. I have Brom's door, and my own purse."

Lira frowned, and hunted for it.

"It doesn't come on like a lamp. It's just there, and it's where it was, like a clock that stopped and started again without losing the time."

Karis had Cael write that down as it was spoken, the whole of it, in the fourth row. She read it over his arm when it was done.

"That is the best of the four," she said. "It is the only one with a measurement in it."

Lira wound the shirt on again, with fingers that were not quite steady, and pulled the great boot over it, and stamped.

"I've spent three months not doing it," she said, to the boot. "I thought that was hard. It's nothing to standing there and asking with everything I've got and being given a step." She looked up at Cael. "I know what's left now. When it isn't me doing the not."

"What?"

"Legs," said Lira. "And they're good ones. Somebody took trouble with them."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

"Now me," said Oryn.

She had given the mule's rein to Seln, and she came up to the stone at her own pace, rubbing her hands together, and looked at Brom.

"The wrist. The one I did, that I read at the fire."

He held it out. She took it between both of hers, as she had taken a carter's palm on a plank at Thornwater, with two fingers of her right hand laid along the inside where the pulse was.

"This is how it goes," she said. She was speaking to Karis, since Karis was the one who would have it written. "It's the short reading; it costs me nothing. I'll have it running, and I'll count aloud so that you can hear where I am. We go over together, him and me. Then back. Then I'll want a third, and I'll tell you what when I've had the two."

"You have never done this," said Karis.

"Nobody has that I ever met. That's why I walked two days."

Her lips began to move, and this time there was sound in them. "One. Two. Three." She nodded to Brom, and the two of them stepped over the stone together, the big man and the square woman, hand in wrist. "Four—"

It stopped. It did not trail away; it stopped as a word stops when a door is shut on the speaker. She stood a stride inside the line with Brom's forearm between her palms, and her mouth was a little open, and there was no count in it.

Cael had seen that look once before, on a mountain, over his own ribs.

"Out," said Oryn hoarsely.

They stepped back, and her lips moved at once. "One. Two." She went all the way to ten this time, with her eyes shut, and Cael saw her shoulders come down as the last of the count went by.

"That's there. It's his, and it's sound, and I could tell you what he had for breakfast." She opened her eyes. "And a stride that way I'd my hands on a piece of warm meat."

"Is it Brom?" said Karis. "Forgive me; I must ask it. His Arbiter stopped at that stone, and yours did. If the thing that you read is his current, and his current is shaped by his Path, then perhaps there was nothing in him to read."

"That's the third." Oryn had not let go of the wrist. "You. Stand where you are, this side. Give me the arm across."

Brom stood on the western side of the stone, where he was an Iron Skin with his Path in the next room. He stretched out his left arm. Oryn kept her two hands on it, and she stepped over the stone by herself, so that she stood inside and he outside, with the mended wrist held between them across the line.

Her lips did not move at all.

She stayed so for a count of twenty, and Cael kept it for her, since she could not. She shifted her fingers on the wrist, and pressed, and shifted them again; then she let go of Brom with her left hand, and bent, still holding him with the right, and laid the left on her own shin.

She straightened.

"Nothing. Not nothing in him. Nothing in my hands."

The wind went over the grass. Nobody at the stone had anything to put beside that.

"He's standing out there with everything he owns. I had it not a minute ago. And I can't so much as feel that he's alive, except that he's warm." She looked down at her two broad palms, as she had looked at them in a hollow of shale, and this time there was no puzzlement in her face. "They told me, and I never checked. Thirty rounds."

"Then the carters were right," said Karis.

"A healer's hands stop working there."

She stepped out. The count came back to her lips before her second boot was down, and she let it run to ten on Brom's wrist, with something like greed, and only then released him.

"So you'll all hear this, and you'll hear it once," said Oryn. "I'm coming in with you. I said I'd see him whole to the ninety-ninth, and I can't do that from a stone. But understand what you've got. If one of you puts a leg through something in there, I can pull it straight. I can splint it, and I can carry my end of you. I can't mend it. Not a scratch. Not till you're this side of that." She pointed at the stone with her chin. "Whatever happens in there happens to six people with no healer."

Cael looked at her as she said it. She had walked two days up an empty road to learn that the one thing she owned in the world, besides a route, would be taken out of her hands at a stone; and having learned it she was going in regardless, with her sleeves pushed back, to be of whatever use a pair of ordinary hands could be. He had not asked her to come. He did not think that he would have had the face to ask it, knowing what a stride had just cost her, and he saw that she would have come all the same.

"Fifth row," said Karis, in a small voice. "As she said it."

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

For a quarter of an hour after that, nobody at the stone had an eye to spare for anybody else.

Cael watched it happen. Five people had each lost a thing, a stride from where they stood, and had it handed back, and every one of them had turned inward to look at it. Oryn was hobbling the mule, with her lips moving in a count that she did not seem to know she was keeping. Brom knelt by the middle box. Karis sat with her eyes shut, and Lira walked up and down on the great boot, a little apart, and Seln stood looking east.

There were five rows to be ruled fair before the leaf went into a box. He took it a cord along the line to the north, to Brom's first turf, where there was a flat place to kneel; and nobody marked his going.

He had seen that it would be so. He had been waiting for it since first light.

He stood beside a square of black turf and priced the thing, as he priced everything, and he did it honestly, since he was about to do it regardless.

The finding in his book said that the hounds answered what went out of a person; and a fragment answering went out of him, as he had felt it go at a ford, where one burst had drawn three. That was the cost, and he set it down first. Against it there was the hour, at which no hound on any road had ever been seen abroad, and there was the choice of what to ask.

The Iron read was the quietest thing he owned. He had refused it on a fan and a lip and a bench, when it would have told him what he was being paid to learn, and each time he had refused because a boy's word could be checked by nobody.

This was a different matter from a map. Six people were about to walk into a place where every one of them believed that all six were alike, and he was the only one who could find out whether that was so.

He opened it.

It came as it had always come, at once and without effort, like an eye that has been kept shut. For a pace and a half on every side he had the ground: the weight of the turf, and the frost standing in it, and a flat stone a foot down that he would never see. He had his own two boots, and the lean of his body over them. It was mass, and the way that mass meant to go, and nothing else.

He was a pace short of the line. He walked.

He had been certain, in the part of himself that kept accounts, of what would happen: a thing taken out of a Path would stop where Paths stopped. He had supposed it since a plank, as the others supposed it, and for the same reason, which was that no other sum came out even; and he had braced for the read to go from him as a count had gone from a healer's lips.

It ran across the stride without a break.

The turf under his left boot was outside the line, and the turf under his right was within it, and he had the weight of both as he had the weight of his own hands. Nothing dimmed. He took another step, and a third, and the ground went on telling him what it was.

He stood still, three strides inside, with his heart going.

Then he did the second thing. He had not been sure, a minute ago, that he would.

He walked in, as a man goes who means to look at the ground that he will presently lead people over, without haste, twenty strides toward the ring. A grey boulder lay there in the grass, as high as his hip, and he walked straight at it. He kept his face to the east; if anyone at the stone had glanced his way, there was only a person with a notebook going to see what lay beyond a rock.

At the twentieth stride he let Wind have his feet.

It was a long way short of a burst. It was the smallest piece of what Lira's fighting had taught him, the lean that takes a body off a line a hair before the blow arrives; and he asked it for a foot. His weight went over without his deciding it. The boulder, which had been in front of him, was on his right hand, and he was past it, and the grass had hardly stirred.

Anybody watching from behind would have seen a person walk round a rock, and no more.

He stood on the far side with the tape drawn tight across his ribs and something going out of him into the cold air, small, as a breath goes out. He listened, and there was the wind, and the hiss of seed-heads, and far off toward the east a bird that got up and settled again. Nothing whatever came through the grass.

He shut them both. He put Wind down, and closed the read as one closes a book, and they went back to where the other seven lay.

He did not know why. He set that beside a healer's word from a hollow of shale, and added nothing to it, as she had added nothing. Five people had lost what they had at that stone, each in a different way, and one of them had asked with her whole body and been given a step. And twenty strides inside it, the things that he carried had answered him as they answered him anywhere.

He walked back along the line, and stepped out over the first turf, and came down to the stone with the leaf in his hand.

Karis took it from him, and read down the five rows, nodding at each. Then she laid it on her knee, and took the pencil, and ruled a sixth.

"And yours?"

She said it to the leaf. It was a clerk's question; she had a table with a row empty.

He had perhaps a breath. He saw Lira, stamping her foot down into a boot the size of a bucket, with her face still stripped from that one step, and he saw a healer flexing her fingers; and he saw that the healer was the plainest reason of all, since she knew nothing of what he was.

To tell it at that stone was to tell it to her, and he could not have said that the things he carried had answered him without saying what they were. There were nine, and every one of them had come out of a person.

One had come out of the mild man who stood six feet off with his hands behind him, looking east. It was the very thing that Seln had reached for at this stone, not half an hour ago, and not found; and Cael had held it shut at every dusk for ninety-six days, so that nobody who might one day speak of it to a carter bound for a ferry should know where a boy had learned it. A healer spoke to every carter on seven roads. She would not have meant the least harm by it.

That was not his alone to give away. It was a real reason, and he distrusted it for coming so readily to hand.

"It was dark before," said Cael. "It's dark now."

Both halves were true. He had looked at that place going over and coming back, and it had been the same dark. Karis wrote. He watched her pencil put the two halves down, one after the other, and he knew what she would take them to mean, and what the other four would take them to mean when they read her leaf; and that the whole was not the truth, though there was not a false word in it.

It was the first thing of that kind that he had kept from any of them in a long while, and he had done it at a stone, at noon, with a pencil going.

"The sun's over," said Lira. She was looking up, with her hand shading her eyes. "If we're going, it's now."

Chapter 30 — The Far Lip

[Measured, watchful narration; hold the quiet ground's pressure beneath the ordinary work]

Six of them went over the stone a little after noon, and the mule stayed where she was.

Oryn had hobbled her on the western side, with a full net and the two panniers still roped on, and the long shape in its oiled cover lashed along the top of the pack as it had been since a mountain. The healer looked at that cover for a breath before she turned away. Then she walked across the line with her hands open at her sides, and Cael saw her fingers close once, hard, as the count went out of them.

They took very little. Brom had the middle box on his back, with the chips in it and the paper, since whatever a surveyor had left would want carrying home in something. Karis had the long cord and the short one. There was the hedging bill, and Lira's knife, and Seln's, and a skin of water.

Seln had the locked case as well, shut, on its strap across his chest. He had looked once at the mule's pack, and once at the stone, and had kept it on him, as he had kept it on every road. Everything else that they owned was either in a loft two days west or under the feet of a mule.

"East, along the old line of the road," said Karis. "I want the cord laid from this stone to the middle, a length at a time, as we laid it round the edge. If I have my sum right, the tenth will end among those stones. If I have it wrong, I should like to be told so by the ground and not by a table."

So they went in as they had gone round. Brom held one end at the stone, and Karis walked the other out until it came tight, and stopped; then he came up to her, and she went on. The other four walked behind, in file, in the track that the cord left. The grass stood to Cael's hip. It closed over each of them as they passed and did not quite rise again, and when he looked back from the third length there was a lane trodden through it, as straight as a ruled margin, with a grey stone and a small brown mule at the far end.

He had his nine fragments as he always had them, and he held them. Wind leaned, since Lira was in front of him. Anchor had fallen quiet at the stake and had not asked since. He had opened nothing after a boulder, and he did not open anything now; but he walked those two hundred yards as the only one of the six who knew that he could have, and it was a strange thing to carry at the back of a file.

At the eighth length the ground began to rise, gently, and the grass grew shorter. At the ninth it was at his knee, and he could see the whole of what stood on the swell in front of them.

It was a floor, and it was round.

It lay on the crown of the rise like the lid of a great jar, grey and pale and quite bare, and the short turf came up to its edge and stopped there as cleanly as a mown field stops at a road. Round its rim, a stride in from the edge, stood the eleven stones. He had counted them from three hundred yards and had the number right.

They were grey, like the floor, and squared, each as thick through as a man's body. Not one of them was whole. The tallest stood twice Brom's height before it ended, and its neighbour came no higher than a knee, and between those two there was every height that a broken thing can have.

"Tenth," said Karis.

She had gone up onto the floor with the cord's end in her hand. It came tight while she was still walking, and she stopped where it stopped her. She was standing at the middle of the round, as near as his eye could tell, with the eleven stones in a ring about her at an equal distance.

She did not say anything about her sum. She laid the end of the cord down very carefully on the grey stone, and set her notebook on it for a weight, and then she paced from where she stood to the rim, in four directions, counting. The four counts came out within a stride of each other.

"Ten cords," she said at last. Her voice was not altogether steady. "I worked it at the stone from the round, with a pencil. And I have walked it now with a rope, from the edge, in a straight line, and there is not a full stride between the two. I have never in my life had a figure come home like that."

Nobody had stepped onto the floor after her. Five people stood on the turf at its western edge, in the track of the cord, and looked.

It was Lira who got the rest of them onto it.

She had not moved from the turf. She stood at the end of the trodden lane with her head tipped back, looking at the nearest of the tall stones, and she was frowning as she frowned at a card.

"There's writing on that," she said.

Round the foot of the stone, a hand above the floor, there ran a band a hand wide, and in the band there were lines. They were sunk in the grey to the depth of a fingernail, fine and even, some straight and some hooked, some crossing others at a slant; they went right round and met themselves. It was only then, with the first rush over, that he noticed what was under him.

Lira had come across it in one boot of her own and one the size of a bucket, and Brom with a hundredweight on his back, and neither of them had rung. Cael came and looked. They held the cord a hand high after that, from crest to crest, and she went along beneath it on her knees with the short one.

She had the brass straightedge, with its pebble on a thread, and she laid it toward each quarter of the floor in turn. "And no pitch. I laid this brass on a mountain for seven days, and on every hundred of it the thread hung off its mark by so many hands. Here it hangs true whichever way I point it. A threshing floor is not as flat as this. A table is not."

"What is it, though?" Brom had let the box down beside her nine crossed twists, and he crouched with one big hand spread on the grey. "It's not slab; slab's got a grain. It's not laid, either. I can't find a course."

There were the honey-coloured stones, such as the walls of Ostrand were built of. There were the dark close ones, like a district hall's, and a pale kind with a sparkle in the break. Cael had knelt down a little way off while she sorted.

He put both palms on the floor. It was smooth, and very slightly rough under the skin, like the shell of an egg. He moved his hands outward over it as far as his ribs would let him, feeling for the thing that every floor he had ever knelt on possessed somewhere: a crack, or a line where one piece met the next.

His fingers found none. He knew that fingers could be wrong on a surface so close, and that the others were all looking at three small stones in a researcher's lap.

He opened the read.

It was the same thing that he had done at the line, done now for work, and he did not count it a third. For a pace and a half round his knees, and a pace and a half straight down, he had the weight of what he was kneeling on, and it was one thing. There was no bed under it, and no joint through it, and no place where it changed. The short upright stood within his reach, and he took in the foot of that as well. It went down into the floor as a horn goes into a skull, and he could find no line between them.

He closed it again. Nothing had come through the grass.

He had known since a hill of plates what he thought of a reading that nobody else could check, and it had not altered. So he took the pencil and wrote in Karis's table, under her level, the only part of what he knew that any one of them could have got with a hand and a pair of eyes.

No seam.

"Nor at the foot of the stones?" said Karis. She had read it upside down.

"Then I shall write that two of us looked." She put it down. "It is a poor sort of catalogue. Round. Level. No seam. Matches nothing. I have written four things about it and three of them are that something is absent."

Cael had expected a good many things of this place, and that had not been among them. He stood on a grey floor with the paper's second sentence going through his head: instruments, and abandoned, and a site. Somebody had sat at a ruled desk and written that, with the sum in words and again in a bracket, and had sent it over a river with a hundred marks in a bag. It had lain a month under a stone. "They live in here because nothing that walks in can fight."

It lay on the cold air. Cael heard it, and so did the rest, and he watched it reach each of them in turn.

A stillhound hunted what went out of a person. Every hold in that country kept its Paths in its pockets on a road because of it; and here was a place, a quarter of a mile across, where a Path could not be taken out of a pocket by anybody. A deer that wandered over that line was a deer. A carter who did was a man with a stick. And five people who had cleared a ford with a declaration and a knife were standing at the door of the den with a hedging bill and two knives, and a healer whose hands had stopped.

Lira was looking west.

They all were. He saw their heads turn, one after another, across twenty-six strides of grey floor and the eleven stones, to the lane that the cord had left in the grass. It ran away from them down the slope, straight, pale in the low light. The grey stone at its end was too small to see. He knew where it was. From the middle of the floor it lay two hundred and twenty yards to the west, and they were standing on the wrong side of the floor from it.

Then they looked at the sun.

It was on the ridge. He had measured two hands under it and spent the quarter of an hour he had given away; now the lower rim of it was touching the hills, red and flattened, and going. The shadows of the eleven stones had run out across the floor and joined. Between them, where the last light struck it level, the grey had begun to shine.

Then four of them looked at Oryn.

She stood a little apart, with her broad hands hanging open. She had told them at noon what they had in her, on this side of a stone, and she met their eyes one after another and did not pretend that it had altered.

And then, all five, they looked at him.

He had the ruling. He was the nearest thing that they had to a captain, and it was his to say which way and how fast. That was the whole of what was in those five faces. Not one of them was asking him anything else.

He stood with it. Nothing that walks in can fight. It was true of five of the six. He had known since a boulder that it was not true of the sixth, and he had told nobody, and he was the person they were all waiting on.

He wrote it there, at the far lip, standing, with the book against his forearm.

It took him less time than it took Brom to shift the box higher on his shoulders and draw the strap tight. He had always written at the start of a thing. He did not know how to begin one without it, and he thought that this might be the last quiet minute of the day.

Ninety-sixth day. The Fallow Ring, at the eastern lip of the floor. Sunset.

The circle is perfect. The stakes are the registry's. The dogs are inside. Everyone's Path dies at the line and mine didn't, and I've told nobody, and I'm going to need to think about why I haven't. Not tonight. Tonight we're inside the one place on the continent where a stillhound can't lose.

He looked at what he had put.

There was a line that came next. He had written it at the foot of every entry since a shelf above a valley with no name, and for the last forty-three days it had ended in the same word. His pencil went to the place.

He did not write it. It would not have been true, and he did not yet know what would be. He shut the book on an entry that stopped short, for the first time since he had crossed the Line, and put it away in Hesk's satchel.

Something lifted in him then, soft, behind the other eight. It came as it came at every dusk, in a meadow or on a road or at the turn of a carter's ruts. It was offering to take him out of the light. He stood ten cords and more inside the line, on the far side of a floor where a Shadow of fifteen years had found nothing to lift, and it came up in him exactly as it always had.

He told it no.

The sun was half gone. Along the foot of the eleven stones the floor had turned the colour of milk. Lira had drawn her knife, and Karis had the last sheet rolled inside her coat, and the healer was lacing her boot with quick hard pulls.

Seln had not yet got up off his knee.

Chapter 31 — Nine on the White

[Taut, lucid narration; keep the Ring's fragment uses, costs, and positions easy to follow]

Seln stood up, and the floor went white.

The sun had gone under the hills while Cael's book was shutting. He had seen the pale thing hold the light on the evening before, from three hundred yards, and had taken it for water; now he stood below its eastern lip, with the rolled edge at the height of his thigh, and saw what it did close to. The long shadows of the stones were gone, and the whole round of it lay level with his hip and gave back the sky, as milk in a pan gives back a window.

He went over the ground once in his head, since six people were about to walk it with the light going.

They stood on the east, at the mouth of the den, and everything that they wanted was on the west. The floor lay between, twenty-six strides across. From its western lip the lane that the cord had trodden ran down through the grass, as straight as a rule, for two hundred and seven yards; and at the end of the lane there was a grey stone and a mule, and beyond the stone a Path was a Path again and a healer's hands were hands. That made two hundred and thirty-three yards from where his boots were.

He had one other mark on that slope. North of the lane a rut came down from under the floor's north-western lip, knee-deep and a stride across, where the rain off the rim had cut itself a road. He had marked the head of it from the ninth cord, and Seln had crossed it on both his rounds in the grass.

"Cael," said Lira.

She had not raised her voice. She was looking between two of the uprights, with the knife held low.

Something grey had come onto the white.

It came over the western lip, where the lane ended, and it came without any sound at all, as everything went on that floor. It was low and long in the back, and it carried its head level, and he had seen that shape beside a white stone in a valley and on a bar of gravel with a river round it. A second came up behind the first, and a third; and then they were coming too quickly to be watched singly, and he counted them as he would have counted fighters onto a yard.

The first was pale, nearly white along the spine, so that against that floor he could see little of it but the legs. The heaviest had a dark stripe from its neck to the root of its tail. Two smaller ones came over shoulder to shoulder and stayed so. There was one long in the leg, which moved like a thing built for running, and one grey to the eyes, which walked a little way onto the white and looked about it and lay down. Three more he could not have told from each other.

"Nine," he said.

"Nine," said Seln. "I am glad to have the figure. I could not get it from their feet."

They did not hurry, and it was that which he liked least. They spread out among the eleven stones as a crew spreads out in its own yard at the end of a day. One sat and scratched. The pale one stood at the middle of the round, by the place where a cord had ended, with its nose down on the grey.

They had gone out by the east at first light, as Seln had read off bare earth, and they had come home by the west, up the one track on the whole of that hillside which six people had made since noon. He thought of a healer at the far end of that track, counting to ten on a wrist, twice, with her Path running; he did not know that it bore, and he left it for whoever kept findings.

"The road's cut."

It was Seln, and he said it as he would have read out a line from a bill of lading.

"What road?" said Brom. "There's not a road in the place."

"The grass. Where the cord went."

Brom looked at the lane then, and at what stood between themselves and the head of it, and said nothing more.

Cael had the ruling, and he made himself look at both ways before he gave it.

Behind him the slope fell away to the east, and the line on that side was nearer by twenty-six yards. It was also the hounds' own door. There were three runs across it and not a stride of it that any of the six had walked; the grass stood hip-high the whole way down, the ground was steep, and in a quarter of an hour it would be dark. If they came out alive on that side, they would be half a circle of open country from a mule. The west was a lane trodden flat by their own feet, with a stone at the end of it that five of them could find with their eyes shut.

"There's a bow on that mule," said Oryn.

She had finished with her boot. She stood up, and for the first time since he had known her she did not seem to know where to put her hands.

"I looked at it at noon and left it lying. I'd come to find out about my hands, and I didn't want anything in them." Her mouth went hard. "That was a healer's reason. Six bolts, in a sleeve on the stock."

"West, then," said Cael.

Nobody asked him why. He saw Seln take up the strap of the locked case by two holes, as he had taken it up at a ford.

"I shall go south about, at forty yards from the lip," said Seln. "I have walked that round twice today. Then down outside the lane, and up it with the thing in my hand. I should not be looked for before three hundred."

"Three hundred. I'll count."

"I know that you will."

He went down off the trodden earth into the grass, stooping, and at his tenth stride there was grass and no Seln. He had done as much at noon, to amuse them, for a count of three.

One, thought Cael. He priced it while he counted, since it was done. It took one of two knives off the hill, and the only one of the six who had nothing wrong with him, and against that it put a bow at the head of the lane. There was a third figure in the sum, which he looked at and did not say: something in his own feet could have had that bow on the floor in forty.

"Round by the south," he said. "On the turf, close in under the lip, and nobody runs. Lira's first, with the knife. Then Karis, and Oryn. I'm behind you. Brom's last, and he's on the floor side." He looked at the hundredweight of paper on Brom's back. "Leave the box."

"No."

"Brom."

"It's eleven sheets and her whole afternoon. It's the only thing we're bringing down off this hill." Brom shifted the plaited strap an inch across his chest, and took the bill in both hands like a quarterstaff, with the hook uppermost. "It weighs what it weighed at noon. I tried it."

Karis did not thank him. She put one small hand flat against the box as she went by, as a person touches a horse.

Cael opened the read.

It came as it had come beside a square of black turf: a pace and a half of ground on every side, and the weight of everything that stood on it. He had the trodden earth, and the hollow going back under the floor, and five people's boots; and something went out of him into the cold, as small as a breath.

On the white, the old one lifted its chin from its paws.

It looked east, at six shapes under a lip, and for the length of one breath it looked at one of them. Then it laid its chin down again.

That was the price of the quietest thing he owned, with the width of a floor between: one head, once. He did not have to work out what the other eight would cost. Any one of them, used here, would bring nine animals to the place where everybody he had in the world was standing within reach of his arm.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

They went along under the lip with the floor on their right hands.

For the first few yards it stood over them like a shelf. Then the turf came up to meet it, and by the south-east it was only a kerb, a hand high, with the white running away level beyond it to the feet of the stones. Lira went in front on the great boot, flat-footed, with the knife out. Karis kept one hand on the breast of her coat, where a roll of paper was, and the healer walked behind her at the carter's pace, since it was the only one she had.

Cael had his eyes on the white and the rest of his mind in the ground.

He was at a hundred and ten, and the pack had begun to move with them. It did not come on as seven had come on at a ford, in a line, behind one that went first. It drifted. A grey shape would get up and walk a few yards toward the southern rim and stand, and another would pass it and stand; and so, by pieces, without any one of them appearing to decide anything, the nine were always a little nearer.

The pale one came to the rim first.

It stood on the rolled edge a yard from Brom's right hip, with its head no higher than his belt, and it looked him over as a man looks over a cart that he may buy. Cael had it inside the read from the instant its forefeet touched the lip, and he felt the weight of it come forward, slowly, off the haunches and onto the forelegs.

"Now," he said.

Brom did not swing. He set the butt of the haft against his own hip and lifted the other end, and the animal brought its throat down onto the ash.

It ought to have had him. Cael saw that as it came, and saw why it had not. A hound springs off its hind feet. On that rim its hind feet had nothing square to push from; they were set on a thing as round as a log, with the edge falling away in front, and so it came over the lip reaching down, with all its weight on its forelegs and its jaw stretched out. The haft took it under the chin. Brom turned his hips, and it went past his knee and onto its side on the turf with a grunt.

It got up. It shook itself from the head to the tail, like a dog out of a pond, and looked at Brom with no ill will whatever. Then it walked off along the foot of the lip, the way that they had come, and jumped up onto the white again.

"It's only a hand," said Brom, hoarsely. He was looking at the rim. "A hand's drop. I'd not have thought it."

"It can't get its legs under it. Keep close to the edge. If you give it a yard of ground it'll have its spring."

"How'd you know it was coming?"

"I was watching its feet."

That was true, as far as it went. Brom took it for eyes, and Cael let him.

The dark-backed one came next, forty yards farther round. It was the heaviest of the nine, and it came to the very same kind of place, at Brom's right hand, and stood, and brought its weight forward in the very same way; and Cael said "Now," and the haft was there.

This one went down harder, for Brom had hit it as he would have hit a post, with both arms and the hundredweight on his back behind them. It lay a breath on the turf with its legs working. Then it too stood up, and shook, and went home along the lip.

"They don't mind me," said Brom.

He sounded more troubled by that than by the teeth.

"I dropped that first one hard enough to stun a calf. And this one walked up to the same place as if I'd never been born. It watched me do it. It was standing there on the floor."

"Nothing told it."

"I told it. I've an ash pole."

"You didn't make the kind of noise they listen for." Cael had the count at a hundred and sixty, and his eyes on a long-legged shape that had begun to pace them along the inside of the rim. "You're a man with a stick, and you can't declare. So far as that floor's concerned you haven't said a word since you came over the stone."

Brom thought about it for three strides.

"Well," he said. "That's a thing I've been wanting to be, by and large. I'd not looked to be it here."

He grounded the haft and walked on, a foot from the lip, with a hundredweight of copied stone on his shoulders. Cael looked at the broad back in front of the grey, and at the wrists, which were the colour of wrists. Brom had stood on a rock in a river once and been the loudest thing for half a mile, on purpose, for three breaths; he was doing a harder thing now, which was to be nobody, with a pole, in the right place.

It was the two small ones that got in front.

Cael did not see them go. He had the whole of his attention in a pace and a half of turf, feeling for the next weight to come onto the rim above Brom, and he had let his eyes follow it down; and when he lifted them the file had stopped.

They were at the south. Fifteen yards on along the kerb two grey shapes were standing on the grass, shoulder to shoulder, with their heads level. They had gone ahead on the white and dropped off the rim where there was nobody under it with a pole, and they stood now on turf, where a hound has all the spring that it was born with.

"Two," said Lira. "In front. On the ground."

She had set her feet. He saw the right one go down whole-soled, a beat behind the left, inside a boot that she had said was like a bucket, and he saw her know it. She had killed one of these with that knife, and she had done it at the end of twenty-five yards of running, on two good feet.

The pair began to walk.

They did not come at Lira. They had seen a knife, and they came wide of it, one on either hand, toward the small pale person behind her and the square one behind that. It was how a thing would come that had learned to take the easiest first, and it was the first sign of sense that he had seen from any of the nine.

"Brom," said Cael. "Front."

"I'm coming."

He was coming at the best pace that a man can make under a box, and it would not be enough, since there were twelve yards of turf between Brom's pole and Karis.

Lira did not turn her head.

"I can't stop two on this foot," she said. "I can't stop one. I can be what they go after."

"You're not to run on it," said Oryn. Her voice was very low. "I told you a month."

"You told me why, too. It's new, and it wants time. It's had sixteen days." Lira had her eyes on the nearer of the pair. "If it goes, mend it at the stone."

She did not wait to be given leave, and he had none to give that would have reached her in time. She took two steps to her right and put her left boot on the rolled edge and went up.

Then she ran.

She ran along the rim itself. It was a thing no wider than a roof-ridge, round on top, with the white a finger below it on one side and the turf a hand below on the other, and she went along it as he had watched her go along a ledge under a mountain, close and quick, with her arms a little out. The great boot came down every second stride with a slap. There was no burst in it and no Path, since there could be none; it was a girl of thirteen on the lanes at Fenmark, who had only legs.

Wind stood up in his own feet to go with her. He put it down, and it was like putting down his own heart.

The pair turned as she passed them. He saw both heads go round together, and both bodies after, and they left Karis as a dog leaves a bone for a thrown stick and went loping along the foot of the kerb under her heels. On the white the pale one had seen her too, and it swung in beside her on the inside, easily, with its head at the height of her knee.

"Go," said Cael to the others. "Now. Round."

The turf in front of them was empty, and Karis went along it at a stumbling trot with the healer's hand in the middle of her back.

Lira had run a quarter of the round. He counted it afterward at twenty yards. She was two strides short of the place where the lane came up to the lip, and she had three hounds strung out after her and nothing whatever in front, when the great boot came down on the outer curve of the roll and not on its top.

He saw the foot go over. It went outward, past the place where an ankle stops, as it had gone on round stones at a river and under a plate of shale; and that made three times.

She fell inward, onto the floor. The knife left her hand and slid away over the grey, spinning, without the least sound.

The pale one took her by the left forearm.

It did not snap. It closed on the arm between the wrist and the elbow, as a door closes on a hand, and its jaws stayed shut. She was on her back, and he saw her do then what he had seen her do at a stone at noon: she gathered the whole of herself, heels and hips and shoulders, and asked.

At noon it had bought her a step. It bought her a yard of floor now, sliding, with the animal's forefeet sliding after her and her arm in its mouth.

"Lira!"

It was Karis, and Karis had never in his hearing shouted anything.

He was on the floor before he had decided to go.

It was twenty yards, and the leg ran every one of them. He went over the lip without feeling it, and the pair, which had come up onto the white at Lira's feet, turned their heads to watch him arrive.

Brom was a stride behind, and he brought the haft down across the pale one's skull with both hands, in a blow that would have broken a door.

The jaws did not open. The hound's eyes shut and opened again, and it settled its forefeet a little wider on the grey; that was all. It had what it had come for. It was not biting to be answered, as seven had bitten at a ford, since nothing on this floor had ever answered; it was only keeping hold, and presently it would do what a dog does with a thing that it is holding.

"Don't let it shake her."

That was Oryn. She had reached the lip with Karis and had not come over, and she stood on the turf with both fists shut.

"Whatever else you do. If it shakes that arm there'll be nothing for me to mend."

Cael came down on the animal with both knees, behind the skull, and put both hands on its head.

It was the size of a calf. He bore the long head down until the jaw lay on the floor, with Lira's forearm lying on the floor between the teeth, and he put the whole of his weight on it and kept it there. He had the thing inside the read, every pound of it; and each time that it gathered itself to wrench he had the gathering a breath before the wrench came, in the neck and the shoulders, and leaned his own weight to the place where it meant to go.

It could hold. It could not shake.

Her face was a foot from his, as white as the floor, and she did not cry out, and she kept her eyes on him.

"Knife," she said, through her teeth. "By your knee."

"I can't let go of its head."

"No. I can see that."

Everything that he carried had come up, as he had not felt it come since a mountain. Compression showed him the skull under his palms and how little it would take. Wind wanted his feet, and hers. And Ember had the place already, as it had had it once in a ford: he was looking into a yellow eye from a foot away, and it would set a point on anything that he looked at for long. There.

He could have ended it in a breath, three ways, and he went through what came after as quickly as he would have gone through a bout. Whichever he chose would go out of him on that floor a great deal louder than a healer's count, and eight heads would come round. There were two hounds within a yard of Brom's legs already, and Karis and the healer stood at the lip with nothing in their hands. He could take one animal, perhaps two; he could not take eight off four people who were standing inside the length of a cart.

It needed room. It needed him a long way from everybody he loved, and them walking the other way; he saw that much and no further, and he had no room at all.

No, he told the three of them. He had said it ten thousand times since a shelf above a valley, and he had never before said it with his hands on the thing that it would have stopped. He was not sure that he was right.

"Two hundred and forty," he said aloud. He had not known that he was still counting.

"What's that?" said Brom. One of the pair had him by the skirt of the coat and was tugging. He let it tug.

"Seln."

The other one tried Cael. Its teeth met in the tail of his coat, and in the cloth of his breeches behind the knee, and it pulled, and stood back to see what he would do. He did nothing whatever except keep a head on a floor, and count.

Seln came up the lane at two hundred and seventy.

He was thirty inside his time. He came over the lip with a long thing under one arm, out of its cover, and no breath to speak with. He gave the bow to Brom, and stood holding his own knees.

"There is a hook for the string," he said, when he could. "A healer does not draw that with her fingers. I did not stay to look for it."

"Pannier," said Oryn. "Near side. It doesn't matter. He's the arms."

Brom had never held one, as Cael saw from how he turned it over; but he had drawn carts and hauled rope all his life, and he found the iron stirrup at its nose, and put his boot in that, and bent and took the string in the fingers of both hands.

He straightened his back, and the string came up the stock and dropped behind its catch with a sound like a gate-latch. When he took his hands away there was a dark line across the pads of four fingers, and he wiped them down his breeches.

Seln drew a bolt from the sleeve on the stock, and laid it in the groove.

"Not from there," said Cael. "You'll have it jump. Get down outside, and lay it on the lip."

It was the lip a third time. A hand's height had spoiled the spring of two hounds, and now it gave a man who had never shot a bow something to rest one on. Brom went back over it and knelt on the turf, box and all, and set the stock on the rolled edge and his cheek against the stock. There were four strides and a foot of white between the iron head of that bolt and the eye that Cael was looking into, and one foot more between the eye and Cael's own face.

"Thirteen feet," said Karis. Her voice was a thread. She could no more have helped it than he could.

"She throws low," said Oryn. "A hand, at that. Lay it on the top of the eye."

"I've never shot one," said Brom.

"I know you haven't. Hold your breath out, and squeeze it as you'd milk a goat."

Cael did not move his hands. He had made the thing as still as he knew how to make it, and that was the whole of what he had to give. Nine fragments lay under his refusal, and not one of them could do what was wanted, which was to let a friend try. He looked across thirteen feet at one grey eye over a bow-stock, narrowed, and at a face that would have done anything on earth sooner than loose that string.

"When you like," he said.

There was a slap, and something went by his wrists with a wind on it.

The head under his hands stopped pulling. There was no struggle in it: it was a weight that had been leaning against him, and then it was only a weight, and he was pressing a dead thing to the floor with all his strength.

"Eight," said Karis.

The pair stood. They had let go of two coats, and they stood as two had stood in the shallows of a river when the one in front of them died, with their heads level, waiting for something to follow.

The jaws had not opened. Seln knelt, and put the flat of the narrow dull knife between the teeth at the hinge, and Cael took the upper jaw in both hands, and it was done as a trap is opened. Lira made one sound while they did it, and it was not loud.

He had her knife in his hand when he stood up. He did not remember reaching for it.
