They got her over the lip to the head of the lane.

Brom carried her the four strides, on one arm, with the bow in the other hand, and Oryn was on her knees in the grass before Lira's back had touched it. Both her hands went round the arm, above the place and below it, as they had gone round a shin on a mountain, and her eyes shut.

"Nothing," Oryn said, to the arm. Her hands were to the wrist in what was coming out of it. "Nothing in my hands."

It was Karis who moved first. She had been bound in a barn once, by a woman with two lanterns, and had watched what that woman did before anything else; and she had both her small hands shut round Lira's arm above the elbow, on the inside, before the healer's had come away.

"Higher," said Oryn. "In, against the bone. Now lean on her as if you meant it."

Her voice was quite level. She was a different person already, and one that he had not met. She was a woman on her knees in the grass with nothing in her hands, and her linen was two hundred yards off on a mule, with everything else that she had left there at noon.

"Cloth. Whatever's clean."

Brom had it out before Cael had so much as thought. It was a strip of plain linen folded in four, which had lived inside his shirt since the middle of the eighty-seventh day; she had tied it round his wrist herself, on a mountain. She tore it across at the fold and put the halves into Cael's hands.

"One on the top, where the holes are, and one beneath. Flat. Hold them."

He held them. The teeth had met through the arm. He knew what that was, from the inside of his own calf, and he knew that his calf had been the smaller matter. He had seen her hurt in a dozen ways since a lane in Ardenmere, and he had never before seen so much of her on the outside.

The healer had dragged the tail of her own shirt out from under the brown coat, and she was tearing it upward, with one hand and her teeth, into strips three fingers wide. She did not wind them herself. She had lifted Lira's forearm across her own knee, to keep it higher than the heart, and she would not let go of it for anything.

"Round, now. Begin at the elbow and come down to the wrist; you're shutting a sack, not rolling a sleeve. Tighter than you like. Tuck the end under, and don't put a knot on the hurt."

He wound, and tucked. It was quick, and nobody was gentle, and when it was done the arm was a pale thick bundle that darkened slowly along one side.

"That stays above her heart." She took Lira's left wrist and laid it against Lira's own right collarbone, and shut Lira's right hand over it. "You hold that there. You don't let it down to balance, and you don't put it out if you fall. If you fall, you fall on your face."

"The foot's gone," said Lira. Her teeth were knocking. "The right. I heard it."

"I heard it too. It'll carry you flat. Put the whole sole down, every step, like a duck." Oryn got her own shoulder under Lira's right arm, and stood up with her. She was the shorter by half a head, and she took the weight as she would have taken a pannier.

Then she looked at Cael. In that light her face was all planes, and there was a thing in it that he had not seen there at noon, when a count stopped in her mouth.

"Move," Oryn said. "I can't fix this here. Move."

He looked back once. The white lay behind them, a hand higher than the turf that he stood on, and it had not dimmed. One shape was stretched on it by the lip, four strides in, pale on pale, and eight others stood or sat among the feet of the stones. None of them had come a yard nearer while a bow was drawn and a girl was bound; they had watched it as the pale one had watched Brom from the rim.

The lane went down in front of him into the dusk, a thin pale stroke with the grass standing dark on either hand, and he could not see the stone at the end of it, or the mule.

"Seln in front," he said. "Karis behind him. Then you two. Brom, wind that thing again and keep it up. I'm last."

Two hundred and seven, he thought, and they began to walk.

Chapter 32 — The Loudest Thing

[Taut, lucid narration; keep the Ring's fragment uses, costs, and positions easy to follow]

There were two hundred and seven yards of lane and eight hounds, and he had both figures by heart before Brom had the string back.

It took Brom three strides' worth of standing still. He set his boot in the stirrup and bent, with the box riding up his shoulders, and drew. When the string dropped home he made a small sound through his nose. It had opened his fingers. Cael could not see how deeply, in that light; he saw only that Brom held one hand away from himself for a breath, as a man holds it after picking up something hot. Then he laid a bolt in the groove out of the sleeve on the stock. That left four in the sleeve, and one in a pale thing on the floor behind them.

They went down in the order that Cael had given. Seln was in front with the narrow knife, and Karis behind him with her hand on her coat. Then came the healer and Lira, as close as two people in one sack: Oryn on the right with her shoulder in Lira's armpit, and Lira's bound arm held up against her own collarbone, and the great boot coming down whole at every step like a duck's foot. Brom walked after them with the bow across his chest. Cael came last, four strides behind Brom's box, with Lira's knife in his hand and the read under his soles. He had the only eyes in the file that were not wanted for carrying somebody, and a rear guard needs room to see what it is guarding.

He looked back at the third stride. The eight were coming down off the lip, one at a time, without haste, and going into the standing grass on either side of the lane. After that there was only grass.

It was dusk in earnest now. The lane was a grey stroke going down between two dark walls as high as his hip. The west had a green light in it still, and behind him the floor lay on the crown of the swell like a moon that had come down to rest.

"A hundred and sixty," he said.

He said it low, for the file. His strides were yards, and he had paced this lane at noon behind a cord.

The grass was moving.

He had been waiting for it, and it was still a bad thing to see. On the south side, a few yards out from the lane, the seed-heads bent and stood and bent again in a slow line that went along beside the file. When he turned his head they were doing the same on the north. No shape showed in it anywhere; there was only the grass leaning, a little at a time, at exactly the pace of a girl putting down the whole of her foot.

Lira stumbled, and the healer held her, and they stood for a breath. On both sides the grass stood too.

"A hundred and fifty."

He did what he had done from the east tier of a yard, and at the head of a gravel bar with four people hurt: he set out what he had counted, and looked for the seam in it.

Nine had come home across that floor in no order, and one of them had sat down to scratch. Two had walked onto Brom's pole from the same place, a minute apart, with the second watching the first. Eight had stood by while a bow was loosed among them. They could have cut this lane ahead of the file at any stride of it, and they had not troubled to; they kept their station on the slowest thing that was walking, and waited for it to stop.

At a ford, seven of their kind had learned inside a quarter of an hour to leave a silent body alone. These had learned nothing whatever since sunset, with one of their own lying dead on their own floor.

They were careless. He turned the word over, and it fitted every count that he had. They had no cause to be anything else. Whatever walked over that line left its Path at a stone, and came on as a deer comes, or as a man with a stick; and in all the years that a pack had lain under that floor, no prey in this place had ever shouted.

"A hundred and forty."

Give it one. He had said that aloud on a gravel bar, and gone down thirty yards to do it. Whichever of them was nearest to a declaration moved first, and the rest fell in behind whatever moved; that was in his own handwriting, by Karis's dictation. He was the only thing between that floor and that stone that had one to give.

He saw then what the room was that he had wanted on the floor, with his hands on a skull. It was a lane, and five people on it walking away from him. He had been carrying the answer since noon; he had stood at a boulder with a foot of Wind going out of him, and thought only of what he had found, and not at all of what it was for.

It would not be enough to draw them off. They would come back to the lane when he fell quiet, or follow him to the stone and over it. On the far side of that stone there were four hurt people and the dark.

He lengthened his stride and came up past Brom's elbow, and along the edge of the lane to the small figure behind Seln.

"Karis. At the stone you'll have it back. How much of it?"

She wasted no breath on why. She thought, walking, with her hand on the roll of paper.

"I have set one point since the mountain, on a lamp-wick. It ought to be very nearly the whole." Her voice was small and dry. "Nine, as before, and the eight joins. I could hold them for a count of six and have something over. I was told not to spend it to the last copper where she was not, and she will be there."

"Along the line. The stone in the middle, and as far each way as nine will reach. Set them and leave them dark. When the last of us is over, join them."

"That is a wall. Across the only door we know of, against animals that hunt a declaration."

"They hunt one. I've not seen one go through sixty yards of fire to reach it. I saw thirty head of horn turn off yours on a mountain."

"That was derived."

"Then it'll be derived twice."

She was silent for four strides.

"Who is last?"

"I am. I've the rear."

She turned her head and looked at him. It was nearly dark, and he could see only the pale shape of her face. He thought that she had heard something that was not about the order of a file.

"Entered," said Karis.

He fell back to the rear. As he passed Brom he said, "At the stone, turn round and keep that thing pointing in," and Brom grunted. Lira had her head down and her teeth shut. The healer's eyes went over him from a foot away, tired and level, as they went over everybody, and found nothing that wanted her hands.

"A hundred and twenty," he said.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He counted them down by tens, and the grass kept pace on either hand.

At a hundred Lira's bad foot dragged, and she made no sound; he knew it only from how the healer's shoulder dropped to take her. At ninety Brom said, without turning, that there was something in the lane behind them, and Cael looked. One of the eight had come out onto the trodden grass thirty yards back, and was sitting there with its tongue out. It got up when they had gone on ten strides, and came after, and sat again.

"Eighty."

He could see the stone. It was a paler thing at the lane's end, the size of a loaf. The mule stood beyond it with her long ears forward, hobbled, and in no fear at all; nothing in that grass wanted anything that she had.

"Seventy."

"Sixty," he said, and the grass on the south side opened.

It was the dark-backed one. It came out low and from the flank, at the smallest thing in the file, with none of the idleness that it had shown on a lip. He had time to think that Karis walked alone, and that he had been a fool not to see what that would look like from the grass.

She went over on her back with the animal on top of her, and he heard the breath go out of her. It struck for her throat, and she got both her hands there first, shut, one fist upon the other under her own chin, as a man of Thornwater had once got a hand between; and the jaws closed across the two fists together and drove them back into the place that they were guarding.

She screamed.

It was cut off almost as it began. It was still the loudest sound that anybody had made on that ground since the six of them crossed a stone; and not one head in the grass on either side so much as turned to it. They did not hunt by that.

He saw all of it at once, as he saw a floor.

Seln was five strides beyond her, turning, with the knife coming up; and between Seln and Karis one of the three that Cael had never told apart had stepped out into the lane and stood there, broadside, with its head level. Lira and the healer were five strides on the near side; Oryn had stopped dead, with her whole weight under Lira, and both of them were looking at the thing on the ground. Brom was a stride behind the two women, with the bow at his shoulder already.

"No line," said Brom. It came out of him like a groan. "They're in it. She's under it. I've no line."

Cael was four strides behind the box on Brom's back, and ten from Karis.

He priced it. He had perhaps as long as it takes a jaw to finish closing.

He could run. It was ten yards; but the animal would hear him come, as it had heard everything all evening and not cared, and it would have all the time it wanted.

He could let Wind have him. It would crack like a whip over the lane and set him down beside her with his feet locked for a count, and it would bring eight animals to the ground where Karis was lying, with him standing in the middle of them unable to move.

There was a third thing, and it was already lifting. It had lifted at sunset behind the other eight, as it lifted at every dusk, with the one offer that it ever made. It did not put anything into the air. It was made to take something out.

It was sealed. He knew the seal's reason as he knew his own name, and he went through it in the half of a breath, since it was the one sum that he had never done carelessly. A defector's craft in his hands would tell whoever saw it where he had learned it. So: who could see?

Lira could, and Brom, and Karis from under the thing's jaw; and Seln, who was looking straight back up the lane, and whose own stair it had come off. Those four knew what he was and had kept it for years. There was no bowman on a bank. There was nobody else nearer than two days' walk, and a pack of dogs carries no tales to a ferry.

That left one. The healer knew nothing of him, and she spoke to every carter on seven roads. She had her back to him. A big man and a hundredweight of box stood between her and the place where he was, and her eyes were on Karis. She would see where he ended. She could not see where he began.

Yes, he told it.

He had not said so to that one since he crossed the Line.

The hiss of the seed-heads against his coat stopped. That was how it came: the world went on, and he went out of it. His boots came down on trodden grass and gave him nothing back; he could not hear his own breath. He went wide of the lane on the south side, through stems that stood to his hip and bent for him and did not rustle, past the box on Brom's back and Brom's left shoulder. Brom's eye came round and slid over the place where he was, as an eye slides over one fence-post among forty, and then came back to it, since Brom knew. He passed Lira on her left hand, a yard out. Her head turned. She was looking at grass that leaned with nobody in it, and he saw her mouth open.

The healer was on Lira's other side, a head lower, with the whole of a girl's weight on her shoulder, and she did not turn at all.

It was ten strides. On the tenth he let it go, with his hands already on the animal's back.

The sound of his own feet came back a beat late, like an echo off a wall. His hands had gone as cold as if he had held them in a spring. And the dark-backed one, which had heard nothing come and seen nothing come, shifted its grip to finish.

He did not try to drag it off her, since a thing that is pulled bites down. He had Lira's knife, and he could not spend the blade either, with two small fists lying under those teeth. He gave it the other end. He put the horn of the hilt in at the back of the jaw, crosswise, where Seln had put a flat blade on a white floor, and bore down on it as on the handle of a pump.

The jaws came open by the width of two fists, and Karis had them out before he could have told her to.

It went for him then, as he had known that it would. It had lost what it was holding, and here was the thing that had taken it. He had been carrying a pace and a half of the world since the far lip, and he had the whole long weight of the animal inside it, and the way that the weight meant to go. It gathered and came, low, at his knee.

He was not there. He did that with his own two feet and nothing in them. A girl on a painted floor had taught it to him before she taught him anything else, and had told him that nothing is thrown which has not first been let go by. He stepped off its line by the width of his body. He took it as it passed, by one foreleg and a handful of hide, and added what he had to what it was already doing.

Five bands of linen said there. He went through them.

It went on a yard farther than it had meant to go, off the edge of the trodden grass and into the standing stems on the south side, shoulder first, and he heard it roll.

Karis lay with her fists under her chin and her mouth open. No sound was coming out of it. Her eyes were on him, and they were quite clear. They went to his hands, and to the place ten strides back where he had been standing, and returned.

"Seln," he said. "Carry her. The stone. Don't stop for me."

"What are you—" said Brom.

"I'm going to make a noise. Walk."

"With what?" said Lira.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

He did not answer her. He set his feet in the trodden grass as he had watched her set hers ten thousand times, with the lane across him and his face to the north.

He had said no at the first stride of every road for ninety-six days, and again at the second, on a bar of gravel and a hill of plates and a mile of grass with a grey thing pacing it. He had become so good at the refusal that he had taken it for what he was. He had kept the nine as a person keeps a purse shut; and he knew now what the purse had been kept for, and the relief of it was so sharp that it was nearly grief.

He stopped holding.

The air cracked.

It broke over the lane as it had broken over a river, and the grass went down flat behind him in a fan. He was twenty feet north of five people, in stems to his hip, and his boots had come down left foot first.

The landing locked. One, and everything that he owned went dumb; there was a boy standing in a field with a knife, who could not have shifted a foot to save his life. He had priced that count before he spent it. The thrown one was on the south side, finding its legs, and the rest were strung along sixty yards of lane. The nearest of them was a good deal more than one count from his ankles.

All along both sides of the lane, the grass had stopped moving at Lira's pace.

It stood. Then it bent, everywhere at once, toward him.

The count was over, and he had his nine.

He drew breath for Pressure. It was a deeper breath than a healer's tape allowed, and his left side told him so from the breastbone to the spine. It gathered under his ribs for the better part of that breath, as it had always gathered, slowly, where anything alive might feel it coming. There was no opponent to send it through. He sent it straight down.

The ground thumped like a drum. The grass lay over in a ring ten yards across, and the force of it came back up through his heels and his knees, as it came back off anything that would not move.

Ember was next. He gave it the one place where he could carry it, which was the tip of Lira's knife; and for the first time since the Line he did not stop at the setting. It lit. A seed of yellow stood on the steel, and then a flame as long as his thumb, burning on nothing, at the end of his arm.

He could see them.

They had come up out of the grass: there were low grey shapes on both sides of the lane and in it, and every head was turned to him, and in every head there were two small green fires where the flame looked back. He counted the pairs. He could not have helped it.

Eight.

Something bright and quick stirred in his right arm and asked what it had asked of every sill and rim and arris since the day it came to him. Edge?

Yes, he told that one too. He had never said so before. Along the knife's cutting side a line of white stood out a hair clear of the steel, as a tall exact person had once made one stand on a lath by saying that it did; and it rang. There was nothing for it to cut. It sang all the same, thin and high, like a wet finger going round the rim of a glass.

He had a light in his fist and a noise at the end of it, and he was the only thing on that whole hillside that had either.

He ran north.

Behind him he heard Lira's voice, once, and it was not his name; it was "Go!" and it was not said to him.

They came after him, and they did not come as they had come all evening. There was nothing idle in them now. They came through the grass as seven had come across a river to a seed of fire on a rock, flat out, with the leaders drawing together and the rest falling in behind; and he had the sound of them on both hands, a dry rushing, like a wind that had found its direction.

There was one thing more that he had refused at every doorway and coping since a river, and he let that off its hold with the rest. Anchor fixed nothing, for he had no point on that hill that he could afford to nail to the ground. It only looked, west, as a dog let off a chain looks first at the gate. It would be within ten feet of a thing before it could tell him what was there.

It was forty yards to the rut. He counted them, with the flame streaming back over his wrist and the edge singing. At the fortieth the ground went out from under his left foot, and he was in it to the knee.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

West was the stone. That was why he turned east.

The rut ran up the swell toward the floor, a little south of east, and every stride that he took along it was a stride away from a lane with a lame girl on it. He put his back to five people and went up the hill the wrong way, with eight animals pouring into the channel behind him.

He had kept the heaviest thing for a place that would hold it.

A Storm lane wanted the air, and to have the air he must give up the ground; at that weight the read would carry one or the other, never both. He let the turf go. It was like shutting an eye. The pace and a half of the world that he had walked in since the far lip went out from under his soles. He was a boy running up a ditch in the dark, with a flame in front of his face and nothing to tell him where his feet would land.

He laid the lane down the rut behind him.

It was a corridor of air the length of a cart and team, high at his end and low at the other, and everything in it went downhill at once. The pale grass stood along both lips of the rut with its seed heavy on it. The lane stripped it. Seed and chaff and dry stem went down that channel in a flood, as thick as meal out of a sack, straight into the faces of whatever was coming up.

He heard them meet it. He let the lane go, and paid.

One. Two. For ten counts after a lane, everything that he had answered him a beat late. He had written it so in Hesk's book, on a road, from a bout. It was a different thing to run in. His foot came down, and then he felt it come down. The flame leaned, and then he saw it lean.

At the tenth count he laid the second.

It was in the second that his left boot came down on a stone. It was a round thing the size of a loaf, bedded in the rut's floor; he would have had it a stride and a half off with the read, and he had not got the read. The foot turned on it, and the calf took the whole of his weight slantwise, along a seam that a hound had made at a ford and a plate of shale had opened on a mountain.

It opened again. He felt it go, like wet cloth parting, and after that every stride on that side had a hot place in it.

Eight. Nine. Ten.

He laid the third. It was as many as he had ever laid; he did not know what a fourth would do to him, and it was not the night to learn. The rut behind him was a river of chaff. Twelve counts, for the third. His own breath reached him late.

He had counted his strides from the place where he dropped into the rut, and he was at a hundred and thirty when he heard it.

"Back!"

It came up the hill from the west, across two hundred yards of dark, and it was a voice that he had never in two years heard raised: mild, and exact, and pitched to carry. It was the word that five of them had said together at a stone, on the evening that they found the line.

A breath after it there was another, higher, and cracked in the middle.

"Back!"

Two. He made five people out of two voices, running. Seln would not have called with Karis still on the wrong side of that stone, and Karis could not call. Lira had a healer under her arm. Brom he had to take on trust; Brom would be the last of them over, and would not spend breath on a word.

They were out.

He stopped running east.

It was as near as he came that night to being caught. He turned in the rut, with the flame swinging, and they were there: grey, and close, coming up out of the chaff with their eyes shut to slits and their muzzles white with seed. The channel was full of them. He could not go back down it, and he could not stand.

He gave Wind his feet a second time.

It answered a beat late. He felt that as a man feels a stair that is not where he thought. Then the air broke, and he was out of the rut and over its southern lip, twenty feet down the open slope, with the knife still lit in his fist.

The landing locked.

One.

He had priced this count too, and the price was a bad one. The dark-backed one had not gone into the chaff. It had run the rut's rim, and whether a boy's hands had taught it something in a lane he could not have said. It was the only one of the eight on the right side of the channel when he left it. It was behind him now, up the slope, and he could not turn his head to learn how near.

He could not have moved a finger.

It hit him low, in the backs of the thighs, at the end of the count, and Compression took it.

It took it late. For the first beat there was nothing there at all, and the animal's whole weight went into his legs as a cart's tail goes into a man in a lane. His knees went. He pitched forward down the hill with its chest on his shoulders, and kept the knife up, and put out the other arm. His left forearm met the ground under the two of them. Then the thing that a fighter had once put through him, and left with him, arrived and did what it was for. There was only one road open to it. The whole of that blow went down one bone into the hill, and he felt it ring from the elbow to the wrist like a struck rail.

The hound had run into a thing that gave like a gate and then did not give. It went on over his head, as a sack comes off a tipped cart, and rolled away down the slope in front of him.

His feet were his own again. He was up and past it before it had found its legs, and running west.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

It was two hundred yards to the stone, downhill. He ran it on a calf that was open, and a side that had been told there too many times to go on saying it.

He had no read. He had a flame at the end of his arm, which showed him ten feet of grass and blinded him to everything beyond. He could not see the stone. He knew where it was as he knew where his own hand was, and he ran down the dark toward the place where a lane ended.

They were behind him. He could hear them come out of the rut, one after another, with a scrabbling of feet on its lip, and then the rushing in the grass. One sound was nearer than the rest, and gaining, and that was a thing with long legs, built for this.

A grey shape went by on his right, as high as his hip, and it was a boulder. Twenty strides.

"Cael!"

That was Brom, from in front and below. Cael saw nothing of him. But Brom could see a light coming down a hill with a boy under it, and something low and fast a few yards behind the light.

At ten feet from the stone the last of the nine told him what it had been looking for.

It was Anchor. It had gone the whole length of that slope with its face to the west and found nothing that it could be sure of. Now it found nine things. They stood in a row directly across his road, a little more than a stride apart, to the right hand and the left, low on the ground, just beyond the stone. Not one of them gave any light. They were places that somebody had fixed and told to stay, as a bar of iron had been told to stay on that same line, three cords to the north. He knew the hand that had set them as he would have known its writing.

She had laid them along the line's inside edge. That was what her feet had been finding since first light: the last hand's breadth of ground where a point would hold, so close to the place where an Arbiter stopped that an animal coming out would meet it with its next stride.

He went over the stone between the fourth and the fifth.

There was grass under him that was only grass, and a mule's shape, and a big man down on one knee a yard in front of him with a bow-stock at his cheek. Brom's eye was not on him. It was on something past his hip.

The string slapped.

Cael turned as he fell. The rangy one was in the air over the stone, at the top of its leap, with its forelegs stretched and the flame's light on its teeth, and it was six feet from the nose of the bow. He did not see the bolt. He saw the animal fold in the middle of its spring, and come down on the western side of the stone like a thing dropped off a cart, and lie.

"Seven," said Lira's voice, from somewhere on the ground.

"Karis," said Cael. "Now."

She was on her knees a stride from the stone, with Seln's hands under her arms to keep her upright. She had no voice to answer him with. Her two hands were out in front of her, shaking, and he saw the right one make the smallest movement that it had ever made.

The line lit.

It went up out of the grass along sixty yards, thirty to the north of the stone and thirty to the south, a wall of yellow-white fire as high as a man's knee and as straight as her wrist could draw a curve that size. He felt her discharge go past him like the door of a furnace. It was the first thing that anybody but himself had declared on that hillside since noon, and after what he had carried down the slope it seemed to him a clean and ordinary thing, like bread.

The seven came to it.

He saw them only as shapes against the fire, and only for as long as it burned. They had been strung out down two hundred yards of hill behind a light, running to a declaration, and the declaration had gone over a stone and gone out; for he had let the flame die and the edge fall silent when the string slapped, and had shut his hand on all nine. What stood in front of them now was a fence of fire with their own road under it.

They split on it. The foremost flung left and the next flung right, and the rest went after one or the other, as thirty head of horn had gone on a mountain. They ran along the inside of that wall to its two ends. Then they were over the line, somewhere in the dark beyond the light, to the north and to the south; and the last that he knew of any of them was a rushing in the grass that went away along the line's outside in both directions, and thinned, and stopped.

Karis held it for a count of six. He counted it for her. At six the wall went down all at once, and she sat back against Seln's knees with her hands open in her lap.

It was full dark. The stars were out. He lay where he had fallen and went over it, since somebody had to.

Two were dead: one on a white floor, with a bolt in its eye, and one a yard from his boots. Seven had gone, north and south, and nobody on that hill could have said more of them than that. Six people were on the western side of a grey stone. Four of the six were hurt, and he would have the count of that by lamplight. He knew already that every hurt but his own had been taken by somebody who had no means of answering. Nine things lay under his hand again, and they had not yet stopped shaking.

There were no instruments, and there would be no hundred marks.

He could say what had been done, as Pike would have said it. A thing loud enough to be hunted had been made in the one place where nothing could be loud. It had taken a pack off five people who could not make a sound that the pack would hear, and a line of fire had kept it from following them out. That was the whole of the win.

The pack had learned nothing from it that it could use. It had never needed to learn anything, and he did not suppose that it would begin now.

And five people had watched him go up a hill with fire in his fist. Four of them had seen one thing more than the fifth had.

Nobody spoke to him. Somebody was striking a flint.

It was Brom who had the flint, and he struck it with the heel of his hand.

The spark took on the third stroke. Karis's small brass lantern had come out of the middle box, and when its flame stood up Cael saw the camp that six people had made without meaning to. They were ten yards west of the grey stone, on the old line of the road, with the mule standing over them and her ears laid back. A long grey thing lay between them and the stone, where it had come down out of the air, and nobody looked at it.

Beyond the stone the slope went up into the dark. At the top of it there was still a faint paleness where the floor lay. Between that and the lamp, along sixty yards of grass, ran a strip of black no wider than his hand, where a wall had stood for a count of six; the frost was coming down on it already.

Lira was on her back in the grass, and the healer knelt beside her. She had the cloth off the arm already, three strips of her own shirt and two pads of a linen cuff, and had laid it in a heap.

"Light," said Oryn. "Here. Lower than that."

Cael brought it down with his right hand. The left would not close properly on the ring.

She put her hands round the arm, one above the place and one below, as she had put them round it at the head of a lane and had them come away empty. Her eyes shut. Her lips moved, and this time there was a count in them; he saw it go to four, and to five, and on.

"There. Back."

She said it to the arm, on a breath, and that was all the notice that she gave it. She had waited thirty rounds to learn what a line did to her hands, and had learned it at noon, and tonight she had no time to spare for having them back. She opened her eyes and looked up at five people, and spoke quickly, as she had spoken on the hill.

"It's deep. It's the deepest thing I've done on a road. I'll be in it an hour, near enough, and I'll hear nothing that anybody says to me, so say it now." She jerked her chin at the dark. "You've a finding about what those things hunt. I've heard it at your fire more than once. A mend's a Path used, and this one's a Path used for an hour, at night, with seven of those somewhere in that grass. It's the loudest thing for a mile, and I can't do it quietly."

"Can it wait for the light?" said Brom.

"It can. The arm can't." Her mouth was hard. "So keep that bow up, and somebody look the other way."

Brom had the bow between his knees already. He set his boot in the stirrup a third time, with four fingers that he had not yet let anybody see, and drew, and Cael heard his breath go in through his teeth. He laid a bolt on it, which left three in the sleeve. Then he walked ten yards to the north and stood there with his back to the lantern, a broad dark shape with a box still on it.

Seln had gone to the south without being asked, and Cael could not see him at all.

There was one thing more to do before she went under. It was Karis's to do, and Karis could not; she sat in the grass with her two hands at her throat and her eyes on him. She held, as a one-armed man at a plank held, that a thing not said was not a finding; and so he said it for her, aloud, as Pike read a line before he wrote it.

"Ninety-sixth day. Dark. The west side of the stone. There were nine. Two are dead, one on the floor with a bolt in it that we'll not see again, and one there." He did not point. "Seven went out when the wall lit, north and south, along the outside of the line. I didn't see where they went after. Did anyone?"

"No one," said Seln's voice, out of the south.

"Four of us are hurt, and she'll have each of those from the one that it belongs to. Six bolts, at noon: three in the sleeve, one on the string, one a yard from that stone, and one gone. The box is whole, and there are eleven sheets in it and on her."

He had come to himself. He looked at the healer when he said it, since she was the one of the six who had no reason to know what she had been looking at.

"Mine's a calf, and an arm that's been struck. And what went up that hill with a light was me. I did it on purpose, to take them off the lane. I've no more to say about it tonight than that it was done."

Oryn looked at him for as long as it took her to draw one breath. She had seen a boy burst sideways out of a file with a crack like a whip, in a place where she herself could not so much as count; she had seen fire in his fist. He waited for what every person with a seal had asked him since a district hall.

"Is that calf worse than this arm?"

"No."

"Is anything you've got worse than this arm?"

"No."

"Then hold the light still and be quiet."

She shut her eyes. Her hands settled, with the fingers overlapping, and her face went as quiet as a pond.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He held the lantern for an hour, and he measured the hour by its oil.

There had been four fingers of it in the glass when Brom struck the flint; he had noted that, as he noted everything. It went down by the breadth of one of them while a square woman knelt in the grass with her eyes shut. He held the flame where she had told him to hold it, and kept it from moving.

Lira did not speak. She had been told once, on a mountain, to lie still and let it, and she lay still, and her right hand was the only part of her that told him anything. At first it had hold of the grass, a whole fistful, with the knuckles standing. A little later it left the grass and found the strap of Hesk's satchel, where that hung from his shoulder beside her, and took two turns of it round the wrist. By the time the oil stood halfway down the fourth finger the strap had gone slack, and the hand lay open on her own breast.

Her eyes were open as well, and they were on him.

He could not read what was in them. He had been able to read that face across a yard since a lane in Ardenmere, and tonight he could not. It was not anger, which he knew, and it was not fear either. She looked at him steadily, as she might have looked at a card that had come up with a name on it which she had not expected.

His left arm had gone dead to the elbow before the first quarter was out. He hung the lantern's ring over that wrist, like a bucket on a hook, and held the wrist up with the other hand. Something in his right arm had begun to ask about the lantern's brass rim. Edge? It had put that question to half the world for a season, patiently, and tonight for the first time it had been told yes; it asked now like a child that has been given one sweet. He told it no, and it asked again.

Nothing came out of the grass.

He listened for it the whole hour, and he learned what that hillside sounded like at night. The pale grass never stopped. The wind went over it from the north in long breaths, and it hissed and lay down and stood again, so that he was always hearing something come and finding that it was only the country. Twice Brom shifted his feet. Once the mule blew, and once, far off toward the north, a bird got up and cried and settled. There was a small dry ticking, close by, which he could not place until he saw that it was the frost, taking hold on the wet cloth in the heap.

Seven animals were somewhere in that dark which hunted the very thing that a healer was doing a yard from his knee, and they did not come. He did not know why. He set it beside a great many other things that he did not know, and held the lamp.

When her hands opened, she did not take them away at once. She turned the arm over in them, toward the light, and looked.

It was closed. That was all that he let himself see: skin, where there had been none, and on it two short rows of small pink marks, one row on the upper side and one beneath, each mark no bigger than a barleycorn.

"Fingers," said Oryn.

Lira moved them. They all went.

"Well?" said Brom, from the north. He had not turned round. His voice was not steady.

"She keeps it."

Brom said something to the dark that was not a word. Cael found that the lantern was shaking, and that it was not his dead arm that shook it.

The healer had not finished. She kept hold of the wrist, and she bent over Lira until her face was a hand's breadth away, and she spoke as she had spoken to Brom about a cuff, slowly, so that there should be no second meaning in any piece of it.

"A mend that deep holds nothing for a season. Nothing. That arm is not to hold. It's not to strike. It's not to catch. Not a rope, not a knife, not a fall, not a friend. Not until I say. And I'll say at first snow, near enough, if it's let alone."

She sat back.

"Blanket. One of the hold's. And a knife."

It was Lira's own knife that Cael gave her, since it was the one in his belt. She set it to the hem of a grey blanket and drew, and the wool dented under it and did not part. She tried it again nearer the hilt. Then she held the blade to the lantern and ran her thumb along it, squarely, as nobody would have dared to do that morning.

"Who's been cutting stone with this?"

Nobody answered her, and she did not seem to want an answer. She held out her hand to the south, and a narrow dull knife came into it out of the dark, haft first. That one cut. She took a strip off the blanket a hand wide and as long as her two arms, and passed it under Lira's elbow and round her neck, and tied it short, so that the mended arm lay across the breast with its hand under the opposite collarbone.

Lira looked down at it. She had been the quickest pair of hands on any floor that she had ever stood on.

"One arm. From here to the snow."

She said it as Brom had once said the hour of a week, to have it exact. Then her eyes went down the length of herself to the great boot, which lay on its side in the grass with the foot still in it, and came up again; and she shut her mouth.

The healer had followed the look.

"The ankle's a tape and a season. I've told you that before."

"I didn't ask."

"No. You were about to not ask, and I'd sooner say it than watch you." Oryn's voice had gone to a thread. "I'll tape it in the morning. I've nothing left to see it with."

She got one hand to the ground, to push herself up, and the arm folded. She did not so much lie down as stop being upright. She went over onto her back in the trodden grass, on the old line of the road, with her broad hands open at her sides and her mouth a little open; and she was asleep before Seln had come in out of the dark to put a blanket on her.

There were six of Thornwater's blankets on that mule, and there were six people.

Seln brought them down, since he was the only one with two hands and nothing wrong with either, and he laid two on Lira and one on the healer where she had fallen. He stayed a breath longer over the healer than a blanket needed.

"She has gone grey to the lips," he said, to nobody. "Her hair is wet through, in this frost, and I do not think that she knows it. I have seen people spent. I have not seen one spent so far who still stopped to answer about a foot."

He cut the bread as well, a round loaf from the hold's oven, into six, with the same knife that had cut the sling; and he left the sixth piece on a pannier lid by Oryn's head, where she would find it before she found anything else.

Nobody made a fire. Nobody proposed one.

Karis had her notebook open on her knee, and she was writing with the pencil held in her fist. Her knuckles were skinned across both hands, where teeth had gone over them; she had looked at them once and left them. When she had three lines she turned the leaf to the lantern and to him.

Throat: pressed, not cut. Air: enough. Voice: none whatever. Hands: skin.

Wall: nine points, eight joins, sixty yards. Count of six. Yours. Not empty: a tenth part left, perhaps. I have done as I was told.

Sheets: eleven. Dry. Not looked at.

He read them, and nodded. She took the leaf back and held the pencil over it, and he watched the point come down to the paper and lift, and come down. He knew what was in that small head. She had been ten strides in front of him with a hound's jaw across her fists, and she had seen a thing arrive that had not come; and after it a crack, and a light, and something that rang. She had nine questions at the least, and she had been waiting all her life for a source like this one.

She wrote one line more, and turned it to him.

I am asking nothing tonight. Entered.

Then she shut the book. She did not lie down. She was looking at his left leg, which lay stretched toward the lamp with the cloth black from the knee to the boot, and he watched her think it through as she thought through everything. The healer was asleep and would be asleep till morning; Seln had the south and Brom the north, and Lira had one arm. That left a person with two skinned hands and no voice.

She came across to him on her knees, with what remained of the blanket strip, and took his boot into her lap.

She bound the calf as she would have ruled a table. He supposed that she had watched a healer do it under a rock, and had kept it, as she kept everything; she was not gentle, and she was very exact, and when she tied it off the knot lay flat. She patted the leg once, absently, as she had patted a box on Brom's back. Then she went and lay down on her side against that box with her back to all of them, in Seln's coat, as she had lain on a mountain.

"Seln," said Cael. "Say yours."

Seln was standing at the lantern's edge. There was grass-seed in his hair and the strap of a locked case across his chest, and his breath had long since come back. He had gone the better part of five hundred yards by himself through that grass with eight hounds on a floor behind him, and come up a lane with a bow.

"Nothing."

"Not a scratch?"

"I have looked. I find that I mind it rather more than I had expected to." He inclined his head, as to a report that had been received, and went back to the south.

Brom had come in. He did not wait to be asked. He knelt down heavily beside the sleeping healer, box and all, and laid the bow in the grass with the bolt still on it, and held out one hand into the light, palm up.

"Hand."

Across the pads of four fingers there was a cut, straight, as though it had been ruled. They had bled down into his cuff and dried. He had drawn that string three times with them, the last time when they were already open, and he had stood an hour in the frost with the stock in that hand.

Oryn did not open her eyes. Her lips moved, in the trodden grass.

"Morning. Wash it. I've nothing tonight."

"I wasn't asking for tonight," said Brom. "I was telling you there was one." He looked down at her with an expression that Cael had last seen on him at the edge of a moss. "Go to sleep. You're asleep."

He washed it himself, from the skin, with his teeth set, and wound a strip of clean linen out of the healer's pannier round it; and he took up the bow again with that bundle and went back to the north.

Nobody had said a word to Cael about a hill. They had eaten bread beside him, and passed him the water, and Seln had put the last blanket round his shoulders without a remark, as he would have put it round anybody. Four of them knew what he was and had not known until tonight that it reached in there. One of them knew nothing, and had asked him whether his calf was worse than an arm.

He had expected questions, and he had been given a blanket, and a sixth of a loaf, and a knot that lay flat. He did not know yet which he would have found the easier to bear.

He wrote while there was oil.

Karis had looked at the lantern's glass before she slept, and held up three fingers, which was what an hour had left in it. He set it on the lid of the box and opened Hesk's book to the page that had stopped short. The entry there was in his own hand and a few hours old; it said that the dogs were inside, and that he had told nobody, and he read it as he might have read the writing of somebody he had known as a boy.

He did not go back to finish it. He began a new one beneath.

Ninety-sixth day, night. West of the stone, on the old road.

Nine hounds, inside. Two dead, both Brom's, with a healer's bow that he had never shot. Seven out, north and south along the line's outside. Not seen after. No instruments were there. No price.

Lira: left forearm bitten through and held; mended at the line, an hour, by lantern. One arm till first snow, by order. Right ankle gone a third time, and not mended. Karis: throat; no voice. Brom: four fingers, on a string. Seln: nothing. Oryn: spent to the bottom, and asleep on the road.

Mine: left calf open on the old seam. Left forearm struck; dead to the elbow. Ribs taped, three days to run; they held.

Then he ruled a line, and under it he put down what he had spent, in the order of its spending, with what each thing had cost and on whom the cost had fallen. He had never had so many to write at once, and he gave each of them its own line, as Pike gave a job.

The read: far lip to the rut. One head turned for it. I had my eyes in the ground when Lira went up on the rim.

Shadow: once, ten strides, in the lane. Four saw it who have always known. The fifth had a man and a box between. I did that sum before, not after. It holds. Cold hands.

Wind: a burst, north off the lane. The lock.

Pressure: once, into the ground. The tape.

Ember: one point, on a knife, lane to stone. Nothing seen beyond ten feet of it. A blister where the hilt was.

Blade: once. An edge on that knife. The knife won't cut wool.

Anchor: looking, nothing fixed. It showed me nine points before they lit.

Storm: three lanes, in the rut. The read goes to the air for those. That's the calf.

Wind: the second burst. The lock had a hound in it.

Compression: in that lock, late. That's the arm.

He went down the ten lines with the pencil's end and counted uses, taking the three lanes singly, and had twelve.

Twelve. With the ford, thirteen.

Deployment since the Line: thirteen.

It stood where the word one had stood on forty-three nights. He had shut the book at a far lip because he did not know what would be true by dark; and here was a true number, and a large one, and there was not a unit in it that had not been paid for on somebody's body, his own or another's.

It was not the whole. He looked at that squarely, with the pencil lifted. There were things that he had done at noon, by himself, a cord north of this stone and on a floor, which nothing had seen and which he had written of only to say that he had told nobody. They were not in the twelve. He would not put them into a count that he could not yet explain, and he would not pretend to the page that they had not happened.

Not in that number: noon. It's on the leaf before this. It gets a line of its own when I can say what it was for.

There was one thing more, and it was the only part of the day that he could write as plainly as a width.

Everyone else's went to sleep at the stone. Mine has been asleep since I was fourteen. Out here that makes me the only one who's awake.

He read it over. It was the kind of sentence that Karis struck out of other people's notes, since it had a likeness in it. He let it stand, since he had nothing truer.

"It worked in there."

He had thought her asleep. He had put the lantern out to save Karis's three fingers, and the stars had come down close over the grass; she lay on her back under two blankets, with her mended arm tied across her, and her face was a pale shape turned up to them.

He did not answer. It had not been a question.

He heard her breathe. She was doing what she had done in a loft at Thornwater, before a ford, when he gave her a plan that she disliked: going through it, a piece at a time, to find the place where she could make it better.

"Yours."

It was one word, and she had left him the whole width of it. She did not say which of them, or how many. She did not say that she had been looking at grass on her left hand, in a lane, with nobody in it.

"Yes," Cael said.

The mule shifted. Somewhere to the north Brom cleared his throat, and was quiet.

He waited for the next thing, and found that he was holding his breath as he had held it under a healer's hand. He had a great many sentences ready for her, and not one of them was an answer. He did not know why. He had not known at noon, and he had kept that from her at noon with a pencil going; and she, of all the people alive, had the right to ask him how long.

"Later."

She said it up into the dark. There was no hardness in it. It was a thing put by on a shelf, with its face outward, where neither of them could pretend that it was not there.

"Later."

She turned her head a little, then, toward him, and he thought that she was going to say something else. She did not. She shut her eyes; and presently her breathing lengthened, and he knew by it that the arm had stopped hurting her enough to let her go.

He sat on beside her with a dead arm across his knee.

The seven did not come, and the stone lay where it had lain, and behind it, a long way off up the slope, there was a faint paleness that he would not have seen if he had not known where to look. He watched the stars go over, and tried to make the sentence that she had given him leave to wait for.

He could not make it. He had the fact, which was that nine things had answered him in a place where a healer could not count. He had nothing to put after the fact. And he knew what became of a thing that was written down before anybody understood it, since it had been done to him. A clerk had found no tier for a boy, and had put a word in capitals where the tier should go, and from that morning nobody had needed to ask what the boy was. A file stopped the asking. He would not do that to this, and he would not hide it either.

It was the better part of two hours before he opened the book again; and he wrote by starlight, large, one sentence to a line, as Karis had written at this same stone on the night before.

I'm not keeping it secret. I'm keeping it unfiled. There's a difference. Lira said later. Later is when I have a sentence. The answer might be: because whatever I am isn't a Path. I've known that since I was fourteen. Out there it was a flag. In there it's the only thing that works. I don't have a word for what that makes me, and I'm not going to invent one at a camp with Lira's arm two hours old.

He shut the book on it, and lay down, and did not sleep for some time.

Chapter 34 — Maps with Holes

It was that same night, the ninety-sixth going into the ninety-seventh, and Seln had the south.

He stood forty yards from the lamp, in grass to his hip, where its light did not reach him and his own eyes were not spoiled by it. He had the line on his left hand. He could not see it. He knew where it was by a strip of burnt stems that began ten yards from his boot, and by a thing behind his breastbone that had gone out at a stone on the way in, and had been there again at the same stone on the way out, exactly where he had left it.

He had called a word up a hill tonight, at the top of his voice, and he could not remember when he had last raised it.

The camp was quiet behind him. He listened to it as he listened to any room that he had his back to, and sorted what he heard: a pencil, and then no pencil; a big man washing his hands without a sound; and the healer's breathing, which was slow and went all the way down.

"Seln. Say yours."

The boy had asked it an hour ago, across the lamp.

He turned that over in the dark, since he had the leisure. He had said once, at a fire in a meadow, that he kept waiting for someone to ask for his report. For fifteen years his reports had been asked for by a slot in a door; for a hundred days after that they had been asked for by nobody, and he had gone on walking the first hour of every road, alone, and saying what he found or not as it bore.

Tonight he had been asked, by name, for the first time. And the whole of what he had to hand in was one word.

It was an accurate word. He had submitted a great many accurate reports, and few of them had sat so ill.

He knew why. He was the cut; he had told a girl so in a loft, in so many words. The cut is the man placed where the subject will run, and he is never where the blow falls. At a ford he had lain in a pool for an hour and a quarter while four people were bled on a bar of gravel thirty yards from his face. And tonight, while a hound took a girl's arm on a white floor, he had been two hundred yards away with his fingers in the lashings of a mule's pack.

It had been right. A bow at the lip had been worth more than a second knife, and he would have gone again. He noted only that it came out the same each time, and that somebody else always paid. He had no column for that, and he found, a little to his surprise, that he would have liked one.

There was the other thing, and he came to it when he had finished with himself, as he came to the difficult page of any file.

He had been looking straight back up the lane. That was his place; the man on point looks behind him as often as before. He had seen the small one go down, and a grey animal step out between her and his knife, and beyond those the two women, and the box. Behind the box there had been a boy with a blade in his hand.

Then there had been the lane, and the grass, and the box.

Seln had not seen him go. Nobody sees that. It is the whole of the craft that there is no instant at which a person is seen to leave; the eye passes over the place and finds it not worth resting on, and goes to something with more in it. He had learned it on a back stair when he was younger than any of them. It had taken him a year to do on purpose, and three more to stop doing by accident whenever a door slammed.

He had known it this time from the outside, by two signs. A big man's eye had slid over a piece of air and come back to it. And along the south edge of the lane the grass had leaned, stem by stem, with nothing leaning on it.

It had gone on for ten strides. Then there had been a boy with both hands on a hound.

Seln had done the sum himself, in the half-breath before. It was the first thing that a person of his trade did on entering any room, and he had done it without choosing to: who is here, and what can each of them see, and where will each of them be tomorrow. There were four who had known for years and had been tried. There was a healer, who was owed everything and knew nothing, and who walked seven roads. She had her back turned and a hundredweight of copied stone between.

He would have said go. He had not needed to. The boy had stood there for as long as a jaw takes to shut, doing the same sum, and had got the same answer; and he had lifted it, and carried it exactly as far as it was wanted, and put it down with his hands already full.

It was correct. Seln looked for a better word and did not find one.

He had wondered, since a night when the boy told him the whole of it in order, what it would be to see his own stair in another person's feet. He had supposed that he would feel robbed. He considered the matter now with some care, standing in frost with a locked case against his ribs, and what he found was nearer to what a mason feels who passes a wall and sees that somebody has laid a course as he would have laid it.

He did not propose to say so to anyone.

The seal was a stranger matter. It guarded the place where a boy had learned that craft, and the place was a man. Seln had spent fifteen years keeping other people's secrets in drawers; he had not looked to end by being one himself, kept shut on a hillside by a person of eighteen who had weighed a friend's throat against it and had still stopped to count who was looking.

The stars went over, and the frost came down, and toward the end of the watch he let himself think about the iron.

He had been keeping off it since noon. It had stood at the back of everything that he did that day, as a figure stands at the back of a room: a square bar, driven at the far end of a measure, with a stamp on its neck that he had seen on every door he had walked through for fifteen years.

Thirty-one.

He had told the boy that he did not know what the number counted, and that he would not guess. Both of those were true. There was a third thing which he had not said, because it was not yet a thing: something in him had answered to that iron, and it was not the Shadow.

He carried what he had carried as a careful clerk carries it, in drawers, each one shut. It was how a man could bear fifteen years of other people's paper and still sleep. But one of them, at the stake, had shifted on its runners, and all day it had stood a finger's breadth open, with nothing to be seen in it but dark.

The big man came down out of the north when the east had begun to grey, walking as a person walks who has stood since midnight, with a bow in his two hands and a rag round one of them.

"Yours is over," said Brom. "Nothing?"

"Nothing."

"Same. I'd sooner there'd been something. I'd know where it was."

"That is very well put," said Seln, and meant it.

He did not go to his blanket. He went along the line to the north, with the burnt strip on his right hand and then the unburnt grass, counting Brom's turfs as he came to them. They lay grass downward, each a cord from the last, and the frost had made them grey. At the third he stopped.

It stood where it had stood. He crouched over it without touching it, as he had crouched at noon, and waited for the light.

It came slowly. First there was a bar, and then the head of it, spread by a mallet. Then there was the stamp.

He did not read the stamp; he knew what it said. He let his eye rest on it as one lets a hand rest on a latch. A man answers for what he takes: he had said that at noon. Iron of that pattern is counted out across a board by a storekeeper who does not look up, and signed for in a book with ruled columns, and carried away in a case with a strap.

A case with a strap.

The drawer came open.

It was a tin, as long as his forearm, with a cap at one end and a lead tag crimped through the hasp. He had it under his arm. He was young, in the memory, with a satchel and one key, and he was carrying the tin from one room to another; that was the whole of the errand. A junior was permitted to break the tag in the second room, before a senior, and to draw out what was in the tin and count it against a docket. He was to count. He was not to read.

There had been eight sheets. They were fair copies, on paper backed with linen, and they were of the east.

He had not read them. But nobody can count eight sheets, corner by corner, and see nothing. He had seen a ruled stroke down the left of each that he took for the Line. He had seen roads beyond it, drawn in dashes, as they were drawn on the printed sheet that lay in a box at the camp; only these had run on much farther before they stopped.

And on some of the sheets, out in the white, there had been a round.

It was a small exact circle, ruled with a compass. He remembered the prick of the point at its middle, where the paper had been dented. There was nothing inside it at all; a dashed road came up to one and went about it and on. At the foot of each sheet there had been a little table of signs, a ford, a hold, a hill, and no sign among them for a round with nothing in it. On one sheet there were two.

He had counted eight, and said eight, and the senior had initialled the docket; and a young man with a satchel had gone down a stair thinking about his dinner.

He had taken those rounds for what a junior takes everything for, which is a thing that he has not been told. He had supposed a post, or a store, with a guard on it. It had never once occurred to him that a place might be left off a map because of what the ground itself did there.

Seln stayed on his heels by the iron a long while, and went over what he had, strictly, as he would have gone over it for somebody else's signature. He had eight sheets, seen once, by a boy who was counting. He had rounds, ruled, with a road going about one of them. He had a stake under his eyes, of the pattern that is signed for, driven on the edge of a circle that a researcher had paced with her feet.

He did not have a leaf to put beside the sheets. He had never seen one. He knew the weight of a tin and the number of its sheets, and he knew that he would be asked for more than that before the sun was high, by a small person with a pencil and no voice.

He could not tell, from memory, where on those sheets a round had fallen. He had the look of one: a water crossed, and dashes running on east of it, and then the white place. To say more than that he needed a ford drawn by somebody who had put a wheel through it.

He stood up, and his knees cracked in the cold.

The camp was stirring when he came down the line. The healer lay as she had fallen. The girl was awake, with her eyes on the sky, and the boy sat beside her with a book shut on his knee and one arm held in his lap like a thing that belonged to somebody else. Karis was sitting up against the box. She had her hand flat on its lid, and he knew that she had not yet opened it to look at eleven sheets, and why.

He went down on one knee in front of her, so that she should not have to lift her chin.

"I should like the carter's map," said Seln. "And the charcoal, if it came east in that box."

By the time the sun stood straight overhead, Karis had a horn cup in both hands and was finding out whether she could drink.

She did it a mouthful at a time, with her chin down and a look of sharp inquiry, as she would have tried a new pen. Across the front of her throat, where there had been a mark the colour of a plum at first light, there was something yellow and old.

She came over all the same, on her knees, since she had been asked plainly. She took his right wrist, which had nothing wrong with it but the cold, and laid two fingers on the side of his neck, and her lips began to move.

He counted with her, as he had counted on a mountain, and twice on a scrubbed table. One. Two. He knew now what he had not known on any of those days. He had stood on a hill in the dark with every one of the nine going out of him at once, and she had been standing on a lane below him with her eyes open.

Five. Six.

At six her lips stopped. He saw the old crease come between her brows; she had the look of a person trying a door that she knows to be locked, for the sake of having tried it.

"I can't mend what I can't read. That's the rule."

"Again," said Lira.

"No." Oryn let go of him, and wiped her hands on her breeches. "And I don't say a finding four times to a patient and change it on the fifth."

Her eyes came up to his, level and tired and a little hungry, as they had come up once over three broken ribs. She put no question to him of any kind. She pressed the edge of the blanket strip down with her thumb, as she pressed the strip on her own heel, and left Karis's knot where it was.

Seln came for them in the afternoon.

He had been at the stake since first light, by himself, with a calfskin and a stick of charcoal and a sheet of Karis's clean paper. Cael had watched him from the camp: a narrow dark figure three cords up the line, sitting on its heels, that drew a little and then sat for a long while.

"I have something to show," he said. "I should like it shown where the iron is. It is three cords, and she may take my arm."

They went at Lira's pace. She walked it flat, in the great boot, with her right hand on Seln's sleeve and her left tied across her breast; and Cael came behind on a leg that gave him eleven strides and then shut like a fist, as it had done once before, on a green rock in a river. He stood until it let go. It was a count that he knew.

The healer had come too. She had not been asked. She looked at the square brown bar in the grass, and at the stamp on its neck, for about as long as she had looked at five people under a rock; and then she let herself down beside it, by stages, and sat with her knees up and the iron against the small of her back.

"That's cold," she said. She did not move.

"Three in two days," Oryn said, after a while, to the country.

He waited.

"The arm. That was last night, and it was one, and it was the size of two. The throat. The hand. Three mendings in two days." She turned her hands over on her knees and looked at them, and let them lie. "That's a route. Near enough, that's what I carry between a hold and the next one, for the people who feed me and shoe the mule. Three serious hurts and a road's worth of small ones. And I've spent it on a road two days from the nearest roof, on a crew that's not on my circuit, sitting against a piece of iron somebody drove where they'd measured to."

Cael sat across from her, with his leg out, and listened.

He had been counting, since a far lip, what the day had cost, and he had supposed the count complete. He had not had this. A woman had added a stop to the only thing she owned, for two reasons of her own, and seven gates that had never been asked were paying for it.

"I'd not have had it," he said. "I have it now."

"Good. Don't do anything with it. Just have it."

She put her head back against nothing, and shut her eyes.

Seln had laid the calfskin on the turf, with a stone on each corner, where the stake's shadow did not fall across it.

"I shall say first what this is worth," he said. "It is one man's memory of a thing that he was told not to read. I carried a case once, between two rooms. There were eight sheets in it, of the country east of the Line. I counted them. I saw what a person sees who is counting."

He took up the sheet of paper. It was thin stuff, the kind that Karis had rubbed stones with, and when he laid it over the hide the carter's brown ink showed through it faintly.

"I have traced three things from his map, and no more. Here is the first water; those are his three strokes. Here is his square with a dot, which is the hold we slept at. And here is his day's measure, a tick to a day, so that what I draw shall be on his scale and not on mine."

He lifted the sheet away and laid it on his knee.

He had drawn it in charcoal. Cael saw a row of short strokes going across the thin paper from left to right, and two days beyond a small square they bent, and went about a neat black ring, and came back.

Cael saw it then, as he saw a seam in a bout when it was already past mending. A paper had asked whether anybody who went into that ring would come out of it. He had carried the answer down a hill himself, with a light.

She thought about that. Then she shut her eyes again, and whatever she made of it she kept.

They moved the dead hound in the afternoon, and Brom was not allowed to help.

That night, the ninety-seventh, Lira lay on her back with one arm tied across her chest and found that she could not get comfortable round it.

It did not hurt. That was the stupid part. She had been bitten to the bone at dusk and by midnight she had a forearm with eight small pink marks on it, as neat as stitching, and when she moved the fingers they moved. It was a perfectly good arm. It was not hers yet. It belonged to a square woman who was asleep six feet away with her mouth open, and it would go on belonging to her until there was snow.

Not a rope, not a knife, not a fall, not a friend.

She had said the whole of it over to herself that morning, to have it exact, as she would have got a card by heart. It was the last part that she kept coming back to. She had spent her life catching things. A lath, a wrist, a rail at the top of a climb; a small pale person who never looked where she put her feet. Her left hand went out for things before she had been told that they were falling.

She was going to have to watch it as she had watched her feet on a river bar, a stride at a time, with the difference that there was no stride to hang the no on.

She turned her head. The boy was sitting up, a little way off, with his dead arm in his lap and his face to the east. He was not on watch, and he had not lain down.

She had run a rim.

She let herself have that, for the length of a few breaths, since nobody else was going to give it to her. Twenty yards on a thing as round as a rail, in a boot like a bucket, on a leg that she had been forbidden to run on, with two dogs under her heels and one beside her knee; and she had been pulling away from all three. There had been nothing in it but legs. She had felt thirteen. She had felt the lanes at Fenmark come up under her as if they had only been waiting.

Then the boot had come down wrong, and here she was.

She left the ankle alone. She had asked a healer once, from the back of a mule, and had been told what it was worth and to whom it was owed; and last night that same healer had watched her not ask and had answered regardless. That made twice told. She would not make it twice asked.

It was the other thing that kept her awake.

She had been looking at Karis. There was a dog on Karis, and Seln's knife was coming up too slowly, and the healer had gone rigid under her arm; and on her left hand, where there was nobody, the grass had leaned.

She knew what that was. She had read it in his book before she ever saw it, in a boy's cramped writing, with sealed beside it and a mild man's name left out. She had seen it since, a handful of times, and never once in front of anybody who did not already know. It had gone by her elbow like a draught, and then he was on the dog.

That was one. She could have carried one.

Then he had set his feet. She had watched him set them, as she had taught him to in a lane in Ardenmere when they were both too young to know what he was; and the air had cracked.

It was hers. That was the whole of it, and she made herself look straight at it. He had had it off her before either of them knew that he could, and for two years it had been the one that he was shyest of, since it was hers and she was standing there. She had stood at that stone at noon, yesterday, and gone up on her toes, and asked for all of it with a panel's worth of wanting; and she had been given a step.

Seven hours later it had gone off in his feet like a whip, twenty feet north, inside.

She tried it for jealousy, as a person tries a tooth with her tongue. It was not that, or it was not only that. It was nearer to what she had felt on a gravel bar when she found out that she was fast: a thing that she had been certain of, about how the world was laid out, was not so, and nobody had asked her leave.

What am I becoming, if nobody's measuring. She had said that to four people at a fire. In there she had been legs, and the big fool had been a man with a pole, and the cleverest person she knew had been a small woman with a roll of paper in her coat. And he had been everything that he ever was, and a light besides.

He had known.

She had not got that from anything he said. She had it from his face, a foot from her own, over a dog's head. There had been a thing in it that she had not seen before in all the years that she had read him across a floor. He had been choosing. A person does not choose against a thing that he does not know he can do.

So he had known on that floor, with her arm in its mouth, and he had held its head and let Brom shoot.

She went through it. It was what she did with a plan that she hated. There had been nine on the white and two at Brom's legs, and Karis and the healer standing at the lip with nothing. If he had gone off like that there, every one of them would have come to the place where he stood, and that was the place where she was lying.

She would have made the same ruling. She would have been sick to do it. She thought, from his face, that he had been.

That left since when. She had the right to it. She could have had it out of him last night with one more word; he had been sitting there waiting for it with his breath held, and he would have told her everything, badly, in the wrong order, with his arm dead and hers tied, because she had asked.

She did not want it got out of him. She wanted it given.

Later. She had put it on her own side of the fire, and it was hers to keep there. It sat in her as the burst used to sit in her calves, wanting out at every stride. She said no to it. She had some practice.

Cael had the last watch, on the ninety-eighth morning, and so he was the only one who saw it.

The healer got up in the grey. She did not go to the mule. She walked the ten yards to the stone by herself, past the place where a dead thing had lain, and stood on the near side of it with her boots together, as she had stood on the first evening with her hands held out over nothing.

Then she stepped across.

He went still. She was one stride inside, and there were seven animals somewhere that he had not seen since a wall went down. He looked past her, at the grass, and kept his eyes moving over it; and he counted.

The first time she only stood, with her palms up, and stepped back.

The second time she had two fingers of her right hand on her own left wrist, and her lips moving. He saw them stop as her boot came down. She stood so for a breath, and came out, and they began again before her heel had left the ground.

She went over the third time by inches, as Karis had, sliding one foot; and the fourth time backward, with her eyes on the camp. She opened her eyes then and looked down, to see where her feet were. They were where the stone said that they ought to be. She did it again from farther back, and that was six.

For the seventh she fetched the mule.

She led the animal up until its forefeet were against the stone, and laid her whole hand on the warm neck under the mane, and stood with her head bent, reading whatever it is that a healer reads in a beast. Then, keeping her hand where it was, she stepped over, so that she stood inside with her arm stretched back across the line.

She was a long time at that one. The mule turned its head and nosed her elbow.

She let go of the mule and walked three strides into quiet ground and stood there, square, with her arms hanging and her face toward the pale thing on the hill; and he counted a hundred before she moved.
