They walked west on the ninety-eighth, and Lira went the whole way on the flat of her foot, since she had been told to.

"Whole sole," the healer had said, at the stone, with the tape freshly on. "Heel and toe together, every step. You don't roll off it and you don't push. If it goes a fourth time, I'm not carrying you to that fence."

"I could ride."

"You could. And if she puts a foot in a rut, you come off, and you come off onto that." Oryn had looked at the sling. "A fall off a mule's a fall. You walk."

So she walked like a duck, across a country with nothing in it but grass, at the pace of a small brown animal that never hurried and never stopped. She had hated that pace for four days on a mountain. She found now that she could not have gone faster if she had been let, and it was restful, in its way, to have the matter settled by somebody else's legs.

It was the arm that she could not get used to.

She had not known how much of walking was done with the hands. Her balance was all on one side. When the wind pushed her she put out the right and nothing answered it from the left; when she stepped over a rut she felt the tied arm start, under the grey wool, and stop against the knot. It did that forty times in the first hour. It was like walking beside a dog that keeps going for the same gate.

The big fool was behind her with the box, and one hand held a little away from its strap.

He made the sound into his sleeve that he had made on a river bank, and she felt better.

It happened at about the end of the first mile.

Karis was in front of her. Karis had not said a word since the lane, and could not, and she had her notebook in one hand and her eyes on a thing that she was working out; she walked as she always walked when she was thinking, without the least idea where the ground was. There was a place where a grain cart's wheel had cut the rut a hand deeper than the rest. She put her left foot into it and went over sideways like a dropped rule.

She went toward Lira's left.

It was not a decision. Lira had caught that small person off a ladder, and out of a chair, and once by the collar on the edge of a wash; her left hand knew the way. Not a friend.

It was too slow, and it was too clumsy. A right arm is not where a left arm would have been. Karis struck it and slid, and went down on one knee in the rut with a jolt that brought a noise out of her throat, a croak, the first sound that she had made since the lane; and the notebook flew.

The healer had not broken step. She was ten yards ahead, on the low side of the mule, and she had her head turned on her shoulder.

It was not praise. Lira knew what praise sounded like; she had been given it on painted floors by people with slates. It was a count, said by a person who kept no book, and she found that she would sooner have had it than a sheet of figures.

She walked on, flat. The arm lay where it had been put. It had started again before she had gone a hundred yards, at a gust, and she felt it reach the knot and stop.

They had a fire that night, at the spring, and Seln made the bread.

It was the first flame that any of them had lit on the Fallow road since the way out, and Cael noticed that nobody discussed it. They were a day west of a grey stone; the ground under them was only ground, and a flint was not a declaration. Seln struck it. He had gathered dead stems of the pale grass by the armful, since there was nothing else in that country to burn, and they went up with a hiss and wanted feeding every minute.

Brom sat on a pannier and gave orders.

"More water than that. It wants to be like a wet clay. Now fold it; no, toward you. You're not folding a letter."

"I have folded a great many letters," said Seln. He had flour to the wrists, and his face was as mild as milk. "I had not understood that it was a disadvantage."

Seln gave it a count of sixty a side. Cael heard him do it, under his breath, exactly; and when the cake came off the stone it was pale gold on both faces, and risen, and there was not a black place on it anywhere.

They all looked at it. In ninety-eight days of road nobody had seen such a thing come off one of their fires.

Finding. A method correctly dictated for ninety-eight days and never once followed by its author. Tested: one cake. I am entering it.

"You can enter what you like," said Brom. "I'm eating it."

She opened her mouth then, and Cael saw her throat work. It was the first time that she had tried since a lane. What came out was a small rough noise with the shape of a word in it, like a hinge that wants oil.

"No," said Oryn, without looking up from her heel. "Tomorrow, if it wants to. Not because you've a joke ready."

Karis shut her mouth, and wrote Tomorrow, and underlined it.

He sat among them with the cake warm in his hand. He had walked a day at a mule's shoulder with nine things shut, and they had gone back under his refusal like dogs that had been run; the heaviest of them lay easier tonight, and the cold had left his fingers at about noon. He had a sore leg and an arm that was coming back. He was, he supposed, mending.

He looked round the fire at five faces. Every one of them had watched a thing go north out of a lane that they had been certain could not happen, and had walked beside him for a day without a word about it. They had not gone quiet, or careful. The big man had let another person make his bread sooner than leave the others without, and the small one had made a joke of it on paper, and Lira had told a carter's boot what she thought of it. It was the same crew that had sat at a fire above a wash, with a healer added, who was looking at her own heel.

He had not known that it could be. He had supposed, at a far lip with his pencil lifted, that whatever was true by dark would cost him this; and it had cost a good deal, on other people's bodies, and it had not cost this.

It came to him that he was being trusted. That was all the silence was. Lira had said later, and three people had taken their time from her; and the fifth asked nobody anything that was not a hurt. They were waiting, without making a show of it, for him to have a sentence.

He did not have one. He ate his bread, and it was very good, and he said so; and Brom told him that there was no call to be unkind.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

By the second noon the leg had stopped counting.

Cael noticed it as a person notices that a noise has ceased. He had been walking at the mule's shoulder since first light, across the last of the pale grass, and he reached for the number of his strides and found that he had none; he had not stood still since the spring. He tried the calf on purpose, a long step and then a quick one. It was sore, and it was a leg.

It had opened on the ninety-sixth evening, in a ditch, with nothing under his soles. This was the middle of the ninety-ninth day.

He looked across the mule's withers at the healer. She was on the low side, as she always was, with her hand on the cheek-strap and her eyes on the road, going at the one pace that she had. She had said the ninety-ninth for his ribs, at a gate, and the hundredth for the other thing. The hundredth was tomorrow.

He had known what the other thing was since a yard at Oxhollow. He had heard her describe it, in a healer's words, and had watched four faces change; and after that he had put it where he put the things that he would look at when there was leisure. There had been a letter to ration, and a line to pace, and a ring. For three days there had been an arm in a sling, and a hill that nobody spoke of. He had been glad of every one of them, and he saw now what he had been glad of them for.

It was a mile to the fork. He walked it at a mule's shoulder with a whole leg, and for the first time in fifteen days he let himself look.

She would lay both hands on him in the morning, and all that she was, for as long as it took. She would do it in earnest, since she did nothing in any other way. He had felt that ninth thing come to him at the end of a bout with a friend who had asked only to be shown straight; he knew, as well as he knew anything about himself, what her morning was likely to be made of.

He wanted it. That was the first thing that he found when he looked, and he was shocked at the size of it. He had wanted very little for himself since he crossed the Line.

The second thing took him the rest of the mile. A woman was walking on the low side of a mule, six feet from him, who had added a stop to the only thing she owned in order to read a boy whom she could not read; and she had not the least idea that the boy might come away from her table with a piece of what she read with.

They came down to the fork an hour after noon, and up the valley with the smoke of a hold standing over the fence in front of them. The east gate was open. He had gone out by it five days before with five other people and a calfskin, to pick up something that somebody had left lying.

It was the bowman who saw them first.

He had no business at that gate. He kept the western one, and in three stays Cael had seen him leave his platform once, to watch six people go out by the east; and he was standing beside the east gate now, with his bow at the length of his arm, like a man who has been coming to the same place at the same hour for five days. He looked at nobody but Lira. He watched her come up the last fifty yards on the flat of her foot, with a strip of grey wool across her and a hand tucked under her collarbone, and he did not lift two fingers from the stave. He took off his cap.

Lira saw it. She put up the great boot an inch, and set it down whole.

There was broth. He could smell it from under the lintel. The steading's woman came out of the long house with a ladle in her hand, wiping the other on her apron, and stopped on the step, and went along them with her lips.

"Six. Well."

It was all that she said, and she said it to the ladle. He thought it the longest speech of approval that he had ever had from her; she had counted them out of that gate, and she had not been certain of the sum.

"There are six blankets," said Seln. He had them rolled on his shoulder. "One is a hand narrower than it went out. I regret it."

"I can see what it went for." She looked at the sling again. "Is that one of mine she's wearing?"

"It's the best of them," said Lira.

"It would be." The woman jerked her head at the long house. "It's on the board. The back room's swept."

The healer had him in the yard before he had finished the broth.

"You. Shirt. All of it."

He got it over his head with one arm and the other, which had come back to him on the road as far as the wrist. He stood by the well's coping in the last of the sun with five bands of linen round him that he had hated on the eighty-sixth day, and measured on the eighty-seventh, and since a certain evening had not once had the leisure to think about.

"Arm on your head. Breath out."

She took the first band at his breastbone, where its end was, and drew it off round his side to the spine in one pull, as she had laid it on. It came with a sound like a page tearing. The other four followed. He had expected to feel something give, and he felt only cold air on a place that had not had any for eighteen days.

She did not put her hands round him to count. She had tried that. She set her thumb on the lowest of the three, where the first small sound had been, and pressed, as she had pressed on Lira's shin under a rock; and she watched his face while she did it.

"Breathe. All the way."

He drew it in. He went past the place where a strip of pitch had told him there some four thousand times a day, and nothing told him anything. He had forgotten that there was so much room in him.

"Twenty-one days. A rib is six weeks. These are done."

"You said they'd be done on the ninety-ninth."

"I said the rule was twenty-one days. I'd have laid money on sooner, and I don't lay money." She was rolling the dead tape onto its peeled stick. "Leg."

He put his boot up on the coping. She undid a knot that she had once called a good one, and dropped a strip of grey blanket on the ground, and turned the calf to the light. There was a seam down it, pale and dry, a hand long, lying over two older marks; she ran her thumb the length of it and did not shut her eyes.

"That opened three nights back. It's closed. Four days, counting the one it went on." She let his leg go. "I've a man in this hold who cut his shin on a scythe at the start of the harvest and it's weeping yet."

He waited for her to ask.

She stepped back, a stride and a half, and looked him over from there, the whole of him, as she had looked five people over from the corner of a rock.

"Still and whole."

She said it as she would have said a weight. He felt it go into him like a key. She had told him that at a ford: when he was not broken she would run the long one, and she wished to feel it not read him properly.

"Tomorrow. First light. The back room, with the door shut, and I'll not have eaten, so nor will you. It's both hands. It's twenty minutes, near enough; I'll not know till I'm in." She tucked the stick into her coat. "It costs me a mending, and there's a bench under that window I owe four days to. They'll keep till after noon. I've looked at every one of them."

"And if it's nothing again? That'd be five."

"Then it's nothing, and I say so."

"I meant—" He did not know what he had meant. He had lain on a table at Oxhollow and felt an instrument close on air, and he had wanted, with a wanting that he had not written down, for this one to close on something. "Will you get anything?"

"You don't get a yes. You get told."

She was not being short with him. It was only how a healer's table was run: nobody was promised what the hands would find; they were told afterward, whatever it was, to their faces.

You get told. He had four people waiting in a loft, and he knew already what he was going to lay in front of them. Those three words would be in the middle of it.

"You lie still," said Oryn. "You breathe slow. You don't talk to me, and you don't hold anything, and you don't help."

"What does helping look like?"

It was an honest question, and he heard, as he asked it, what else it was.

"I'll know."

She went to her bench.

There were five people on it, under the window of the back room. They had seen a mule come up the valley and had come out and sat down, as eight had sat down at Oxhollow, and one of them was a man with his shin wrapped. She did not eat first. She went along them at her stride and a half, with two fingers for each wrist and her lips moving to ten, and at the end of the bench she turned round.

"Not one of you is worse than when I left, and one's better and won't care to hear it. I'll do what wants doing after noon tomorrow. I've a thing in the morning that needs all of me."

They got up, the five of them, and went back to whatever they had been doing; nobody on that bench had ever argued with her about a day. Cael stood by the well with his shirt in his hand and the cold on his ribs, and watched five people give up a morning to him that not one of them knew they were giving.

It was the same yard. He had not looked at it when he came in. There was the sweep of the well, and the cart-yard, and a boy forking straw into the barn under the loft where two boxes waited; the geese went by in a line, and somebody in the long house was scouring a pot. He had gone out of this place five days ago and stood on a floor that matched no stone in the world, and held a hound's head, and carried a light down a hill. Nothing here had altered by so much as a goose, and he found that he had been counting on that without knowing it.

Lira was at the foot of the loft ladder, looking up it, with one hand on a rung.

"I've climbed that with a foot on a stave," she said, when he came over. "I'm working out how you do it with an arm that's not allowed to hold." She kept her eyes on the rungs. "Don't help. I'd like to know."

She went up it sideways, in the end, with her right hand and both knees, and her left elbow tight against her ribs; and at the top she sat down on the loft's edge with her legs hanging, breathing hard, and looked at the sling as a person looks at a dog that has stayed when it was told.

He drew the ladder up himself, hand over hand, and laid it along the edge of the loft.

Karis lifted one finger from the notebook. Her throat was the colour of an old apple by that light, and she had spoken twice that day, a word at a time, in a voice like a rasp on wood.

Her page was a single leaf, and she had been two years in the making of it. It had a curve on it, for how quickly each of the nine had come, and a column for what each had cost him afterward; and at its head, in her small exact hand, stood three words with a rule under every one. She had never in his hearing called it more than a model. He had its three words by heart, and so had the others, since she had read them out on the night that the eighth was priced.

"So I've laid tomorrow beside her page, a piece at a time. It wants to be sustained. She says twenty minutes, with both her hands on me, and I've never stood a bout that was a quarter as long. It wants stakes, on both sides. Mine are that I'm three days off that floor, with every one of the nine still shaken by it. Hers are that she's spent three mendings on us and she's late at the top of her round, and she means to lay out a fourth on a boy who has given her nothing four times. The oil lasted him long enough to write it, with the others asleep or pretending to be.

He did not put it under the day's heading. He had written two such leaves before this one: the first in a week of rain, with four people's initials at its foot, and the second at a sill, on the night before a bout with a friend who was not to be told. He turned to a clean page for the third, and began it with the two words that were the point of the whole.

Written before. Tomorrow morning, the back room, the door shut. Oryn runs the long reading. Both hands, all of her, all of me, twenty minutes. I lie still. I'm still and whole for the first time in front of her; she said so in the yard, with the tape off.

The conditions, as I have them. Sustained: twenty minutes at contact is longer than any bout I've stood. Stakes: I'm three days off the Ring and the nine are still settling; she's three mendings down and her route's late at the far end and she's spending a fourth on a patient who's given her nothing four times. Earnest: she'll do the thing she does as well as she does it. Karis: the model says real, not fight. I don't know if the model's right. Nobody does. Tomorrow's the first time it could be tested and I'm the test.

The price. She doesn't know what I am. She can't consent to what she can't know about — not won't; can't. My reasons are good, and they're the reasons of somebody who wants it, and the real one is that I don't know what she'd say. Entered.

If it takes what she's using on me, it takes it from the one person on this road who came to help. I don't know what it costs a source. It's never shown. Tomorrow's the first time it could, and if it does, she pays, and I chose that for her.

After: I tell her. In full. On her table, before I'm off it. Whatever it costs me, including the route walking north without me on it.

I want it. Write that too.

Write it before, not after. That's the whole difference between me and the system.

The flame had gone down to a blue bead, and he read the leaf through once by it, quickly, from the top.

It was not a good page. He had hoped a little that it would look better written; that somewhere between the pencil and the paper it would turn into the kind of thing that a careful person does. It had not. It read as what it was: a boy wanted something, and had found that he could not have it honestly, and was going to take it and pay afterward; and he had set down the price first, in a hand that would be dry by morning, so that he could never claim to have been surprised.

That was all that the last line meant. A registry had read him for years, and written down what it found, and had never once told him beforehand what it was reaching for or what the reaching might cost him. He was about to reach for somebody else in the same way. The one thing that he had which that office had not was a leaf with tonight's date at the head of it.

It was a thin difference, and it did not make the thing allowed. He was exact with himself about that, since he was trying to be exact about all the rest. To cross the yard now and knock would be right. To say in the morning, before she had so much as washed her hands, what those hands might lose, would be right. Four people had shown him both doors. A leaf written first opened neither of them; it meant only that when he walked past them he would be doing it with his eyes open, and could never afterward tell anybody, himself least of all, that he had not known.

He held to that much, since it was all there was.

The bead went out. He lay down between two sacks of barley with the book under his hand; and in the dark Wind leaned a little toward where Lira was breathing, and the heaviest of the nine shifted, like a sea a long way off, and was still.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

It was barely light when he crossed the yard.

There was ice on the trough. The geese were asleep in a heap by the long house wall, and on the platform by the western gate a lean man turned his head, and turned it back. Cael had eaten nothing. He had his shirt on and no coat, and his feet were bare inside his boots.

The door of the back room stood open. He stopped on the sill, since something in him was asking about the sill, and since he wished to have the room exactly; he thought that he would be remembering it for a long time.

It was small. There was one window, in the eastern wall, a square of grey with its shutter folded back, and a bench under the window. A table stood in the middle of the floor, a scrubbed plank on two trestles, long enough for a man to lie on, with a three-legged stool at its head. Along the sill, under the light, a strip of canvas had been unrolled, and on the canvas her things lay in a row: the tape on its peeled stick, a flask, shears, a hank of clean linen, a horn cup, a bone needle. He had seen them come out of a pannier in a dozen places. He had never before seen them set out in her own order, where her left hand would find each of them without her eyes.

The healer was washing. She had a basin on the bench and her sleeves pushed above the elbow, and she did not turn round.

"Shut that. Boots off, and the shirt. On your back, with your head at the stool."

He shut the door, which had a peg on a thong for a latch.

The plank was cold under his shoulders and very clean, and there was a folded sack for his head. He lay and looked at rafters with barley dust on them, and listened to her drying her hands, a finger at a time.

Nine things lay in him, and he went along them as he went along anything at the start. Wind was in his feet, and still. Pressure sat under the breastbone. The read was shut, as it had been since a rut. Compression lay in his frame, and Ember in his right hand, with nothing to look at. The bright quick one had asked about the table's edge when he lay down, and Anchor about the sill, and he had told each of them no. The heaviest lay low, like weather that has blown itself out.

The ninth had drawn itself in very small. This was the first light, and not the last; that one came up at dusk.

She had told him in a yard to hold nothing. He had spent a hundred days in learning to refuse the nine, a stride at a time; and now he was to lie here for twenty minutes and neither refuse them nor let them go, and he did not know the name of that.

She came to the table's side, smelling of pitch and cold water.

"Breathe like a man asleep."

He tried it; he had watched Brom do it often enough. The breath went in to the bottom of him, where a tape had stopped it for three weeks, and out again slowly.

"Slower than that. You're thinking. Stop."

Two fingers came down on the inside of his right wrist, and two more below the hinge of his jaw, and they were warm from the basin. Her lips moved. He did not count with her this time. He lay under it and felt the count come to five, and to six, where it had stopped on a leg at a stone; and it went on to ten.

"Nothing. As before."

She said it without any disappointment, as she would have said that a door was shut. It was the fifth time. She took her fingers away and shook both hands out from the wrist, twice, hard.

"That was the short one, so that I'd know I hadn't dreamed it. Now the other." He heard her push the stool aside with her foot, for she did not mean to sit. "I'll be a while finding my way in, and then I'll be in, and I'll not hear you. If you must move, say so first. If I say lie still, you lie still."

"Yes."

"And don't mind my talking. I talk, in a long one. It's how I keep my place."

Her left hand slid in under the back of his neck, broad and warm, and took the weight of his head. Her right came down flat on his breastbone.

It lay exactly over the place where a small bright thing had gathered on a morning in a windowless room, and looked at him for eleven seconds, and gone out. He had gone looking for that place on a hillside five days ago, with five people abreast of him, and had found it dark. Her palm was on it now. She could not have known that; it was only where a healer puts a hand.

"Still," said Oryn, and shut her eyes.

Chapter 37 — Minute Twenty-One

[Taut, lucid narration; keep the Ring's fragment uses, costs, and positions easy to follow]

He counted breaths, since it was the only count that she had left him.

A man asleep draws twelve to the minute. He had timed Brom against Hesk's clock once, on a road, for want of anything better to do, and had kept the figure. Twelve to the minute made sixty in five, and two hundred and forty in the twenty that she had named; and he lay on a scrubbed plank with a healer's hand over his breastbone and began at one.

For the first dozen there were only her hands. They were warm, and broad, and they did not move. He could feel the short nails of the left one against the back of his skull, and the heel of the right resting on bone. He could feel her pulse in it, which was slow.

"That's skin," said Oryn.

Her voice was lower than he had ever heard it, and it came from a little way off, as a person's does who is talking in her sleep.

"That's breath. That's a heart, and it's a good one; somebody's run it hard since it was small. Those are the three I taped, and they're done. I said that they were."

She was silent while he drew six more.

"Past that, now."

He had thought about what it would be. He had lain awake over it in a loft, with the book under his hand. He had been read by a great many things, and the only one of them that he could do himself went down: it opened under his boots like an eye and took the weight of whatever was beneath, a pace and a half, straight into the ground. He had supposed that a healer's reading would do the same, and that he would feel it come down into him from her palm as a plumb-line comes down a wall.

It did not go down. It went along.

He felt it leave her right hand at about the thirtieth breath. It was not warmth, and it was not a touch; it was nearer to what a person feels when somebody else's attention comes to rest on the back of his neck. It set out from his breastbone toward his feet, and it went the whole length of him without haste, as a joiner runs his thumb down the edge of a plank to learn whether it is true. When there was no more of him to go along it turned, and came back up the other side, and he felt it arrive under the nape of his neck, in her left hand, where she was waiting for it.

Then it set out again.

He lay very still. It was not even, and that was the first thing about it that he could have sworn to. Down his right side it bore a shade more lightly than down his left, and came a hair late. Each time, the heel of her hand on his breastbone eased and settled with it, by so little that he would never have caught it without three weeks of a tape to teach him what a hair was. He knew that unevenness. He had walked behind it for a day and a half down a mountain before he saw what it was: a raw heel, taped, and favoured for so long that it had been built into everything she did.

It was only after that that he found the beat. It was slower than his heart and slower than his breath, and it did not vary. It was the pace that she kept on a road, below a mule, and she was going through him at it.

He could feel her keeping time. He had not expected that, of all things: that he would lie under an instrument and be able to tell that it was a person. A brass plate in a district hall had waited over him for eleven seconds, and he had not felt it wait; an assessor's panel had read him across a floor, and he had got nothing from it but a number on a slate. This one limped.

He had been afraid, coming over the yard, that it would be like being searched. He had been searched by a good many careful people; he knew the hands of a clerk going through a satchel, and the eyes of a panel going over a stance for the thing that was wrong with it. This did not rummage. It went down him and came back as a carter goes down his own road, looking at what was there, and it took up nothing to see what lay beneath.

"There," said Oryn.

It was at the fifty-fourth breath.

"There it is. I've got the moving. I had that much at a ford with two fingers." Her hand had not shifted on his chest. "Now I go and look for what it's moving in."

He drew the sixtieth, slowly, like a man asleep. That was five minutes, and she had only just come in.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

She talked, as she had told him that she would.

He had supposed that it would be like the talk at a bench, short and to the purpose. It was nothing of the kind. It was the low running murmur of a person who is feeling her way down a passage in the dark and saying what her hands meet, less to be heard than to keep herself from being lost; and he lay under it and counted, and tried to do as he had been told, which was nothing.

It was a good deal harder than refusing.

He had refused the nine at every stride of a road, and he knew that work as he knew the weight of his own boots. He was not to refuse them now; a refusal was a holding, and she had said that she would know. He was not to let them answer either. He had to lie as a house lies when somebody goes through it with a lamp, with every door standing as it happened to stand, and he found that he had never in his life left a door alone.

Her current went down the length of him and came back.

Eighty-four. Something in his feet turned over like a sleeper who had heard his name. It was Wind. He did not tell it no, and he did not let it rise. He let it turn over, and it settled.

His right palm grew warm on the plank. He left it where it lay.

She was silent for several breaths. He felt the thing that she was doing go more slowly along his left side, where three ribs had been, and then down the leg that a hound had opened, and stop there, and go on.

"Everyone I've ever had my hands in, this is the part where I know." She said it as a finding about herself. "Iron Skin, you feel the banks first — dense, walled, everything held. Ember, the banks are a fire's, hot at the edge. Wind you barely feel the banks at all, the water's too fast. But there's always a bank. It's how you know which river." A pause, long, her current going along Ember and stopping at the ignition point and lying there as if it had found a stone in a bed. "I can't find one here. I keep putting my hand where the bank ought to be and there's more water."

He was at a hundred and eight. That was nine minutes.

He had begun to be able to tell where she was. It was like lying in a field with his eyes shut while somebody walked round him: he had her by a sense that he had no name for, now at his knee, now under his heart. And as she came to each place, the thing that he carried there did what it would have done if a stranger had come to its door.

Compression lay through the whole of his frame, and it did nothing at all; it had been built to wait for a blow, and no blow came. The read wished to open. It wished it very much. There were two hands on him and a square woman standing over a table, and it could have told him the weight of her to a pound and which way she leaned. He left it shut. He did not hold it shut. He found, after a while, that there was a difference, and that it lay in whether his jaw was tight.

"You're helping," said Oryn.

His eyes came open. She had not opened hers.

"Your neck went hard. Let it go. I don't need you to keep anything out of my way. I need you to lie there."

He let it go. It took him three breaths.

"That's it. That's a man asleep."

She went on down.

It was at about the hundred and thirtieth that she came to where the ninth lay, and that one did a thing that none of the others had done. It drew in. He felt it go from her as a snail's horn goes from a finger, small, and smaller, into some place behind the rest where even he could hardly have put a hand on it. He had not asked it to. He had not asked anything of it since a lane. It was a thing made for not being found, and somebody was looking, and it had hidden by itself, as its first owner had hidden on a back stair before he was old enough to choose.

Her current went over the place and did not check.

He breathed out. He had not known, until then, that he was afraid of what she might say.

The heaviest of them she passed last, low down, under everything. He had felt it shift in a loft the night before, and it had been restless since a ditch; it had three lanes still in it, like a sea with a swell left over from weather a long way off. He waited for it to rise at her.

It did not. It lay quiet under her hands. She went along the top of it as a boat goes over deep water, and it did not so much as lift.

A hundred and forty-four, he counted. Twelve minutes. He lay with his neck loose and all nine doors standing as they stood, and for the first time since a morning in a windowless room there was somebody in the house besides himself.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

It was in the thirteenth minute that he understood what was strange about her.

He had been waiting for it without knowing that he waited. He had lain under hands before, and under eyes; he knew to the breath when it came. The thing reaching for him would find that he was not what it had been built to hold, and then it would change. A brass plate went dark. A panel's faces shut. A clerk with a form that had no box for him wrote a word in capitals, because he could find no tier to write; and after that there was a file, and a watcher at a gate.

They had all been afraid of him. He had first seen it on the morning of his Kindling, and had not had the word for it then. It had looked like anger, mostly.

She had found it eight minutes ago, and he had heard her find it: there it is, I've got the moving. She had been walking up and down the length of something for twelve minutes that was like nothing she had ever put her hands in, and her voice was the voice in which she had told an ox-driver that four small bones were broken.

She was not afraid of him.

He turned that over, slowly, at a man asleep's pace. She had watched him go up a hill with fire in his fist, in a place where she could not count to four, and she had asked him whether his calf was worse than an arm. She had read him afterward and found nothing, and said so, and left his leg in its cloth.

It was not courage, and he did not think that it had so much as occurred to her that courage was wanted. It was her trade. A healer who stood amazed at a broken leg would never set it; she had spent her working life walking up to the worst thing in a yard and asking which it was, and her craft had no room in it for being impressed. He was the strangest thing that she had ever touched, and to her that made him a difficult reading, which she was doing as well as she knew how.

He had been a case to a great many people. He had never before been a patient.

Something in him eased that had been braced for longer than he had carried any of the nine, and he let it; and she did not tell him that he was helping.

She had gone quiet. He counted through the fifteenth minute, and the sixteenth, with nothing over him but her breathing and the slow going-along; and he felt it change. It was no weaker, but it had been a walk, and now it was a search. She went down one side of him and stopped, and came back a hand's breadth, and tried it again from a little farther in, as she had tried a stone with her feet at dawn, eight times. She was looking for an edge: under his heart, and along his arms to the fingers, and in the long muscles of his back. She was not finding one, and she would not leave off.

The sweat had come out on her. A drop of it fell on his collarbone.

Two hundred and four. That was seventeen. Two hundred and sixteen.

Her right hand pressed down a very little on his breastbone, as though she were leaning on a door.

"I'm going to say what I've got." Her voice had roughened. "I say it while I'm in. It's truer."

He did not answer, since he had been told not to speak to her.

"I can feel that there's movement. More than one. I can't count them — I can't find where one stops. There's no channel. Everyone has a channel; I feel the banks and I know the Path. I can't find the banks in you. I've looked for twenty minutes. It isn't that you're broken. It's that I can't find anything shaped like the thing I read."

It was the longest thing that he had ever heard her say with her eyes shut.

More than one. She had it, and she did not know what she had. She had gone through a house with a lamp and counted more rooms than a house ought to hold, and she had stood in every one of them and could not find a wall.

He was at two hundred and twenty-eight. That left one minute of her twenty.

Her hands did not lift. He felt her draw a breath all the way down, and let it go, and there was something in the going that he had not heard in her at a bench or on a hill or beside a bar of cold iron. She was not tired; he knew what her tiredness sounded like. A person who had only ever owned one thing had put the whole of it down on a table and found that it would not buy what was there.

"Eleven years," said Oryn. "I've never had my hands in something and not known what it was."

She did not take them away. She leaned on them, and went in again.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

It came then.

He knew it before it had finished coming. He had felt it nine times. The first four he had hardly known that he was there for; after that he had learned to be present. It had always come in the thick of a blow, or at the end of a bout, with his arm ringing. It had never before come into a quiet room.

There was a place in him that stood empty. He had not known of it until it was offered something.

And along the slow current that she kept, the one that set out from her right hand and came home to her left, he could feel a shape. It was not his. It was the way she went: the keeping of time, and the feeling ahead for a bank, and the patience of it, which would walk the length of a person eight times sooner than guess. It was the thing that she read with. She had laid the whole of it open on him for twenty minutes, in earnest, at a cost, and she was pressing it against him now harder than she had pressed it yet.

It stood at his breastbone, under her palm, like a hand held out in the dark.

He could stop it.

That was the first thing that he was sure of. He had refused nine things a stride at a time for a hundred days, and he was better at that one act than at anything else he did. He had only to say no, at the first stride, as he had said it on a gravel bar. Her current would go by the empty place and find it shut, as it had found the ninth; she would come to the end of her twenty minutes and lift her hands and tell him that there was nothing, as before. He would get down off her table with what he had lain down on it with. Nothing would have been taken from anybody.

He went through what came after that, as quickly as he had gone through it on a white floor with his hands on a skull.

It would be right. He did not hide that from himself, lying there. Four people had said so in a loft, and nothing that he had written afterward by a bead of oil had altered it by a hair. There was even an honest way to do it: he could shut the place, and when she lifted her hands he could tell her all the same what had stood open in him while she worked, and what he had come within a breath of taking.

That was the right road. He saw the whole length of it, and he did not want it.

There was another way to stop, and he looked at that one longer, since it was the one that he would really have taken. He could shut the place and say nothing. He would walk out into the yard having wanted a thing with his whole heart, and having climbed a ladder to say so, and having written it on a leaf with the price beside it. Four people would be glad, and he would let them be; and the leaf would turn into a page about a boy who had thought of doing wrong and had not. That stopping would be a lie, and he would not add it to the rest.

So he knew which was right, and he chose against it. He was exact about why. It was not that a leaf permitted him; a thing written down beforehand is only a thing done on purpose. It was that he wanted to know what he was more than he wanted to be in the right, and the one instrument that might tell him was standing at his breastbone. He would answer for it within the minute, on this table, to her face.

He looked at it squarely, with his neck loose and his eyes open on a rafter.

He reached. Directed. Open-eyed. Still.

It was a small thing to do. He had not known how small. He did not so much as shift a finger on the plank. He opened the one door in the house that had been shut, and something came through it at her pace.

The place behind his breastbone took on weight. It filled slowly at first and then all the way to the brim, like a cup under a careful hand; and he lay under a healer's palm and kept his eyes open through all of it.

The lines came after. They stood where they had always stood, plain, in the place that belonged to nothing else, and nobody in that room could see them but himself.

Ten.

He read it through, from the top, with her hand still on him.

It said unnamed, as it always said; and he knew the name, and how she laced a boot. Iron: it was as light as the one before it, which a friend had given him on sprung oak. He lay and looked at that. He had wanted it with his whole heart in a loft, and had told four people why: that he might look. It sat under his breastbone now, as real as the other nine, and he did not try it. He did not know how. And he had a healer's hand on him still, and a debt to pay before he had any right to learn.

It was the first that had ever come to him lying down. It had come out of nobody's blow, in a room with a basin in it, from two hands that were trying to learn what he was made of. That was one.
