"My paper is in the middle one," said Karis.

"It will be there at noon. If the floor is as empty as it looks, you will come up for it yourself, and I shall carry it down." He turned to the healer. "You said that somebody should stand outside the line."

"I'll stand at that stone with my sleeves up. I said it, and I meant it." Oryn was sitting on her heels. "I've learned what my hands are worth on the far side of one. If a thing goes wrong in there, you bring it to me. It's two hundred yards. I've seen an arm carried as far."

"Then this stone is the objective, as the other was. Whatever is seen, whatever is heard, the word is Back, and every one of us comes to it by the straightest way." Seln looked at each of them in turn. "It is a good plan for a place with nobody in it. I do not know of a good plan for the other."

He looked at Cael last.

"I said a thing at the fire in the meadow, and I told you that I should say it again here. If there are hands, in the dark, at arm's length, you do as you think fit. If there are eyes, you are a boy with a knife. Nothing that a pair of eyes could carry to a boat."

"I heard it."

"I am saying it to five people now, so that when you stand still with all of us looking at you, four of them will know why."

Karis had got up while he was speaking. She went to the middle box and undid its cord, and lifted the lid a hand's breadth, and felt down the inside of it without a light. What she drew out was a single leaf. Cael knew it by its ruling, even by the fire: six rows, and a numeral struck through at the head of the sixth, and three lines of small exact writing against it.

She folded it once and put it inside her coat, against her shirt, and tied the box again.

"There is nothing else in there that says a word about him," she said, to nobody. "That one goes where I go."

He wrote the night's log with his back against the old iron.

Hundred and thirteenth day, night. At the edge of the second one. A stone, and two bars, both numbered thirty-two; one five cold terms old, one a cold term or two, with a mark under its number that Seln won't read. A floor with no stones on it, and a hole, and a stair. Nobody on the ruts.

Tide: once, on the healer, on the ridge road. I asked twice today and she granted the second. The short count and then a minute of the long, at one sitting; I am counting that as one, since it was one asking and one yes. At three there were banks. I knew the Path by ten. In the minute, one channel and one thing in it, going somewhere. It cost her nothing that she would notice. It cost me the use of that hand for an hour, and most of a loaf.

She says not tonight for the other, and she is right.

Deployment since the Line: fourteen.

He slept a little toward morning. When Brom woke him the stars were going out, and the frost lay so thick on the old road that it showed like a chalk line all the way down to the floor. Seln was coming back along the ruts from the north, and he shook his head at them from thirty yards away.

They ate cold. Brom put his boot into the stirrup of a healer's bow, and set the hook on the string, and straightened his back; the string came up the stock and dropped behind its catch, and he laid one of the five bolts in the groove. Karis had her lamp and her notebook and a flask, and Lira drew the knot of her sling tight with her teeth.

Then Seln stepped over the stone.

Chapter 49 — Forty Steps

[Building, spatially clear narration; sustain the Stair's danger without rushing its decisions]

A hawk over that place at first light on the hundred and fourteenth day would have seen three rings, one inside another, and a line drawn across them.

The outermost was the carters' road, two pale ruts going the whole way round the low ground. Forty paces inside it lay the edge that could not be seen, where a grey stone sat on the turf between two iron bars. And in the middle, two hundred and twenty yards from the stone, was the floor, as round as a coin, with a square hole at its centre no bigger than a cart. The line across all three was the old road. It came down off the ridge from the east, over the brow where the ruts turned aside, between the two bars, and straight on down the frosted grass to the floor's edge.

Six people stood at the stone. The sun was coming up behind them over the ridge, and their shadows went before them down the old road.

Seln was already over. He walked as he walked every approach, without haste, with his hands a little away from his sides and the strap of a locked case across his chest. When he had gone ten yards he lifted two fingers, and Lira stepped over the stone after him, on the whole sole of the great boot.

"Gone," said Karis, ten yards behind Lira.

She said it quite quietly, at the stride. She had crossed such an edge more often than any of them, and she had told Cael at the fire that she did not expect ever to grow used to it; but she did not break her pace.

He went fourth. He felt the turf under his boots and the cold on his face, and nothing else whatever; the place behind his breastbone was as dark on the far side of that stone as on the near. The ten things that he carried lay as they had lain. He had made up his mind in the night that he would ask none of them for anything this morning unless the roof fell in, and he walked down the old road ten yards behind a small straight back with his hands empty.

Brom came last. Cael heard him grunt at the stride, as he had grunted on the Fallow, like a man who has felt a door shut behind him. The healer's bow was on his left shoulder, spanned, with a bolt lying in its groove.

The healer herself had not moved; he glanced round once and saw her, square and brown against the sunrise, with her sleeves pushed up to the elbow and two mules and three boxes on the slope behind her.

He was facing the floor again when he heard the sound.

It was not loud: a short dull knock, like a mallet on a wet post, and after it a hiss of breath between somebody's teeth.

He turned.

Brom was five yards inside the stone, where he had taken one step that he had not meant to take, and he was standing very upright, with his head a little on one side, as he stood when Karis told him something that he could not at once believe. A hand's length of ash wood stood out behind his right shoulder, with three grey feathers on it.

"Ridge," he said.

Cael looked up the old road, into the sun, and had to put his hand over his eyes. On the brow, where the ruts turned north, there was a shape standing that had not been there when Seln walked the ruts in the dark. It stood forty paces above the stone. There was a second shape beside it.

Forty paces to the stone, and five yards beyond: that made forty-five. He knew that distance, since he had walked a mile once in front of a cart with a grey thing keeping it behind him in the grass, patiently, waiting upon a signal.

"Back," said Seln's voice, from far down the road.

It was the word, and all four of them came round to it as they had agreed. But the healer had not waited for a word. She was over the stone already, running, with her coat flying out behind her; she had seen a man hit five yards from where her hands worked, and she had come to fetch him out.

Cael ran too, and he was thinking as he ran.

Something was wrong with that shot, and though he had only fifteen yards to cover, it took him the whole of them to say what. A bow on that brow could have let all five of them walk down to the floor, and had them two hundred yards inside, with nothing over them and nowhere to go. It had chosen to shoot the last man instead, when he was five strides from the way out, with a healer standing in plain sight at the door.

A shot of that kind did not want them to go on. It wanted them to turn round, or it wanted somebody to come in.

He was twelve feet from the stone when he made up his mind. He had refused Anchor, the thinnest of his ten, at these two irons the evening before, and again in the frost an hour ago. He let it look now, on purpose, with his eyes open; and since he had stopped dead to do it, he stood on a frozen road for the length of two counts while a friend with a bolt in him was being turned about by the arm.

At twelve feet there was a greyness in the air between the bars, like breath. He took one stride more, and it was there.

Three lines were going across the old road.

They came from the old iron, on the north side, and they went to the newer one, eight feet away, at the height of a knee and a chest and a hand above a tall man's head. He saw them arrive, and they did not creep; they swung across as a gate swings to, all three together, and caught on the newer bar, and ran on past it to the south until they were beyond his seeing. On the north side they ran away from the old iron along the turf in the same three courses, and went out of his sight in that direction too.

He had seen such things once before, in a chalk cut on the Ostrand road, and he knew the craft as he knew his own handwriting. A point was set against a surface and told to stay, and a line was drawn from it to the next.

But these were not hers.

The woman in the cut had laid nineteen points round him while he fought her, each as fine as a fishing line, from fifteen feet, with the stillness of a person threading a needle. Whoever had laid these was forty paces off. And they were thick: every one was as thick as his wrist, and there were three where she would have used thirty. It was the same trade in a different hand, as a ship's cable and a stitch are the same trade: this hand threw.

"Stop," he said. "It's shut."

The healer did not so much as turn her head. She had Brom's left arm across her shoulders and she was bringing him up the road toward the stone at a stumbling run, with her eyes on the grey wool of his coat where a dark stain was beginning. She had three strides to go, and Cael saw her thinking of nothing in the world but those three strides, at the end of which she would be a Tide again.

"Oryn. Stop."

She walked into it.

Her right shoulder met the middle course exactly as a shoulder meets a door that somebody has shut in the dark. She stopped as if she had been struck. Brom's weight came on past her, and his chest found it, and he made a sound that Cael did not wish to hear again; and the two of them stood swaying against nothing at all, a yard short of a grey stone, with the sun in their faces.

She put up her free hand. She laid the palm of it on the air, at the height of her eyes, and pressed.

Then she looked at the hand.

"Four," she said. Her lips had been moving. "I can't get past four."

"There's a fence across it. From that bar to that one, and on round. You can't see it. I can." He had her by the elbow. "It wasn't there when you came over. It went up behind you."

She understood him. He saw her understand all of it at once, as she understood a break under her hands: the bolt, and where it had been put, and for whom. Her face did not change. She shifted Brom's arm higher on her shoulder.

"That was for me, then," said Oryn. "That bolt."

Seln was beside them, having come back up forty yards of road without a sound, and Lira and Karis were behind him.

"They are standing up," he said.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Cael turned on his heel, slowly, all the way round, and counted what the morning had on its rim.

There were two on the brow to the east, where the old road came over. One had a crossbow, with its nose on the ground and his boot in the stirrup; he was drawing the string with a hook, steadily, like a man doing a thing that he had done ten thousand times. The other stood two yards south of him and had nothing in his hands at all, and his arms were coming down to his sides.

There were two on the southern rim, a quarter of the way round. They had risen out of the white grass behind the ruts while he was looking at the brow. One of them was kneeling over a bow, and the other only stood, a little apart, with his arms folded.

There was one on the west, a long way off beyond the floor, so small that Cael could tell only that it was upright and that it held something across its body.

And there was one on the north, kneeling.

That made six, and four of them had bows. Every one was the grey of the road in a dry month. They wore hoods, and under each hood there was a cloth drawn up across the face, of the kind that carters wore against dust. Not one of them had called out, or so much as lifted a hand to another. They stood at four stations round five hundred yards of grass, outside an edge that none of them had needed a stone to find, and they looked down.

"Six, and four bows," said Seln. "I walked past every one of those places twice."

"Can we rush the two?" said Brom. He was grey round the mouth, and his voice was quite steady. "It's forty yards."

"Through that?"

Brom looked at the air in front of his chest.

Nine fragments had come up in Cael at once.

He had not called them. They had risen as they had risen in a lane on the Fallow, each offering what it had. Wind was in his feet, and though it could not take him through three courses of that fence, it could take him a long way along the inside of it, faster than a hooded man could run round the ruts. Storm, the heaviest of them, lay ready; there was a rut at his feet, running straight up the hill to the brow, with seed on the grass at either lip. Ember had fire for his hand, and there was a great deal that a boy could do from where he stood, in a place where four of his friends could do nothing.

And six pairs of eyes were on him, from four sides.

Nothing that a pair of eyes could carry to a boat.

He held them. He stood on a frozen road, with a bolt in Brom's shoulder and a healer staring at her own hand, and refused nine things one after another in the only country on the continent where every one of them would have answered. He had done as much once before, on a white floor, with a girl's arm in a hound's mouth. It was no lighter. Seln had told him that it would not be.

Lira was looking at him.

She had seen it on the Fallow from a foot away, and she saw it now from three yards. He watched her know what he was doing, and why, and what it was going to cost somebody before the day was out. Then her eyes left his face, and went up to the brow, where a man had got his string behind its catch and was reaching to his belt for a bolt. They went south, and west, and north, right round, in the time of one breath.

"He's nearly spanned," she said. "And there's not a yard of this grass that one of them can't see."

Her gaze had come down the old road to the floor, and stopped.

"There's one place."

She did not wait to be answered. She stepped in close under Brom's good arm, and with her right hand she lifted the healer's bow off his left shoulder by its stock, spanned as it was, with the bolt held in the groove under her thumb.

"I can't span it," she said to him. "I can carry it."

Then she ran.

She ran down. She went away from the stone, and from the two mules, and from the only ground on which a Path would answer, straight down the middle of the old road toward a bare grey floor with a hole in it. She ran on the whole of her foot, slapping, like a child in its father's boots; a healer had told her four days ago that a certain bone was her own again, and she was using it.

"After her," said Seln.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

They went as a unit, since they had been one for a long time.

Karis was away first, with her coat held up in both fists. Brom ran. A bolt in the shoulder is not a bolt in the leg, and he went down that road like a bullock, with the feathers of the bolt nodding at his shoulder and the healer at his left hand, matching him stride for stride with her fingers hooked in his belt. Seln ran a yard to his right. Cael came last, since somebody must, and since if any of them fell he wished to be the one who saw it.

It was a hundred and ninety yards of grass. He had paced none of it, and he measured it now with his lungs.

At sixty the bolt came.

He heard that one. It went over his right shoulder with a sound like cloth tearing, and he saw it strike, far ahead, on the grey of the floor between Karis and Seln. It did not stick. It skipped, as a flat stone skips on a pond, and went skating away across the plate with its feathers spinning.

"Two," said Seln, running. He had not turned his head. "Both from the gate."

Lira was on the floor. She had not slowed, and her boots made no sound on it at all.

Two more came out of the sky.

They were not aimed, or not as the first had been. Cael saw them only when they were falling, two dark strokes dropping steeply from the north and from the south. They had been lofted from better than two hundred and fifty yards by people who knew to a hair how far their bows would throw. One struck the plate ten feet from Brom and leapt up again, end over end, and the other came down beyond the hole and slid.

"Three. Four."

He was on the floor himself then. It was as cold through his boots as the other had been, and as silent, and thirty yards of it had never seemed so far. The hole was in front of him. It was two strides square, with an edge as sharp as a box's; and on its near side a step went down, and another, and a third, each of them white with frost and sunlight.

Lira's head was already below the floor. Karis went in after her. Brom took the first step sideways, with the healer under his arm, and the dark had them.

Cael looked back from the lip, since he was the last, and since it was his to know.

The six had not moved from their stations. On the brow a man was setting his boot in a stirrup for the third time. Nobody was running down the slope, and nobody was shouting. They had watched six people go into a hole in the ground, and it seemed that this was a thing that they had expected to see.

He went down.

Blade, in his right arm, which had come to him from a friend's sword, asked its one word at the first step, where the stone turned a sharp corner under his heel. Edge? He told it no, and it asked at the second. He counted the steps by its asking, since he could count them no other way. Below the third the light stopped as if it had been cut off with a knife, and he was going down into black by the feel of a wall on his left hand, at a run, behind the sound of other people's boots.

Eighteen. Nineteen.

Somebody cried out below him.

It was Lira's voice, and it was cut short. There was a scrape, and a thud of something soft against stone, and then her breath, loud and ragged in the dark.

"Keep on," she said, between her teeth. "I've got it. I've got the bow. Keep on."

Twenty. The air changed at that step, as if he had gone through a door; he had no time to learn how, and went down through it with the edges asking under his feet.

At the fortieth there was no forty-first. His boot came down on the level, and he walked into Seln's back.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

"Stand where you are," said Seln's voice, close to his ear. "All of you. I am striking a light."

There was a scrape of steel, and a spark, and another. Karis's breath went in and out somewhere to the left. Cael knew what she was doing as well as if he had seen her. She had put out her hand in the dark to set a point on her own wick, as she had done every night of her life since she was fourteen; and there was no hand to reach with.

The tinder caught. Seln held it to the lamp, and the small brass thing took the flame and steadied. Nobody had spoken since the fortieth step, and the only sound in that place was six people getting their breath.

It showed them a room.

It was square, and Cael put it at ten strides each way. The floor was the same grey, level and seamless. So was the roof. He looked up, and it took him a breath to understand what he was looking at: the roof of that room was the underside of the floor that they had run across. There was no beam in it and no arch; it lay over them like a lid, and he judged it a foot above Brom's head.

The walls were cut.

Karis made a sound in her throat. From the floor to the roof, on all four sides, the grey was covered with the fine sunk lines that had been round the feet of eleven stones on the Fallow: straight, and hooked, and crossing. They ran in bands, one above another, each as tall as a man's forearm. There was more of it on one wall of that room than on the whole of the other place.

And in the middle of the floor, where the lamp only just reached, something lay.

It was a dark oblong, the length of a man's arm, and it had a look of leather or tarred cloth about it, as a case has. From one end of it a pale line ran out along the floor toward the wall that they had come in by, and stopped.

"A cord," said Brom thickly.

"Nobody goes near that," said Seln.

He had spoken more sharply than Cael had ever heard him.

"It is what the paper says we were sent for. Six people brought us to this room this morning by a road that they had prepared, and that is lying in the middle of it. It has lain there a good while, by the dust. It will lie there until I have read the floor round it, with more oil than we have." He took the lamp out of Karis's hand and gave it to the healer. "That is for him. Use it."

He went back to the doorway.

It was a plain square opening in the wall, the width of the stair. Seln stood in it with his back to the room and looked up forty steps at a small square of blue.

"They can shoot the bowl," he said.

He was speaking to himself, as a man does who is taking an inventory. He put his hand on the stone of the door's edge, and then on the wall of the stair, and measured something with his eye.

"They can't shoot the stair."

"Why not?" said Lira. She was sitting on the lowest step with the bow across her knees and her left side turned away from the light.

"They are two hundred and sixty yards from that hole, on every side, and very little above it. A bolt that comes in at the top must come in nearly level. It strikes the wall or the upper steps." Seln turned round. "From the rim, nobody can see into this. Nobody can see so much as the fourth step. And anybody who comes to the edge of the hole to look down is a black shape on a bright square, to a person sitting where you are sitting, with that."

Lira looked at the bow.

"I've one in the groove," she said. "There's four more in the sleeve on his belt, and I can't span it."

"I can span it. I trust that I shall not need to." He took the leather sleeve from Brom's belt as he spoke, and laid it on the step beside her. "Go up six. Sit so that you can see the square and it cannot see you. If anything stands in it, do as the man on the gate-walk taught you."

"Shooting's stopping," said Lira.

She got up, with her jaw shut, and climbed six steps on her whole foot, and sat down again with the stock laid along her right knee. That was the thirty-fourth, counting from the top. Cael saw her set her boot on the step below, heel and toe together, and let her breath go out.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The healer had Brom on the floor by then, with his back against the wall beside the door.

She had cut his coat away from the shoulder with Seln's knife. Karis held the lamp where she was told. In its light the thing was plain enough, and Cael made himself look at it, since it was his crew's: the bolt had gone in behind, a hand below the top of the shoulder, and its iron head stood out in front, under the collar-bone, by the length of a thumb. There was not much blood. What there was came slowly.

Oryn put her two hands round the shoulder, above the wood and below it, and shut her eyes.

Her lips moved. They stopped. She opened her eyes and took her hands away, and for the length of one breath she looked at them as she had looked at them on the road, in front of nothing.

"No," she said, to the hands. "Well. I knew that."

Then she became somebody else, as Cael had seen her do once before, at the rim of a white floor, with a strip of her own shirt in her teeth. She took the lamp from Karis and held it close, and looked at the wound from in front and from behind, for a long time, without touching it. She laid two fingers on the inside of Brom's left wrist and counted, with her lips, to a good deal more than ten, and put her ear to his back.

"Breathe in. All the way. Does it catch?"

"No."

"Cough."

He coughed, and went greyer.

"Shut your hand. That one. Now open it." She watched the four dark lines go across and come back. "Is it cold? Can you feel me pinch?"

"I can feel you pinch."

She sat back on her heels.

"I can see what's wrong. I can't feel it and I can't touch it. Tape it. Leave the bolt."

"You'll not draw it?" said Seln, from the door.

"It's high. It's missed the lung and it's missed the big vessel, or he'd not be talking. Leave it in, because the bolt's the plug. When my hands work again I'll take it out and close what it opened. Not before."

"Tape," said Lira's voice, from up the stair. A small hard roll came down the steps, one at a time, and lay on the floor in the light. "It's what I've left from the ankle. It's hers anyway."

Oryn had it in her hands before it stopped rolling. She laid the first strip round the shaft in front, close, and the second behind; she did it by lamp and by eye, as a carter's wife would have done it, and it took her a quarter of the time that it would have taken anybody else in that room. When she had done she pulled what was left of his coat across.

"You'll sit there. You'll not lean on it, and you'll not be brave." She wiped her fingers on her breeches. "I said in a loft that somebody ought to stand outside one of these with her sleeves up. I was outside. I'd my sleeves up. And I'm in here with a roll of tape, and that's a clean wound that I could shut in an hour on the far side of a rock." Her voice was low and quite even. "I came south for exactly this. Enter that."

"It's entered," said Cael.

"I know that it is. I wanted to hear myself say it."

She stood up with the lamp, and turned, and held it toward the stair.

"There's nothing," said Lira.

"There's a sleeve on that sling that was grey this morning."

For a breath there was no answer. Then Lira came down the six steps, slowly, and into the light; and the wool across her breast was dark and wet from the elbow to the wrist.

"It was the twentieth step," she said. She was looking at the wall above the healer's head. "The ankle went. I'd the bow in my right hand, so I'd nothing to put out. And then it was out. I never told it to. It hit the wall, and it took me, the whole of me, and I stood up off it."

Not one of them repeated what she had been told about that arm, since they all knew it, and so did she.

The healer undid her own knot and drew the wool down, and two of the eight small marks had opened, the lowest of each row, and were bleeding steadily.

"The rest have held," she said, after a long look. "It's not gone through. It's opened where it was newest." She was already tearing a strip from the tail of Cael's shirt, which he had held out to her. "I can't shut that either. I can bind it, and I can tie it higher, and you can keep it against your chest until there's a sky over us."

She bound it. She tied the sling again, shorter, so that the hand lay almost at the collar-bone.

"Back up your six steps," said Oryn. "And if you put that arm out for anything again, I'll take the other one off you myself."

"Yes."

When Lira's boots had stopped on the stair, the healer looked into the lamp. It had held a finger and a half of oil when Seln lit it. There was a finger now.

She blew it out.

The dark came down on them like a cloth. Far up, at the head of forty steps, there was a small square of sky. Two of the six under that lid were bleeding, and it was not yet the middle of the forenoon.

Chapter 50 — The Square of Grey

[Building, spatially clear narration; sustain the Stair's danger without rushing its decisions]

They had the day in that room by the colour of one small square.

It stood at the head of forty steps, a man's height on each side; for the first hours after the lamp went out it was grey, and everything else was black. Cael learned the room by its sounds.

Lira sat on the thirty-fourth step, six above the floor, with the bow along her knee, and Seln stood below her in the doorway at the stair's foot. Brom was on the ground against the wall to the north of that doorway, with three coats on him, and the healer sat on her heels at his left hand. Karis had put her back against the wall opposite; and in the middle of the floor, where nobody went, a case lay in the dark with its cord.

That was six below, and there were six above; he had Seln's word for it every hour.

Seln went up for them himself. He climbed to the fifth step from the top and no higher, and lay along the stair with his chin on the stone, so that his eyes came level with the floor outside and nothing else of him did. From there, he said, the rim stood all round against the sky like the edge of a dish, and he counted what was on it. Then he came down, without a sound, and said it to the room in his mild voice.

"Six. Two at the gate, two south, one west, one north. None has left his place."

"What are they doing?" said Brom, the first time.

"The one at the gate with the bow is doing what you would do. He is finding his range."

They heard it for themselves before he had finished speaking.

It was a small hard tick on the roof over their heads, like a pebble dropped on a lid, and after it a long dry skittering that went away across the stone. Karis drew her breath in, and nobody spoke until it had stopped.

"That is five," said Seln. "He means to learn whether he can put one into that hole from where he stands. The stair runs down to the west, and he is to the east of it and a little above. He is the only one of the four who could."

"Can he?" said Lira, from the stair.

"I should say that it will take him some time."

It took him the better part of the forenoon. He did not hurry. A tick came, and a skittering, and then nothing for as long as it takes to walk a quarter of a mile; and then another. Some fell short and rang on the far side of the roof, and one struck so near the hole that they heard it skate past the lip.

"Six. Seven. Eight," said Seln, at intervals, from the doorway. He might have been reading out a floor schedule. "Nine. Ten. Eleven."

The square had gone from grey to white. It was near noon, and bright up there, and a little of the brightness came down as far as the tenth step and lay on it like spilt milk.

Then there was a sound that was not on the roof.

It was in the stair. It began high up, a crack and a rattle, and it came down toward them very fast, striking one edge and the next, like a stick drawn along a fence. Cael heard Lira's breath stop, and he heard the thing leap, and strike, and slide.

It stopped.

For the length of three breaths nobody moved. Then Lira spoke, and her voice was quite level.

The white lasted a long time, and they filled it with small things, since there was nothing else to fill it with.

There was the water, of which they had five flasks among six, since the healer had come over a stone at a run with nothing in her hands; and Brom, who could not lift his right arm, had them all set down in front of him in the dark and shook each of them at his ear.

The square was going grey when he had it.

He had been at it since the morning, as he went at anything: a thing at a time, from the beginning, leaving nothing out. He did not have an answer. But he could state the whole of the question, and he had learned at a healer's table that this was most of the way.

He went up thirty steps on his own feet, like anybody.

At the fourth from the top he stopped. The square was over his head, and it was the colour of slate; he could see one star in it. Below him the stair went down into black, and he knew that a girl with one arm was looking up it at his back. He knew that Seln had turned round in the doorway and was facing the room, which was his way of saying that he had seen the thing before and did not need to see it again. The cold began at fifty.

He had been waiting for it. A thing made for hiding costs from the moment that a person wakes; he had paid that on every day since it came to him, by carrying it shut. To have it open was a different bill. It began in the ends of his fingers, as it had begun in a lane on the Fallow, and it was not the frost, since it came from inside. It made no sound, since nothing that he did made any sound. But he stood for ten breaths with his heart going, and his eyes in the ground again, and gave the read back to the turf before he took another step.

At a hundred and fifty there was a noise that nearly stopped that heart altogether.

It was the grey mule. She was hobbled above the stone with the brown one, and she had put up her head and brayed at the dusk, long and rusty, as she had no doubt brayed at every dusk of her life. The brown mule did not bray. She had turned her ears, both together, down the old road. She was looking straight at the place where he stood.

On the brow, the sitting shape turned its hood toward the two beasts.

Cael walked on, and he could not feel his arms below the elbow.

At fourteen feet from the newer bar there was nothing.

He had known that there would not be. He could see the iron itself, a dark stroke above the frosted turf, and the grey stone beyond it; and the air between that bar and its fellow was as empty as any air. He took a stride, and another, and let Anchor look.

At twelve feet there was the greyness, like breath on glass. At ten, they were there.

There were three courses across the old road, at the knee and the chest and over the head, exactly as he had seen them thrown in the morning; they were as thick as his wrist, and they had not slackened in a day. He went along them with that other sight to the newer bar, where he had watched them arrive, and looked for the place where they were made fast.

It was not there.

He stood in a ditch with the cold in his elbows and looked again. The three courses came to the newer bar and touched it, and there was a point where each of them met the iron; but they did not end. They went through those points as a rope goes through a ring, and on, southward along the edge, out of his sight.

He had got it wrong. He had watched three lines fly across a road toward a bar, and had taken the bar for the end of them. A rope is not made fast where it lands; it is made fast where the hauling starts.

He turned his head, slowly, to the north.

The old bar stood eight feet away across the grown-over road, under its five cold terms of rust. It was there.

It was on the far side of the iron, the side toward the brow, a hand above the turf, and he saw it through the bar, as a person sees a lamp through his own fingers. It was a single point, as big as a fist. Three courses came into it from the south, across the road; and three came into it from the north, round the whole of that great circle, the other end of the same rope. Nothing came out. Everything that held six people in a low place on the hundred and fourteenth day was hauled taut through that one point and belayed there, like the whole of a ship's rigging brought down to a single pin.

He could see it. He had been able to see a line across a doorway once, with a girl's shoulder pressed against it, and it had done him no good whatever.

He lay down in the rut on his left side, with the bar at the length of his arm. It was against him now, as the first had been against his coat; and he was inside what it held.

A thing set against a surface and told to stay.

He told it not to.

He had not known how much ground it held until it stopped holding.

Forty paces above him, on the brow, a standing shape flung both its arms forward out of its sleeves, as a man does when a rope is dragged through his hands.

He let Shadow go while he lay in the ditch, with his arm still round a bar of the registry's iron.

It went out of him as it had come. The sound of his own breath returned, loud and ragged, and after it the creak of frozen grass under his hip and the grey mule shifting her feet above the stone. The two on the brow were on their feet; the one with the bow had it up across his chest, spanned, and the other was holding his own hands out before him and looking into them.

Cael stepped out of the rut and walked across the edge, between the old bar and the stone.

He had priced this on the stair. There was one bolt in that groove, and when it was gone, a boot must go into a stirrup and a hook onto a string, and a back must straighten; he had watched that man do it once, from a frozen road, and it had taken him something over twenty counts. He had been told on a bluff never to spend the Wind near a thing whose single blow he could not price. He could price this one to a hair.

For ten counts after a lane, everything that he had came to him a beat late.

He had run up a ditch on the Fallow in that lag, with hounds behind him, and he knew it; but he had not known what it was to close with a man in it. His boots struck the turf, and then he was told that they had struck. The brow came up to meet him. He saw the stock begin to move. Then he saw where it was, which was a good deal nearer.

It was coming round at his head like a flail. He got his right arm up. It was a dead arm, and it was late, and for the first beat nothing in him answered at all; a pound of ash wood and horn met the bone of his forearm with the whole of a strong man's swing behind it. His knees began to go.

Then Compression, which a fighter had put through him on a circuit, long ago, arrived and did what it was for.

There was only one road open to it. The blow went down the bone into his shoulder, and down his spine, and through both his heels into the hill; and the hill took it. The stock stopped against his arm as it would have stopped against a gatepost. He felt it ring from the wrist to the elbow, and he knew that he would be paying for that for a week.

The hooded man had both his hands stung off the bow. It fell between them.

Cael did not strike him. He could have; the man stood open, a yard off, with his cloth blown half across his hood and grass-seed in the folds of it, and there was nothing in that hood that Cael could have sworn to afterward but that it was the height of a person. He looked at it for the length of one late breath, and turned away from it, to the south.

The other stood two yards off.

He had not run, and he had not reached for anything, since he carried nothing to reach for. He stood with his feet apart on the trodden ruts, and both hands held out before his chest, bare, with the palms turned toward Cael and the fingers a little spread. They were quite still.

Cael knew that stillness. He had knelt under it once in a chalk cut, and it was the stillness of threading a needle. In another breath there would be something set against the front of his coat, and told to stay.

He did not let Anchor look. He had no need to; he had the hands.

They were a man's hands, broad, and short in the finger. That was all that he was ever to know of their owner. There was a pale band round the third finger of the left, where a ring had been taken off before the work began.

His own left hand had found his knife. He could not feel the hilt. He drew it, and held it out at the full length of his arm, with the point a hand's breadth under those two open palms; and he asked Ember for the one thing that it had.

A point of fire stood on the knife's tip.

It was no bigger than a candle's. It lit the palms from beneath, and the grey cuffs, and nothing above them. He held it there. He said no word, and he did not move the blade nearer by the width of a hair.

A person cannot thread a needle with a flame under his hands.

He saw the fingers want to. He saw them hold their stillness for one breath, and for a second, with the heat coming up into them. Then they closed, slowly, and the hands drew back, and went down to the man's sides.

The man took one step backward. He took another. He did not turn his hood away from the flame until he was five yards off; and Cael did not follow him by a single stride.

It was the bowman who ended it. He had got the chaff out of his cloth, and he bent, without haste, and took up the bow from the turf. He did something to the lock of it with his thumb, and a small dark thing like a walnut came away into his palm and went into his coat. He drew a short knife across the string, and then he laid the bow down again in the ruts, carefully, on its side, as a workman lays down a tool that was only lent him.

The two of them went north along the carters' road, side by side, at a trot. They did not run until they were sixty yards off.

Cael turned to the low ground, and lifted the knife over his head.

The lag had gone out of him. He stood on the brow in the last of the dusk, with a point of fire at the end of his arm where anybody on that rim could see it, and he looked for the other four.

To the south there were two shapes still. One of them, the one that had stood all day with its arms folded, raised a single arm above its hood and let it fall. Then both stooped, and straightened, and went away over the rim to the south, with nothing in their hands.

When he looked to the north, there was nobody there at all.

The west was the last. The sky there was green yet, low down, and the rim stood against it as black as a cut edge. A small upright shape had stood on that edge since first light and had never once loosed. It bent now, and laid something down. It walked away; and at the top of the rim, where another step would have taken it out of his sight, it stopped, and turned itself round, and looked back across five hundred yards of grass at a boy with a light.

He saw the hood against the sky. There was the shape of it, and the shoulders under it, and inside it there was nothing whatever. Then that was gone too.

Six. He counted them off that rim as Seln had counted them onto it. He let the fire go out, and walked down forty paces to the grey stone, and called one word down the old road into the dark.

"Back."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

They came up out of the low ground in file, as they had gone down.

He heard them long before he saw them. There was no need for quiet now. Brom's breathing came first, heavy and careful, and then a shuffle of boots on frozen turf; and at last five shapes grew out of the dusk on the old road, with a small one in front that made no sound at all.

Seln stepped over the stone, and stood a breath on the outside of it. Cael saw his shoulders come down by the width of a finger, as a man's do when a Path that he has done without all day is handed back to him.

Karis was next, and she had said that she would never grow used to it. She crossed, and stopped, and put out her right hand in front of her in the dark. A point of light stood on the air above her palm, as small and steady as a star.

"I have a hand," she said, to nobody. Her voice shook. "I have a hand again."

She set the point on the wick of her lamp.

The healer came over between two of them, with Brom's good arm across her shoulders and his weight on her. She took one stride past the stone. She stopped dead, with her eyes shut and her lips moving, and her free hand closed on Brom's wrist.

The count went to four, and on, and did not stop.

"There. Back," she said. It came out of her on one breath, hoarse, as a person speaks who has been holding it since the morning. She opened her eyes and looked at her own left hand in the lamplight, back and palm. "The clock started again."

Then she was a healer.

"Down. Here, on the blanket, on your left side. You, bring that light and hold it where I point. You, the pannier, the one that's on the grey." She had Brom on the turf before any of them had moved. "And somebody give me a knife that'll cut ash."

It was Seln's. She had him kneel behind Brom's shoulder and cut through the shaft below the iron head, a notch at a time, while she held the wood still in both her fists so that it should not turn. It took as long as it takes to say a line over twice; then the head came away, and she threw it on the grass, and put one hand flat on the front of the shoulder and took hold of the feathered end with the other.

"Breathe out," she said. "All of it. I'll not lie to you; you'll know that it's leaving."

She drew the shaft back out the way that it had come, in one pull.

Brom made no sound that could be heard at ten yards. His boots moved on the turf. Her two hands were round the shoulder before the wood was clear, one above the place and one below; her eyes shut; and Cael, who had sat all day in a stone room and heard her count that man's heart with two fingers, saw her lips reach three and stop counting, since she had what she wanted.

It was an hour, by the stars. Lira held the lamp for all of it with her one hand, sitting on the grey stone, and did not once let the light shake.

"That's one," said Oryn at the end of it. She sat back on her heels. Her face was the colour of the frost. "It's shut. It went through the meat and missed everything that matters, and you were born lucky. You'll carry nothing on that side till I've said so."

"I've another side," said Brom.

"I've seen it. Be quiet." She turned on her knees. "You. Give me that arm, and give me the lamp to somebody else."

Lira gave the lamp to Karis. She held out the sling without a word, and the healer undid her own knot, and unwound a strip of Cael's shirt that had gone stiff and dark, and put her two hands round the forearm.

It took a quarter of an hour. When she had finished she did not let go of the wrist at once.

"It held a stair. It's not going to hold anything else this season."

"It did hold it," said Lira. Her voice was small. "I'd have gone down the other twenty on my head."

"I know that it held. I felt where. I'm not scolding the arm." Oryn drew the wool up and tied it, shorter than before, so that the hand lay high against the collar-bone. "That's two, on a road, after three at a bench yesterday. There isn't a third in me tonight for anybody, and I'd thank you all to stay whole till morning."

He paid the rest of his own bill sitting against the old iron, with his knees drawn up.

It came all at once, as it had come at the stone on the Fallow. Across his left palm there was a white weal as long as a finger. He had held a knife with a flame on its point in a hand too cold to know that the hilt was hot, and he had found it out only when he tried to open that hand again. He could not stop shaking. He had had a week of barley sacks and tables to rest in, and he had spent the whole of what it gave him between a stair and a brow, in less time than a kettle takes.

The healer looked at the palm from her stride and a half.

"I can't touch that. You know why." She threw him what was left of Lira's tape. "Wind it round, and keep it out of the frost. It'll close faster than it ought to. Yours always do."

Seln had gone to the mules.

He went round the three boxes under their blanket with the lamp held low, and stooped over each cord in turn, and touched nothing. When he came back his face was as it had been all day.

"I tied those to be read. There is a stem of grass laid under every knot, and each is where I laid it." He set the lamp down. "Six people with a quarter of a mile of rim apiece do not leave it to look into a mule's load."

"What did they see?" said Cael. "Tell me as you'd write it for them."

"A fence that failed at dusk, at its knot, which was set on an iron bar that stands upon the very edge of the place; and directly afterward a boy, who stood up out of the old road beside that bar and declared. Nobody on that rim saw anything between the stair and the bar. I asked Lira what she saw from the thirty-fourth step, and she says that she saw a stair. They will write that he crept up a rut in bad light while they were watching a hole, and that a knot tied a hand's breadth from such an edge is a knot which nobody should have trusted. A man who lays fences for his living would far sooner put that on paper than the other thing, and he has no cause to think of the other thing at all. It holds."

He turned, and went up the old road to the brow by himself.

When he came down he had a crossbow in his hands.

He brought it into the lamplight and turned it over, slowly, as he turned over any paper. It was a good bow, heavier than the healer's, with a prod of horn and sinew, and its string hung cut from one end. He ran his thumb along the underside of the stock, and under the stirrup, and across the butt.

"There was a maker's stamp here. It has been taken off with a file, and the place oiled. There is no armoury number. It was bought for one day, by somebody who meant from the first to leave it lying." His voice had not risen. Cael had never heard it so quiet. "I walked past the place where that man lay, twice. I have sat in a hole since sunrise with his bolt on the stair. I have his bow. And I could not tell you tonight whether he was tall."

He took the thing by its two ends.

Cael had known him for two years. He had seen him carve a goat, and wax a seal, and stand in a doorway with his back to a room, and he had never seen him do a thing in anger. Seln lifted the crossbow over his head and brought it down across the grey stone with the whole of his narrow strength, and the stock broke in two at the lock. He stood over it, breathing.

"No faces."

He laid the two pieces on the turf, side by side, and went and sat down by the mules.

Cael opened Hesk's book on his knee. Lira had put it into his lap when she came over the stone, with the strap done up, and had said nothing; and he held the pencil in his bandaged left hand, since the right would not close.

Hundred and fourteenth day, night. Outside the stone. All six out. Brom: a bolt through the right shoulder, drawn and mended, an hour. Lira: the arm opened on the stair wall and is shut again, a quarter. Thirteen bolts loosed at us in the day, and one hit. Ours: five, and none shot.

He ruled a line, and put down what he had spent, one thing to a line, as he had on the Fallow.

Anchor: looking, at the two bars, first light. I saw the fence go up. I stood two counts to see it, and Brom had those two counts with a bolt in him.

Shadow: once, from the fourth step to the old bar. Lira saw it go, from below. Seln turned his back. Three were round the door. The six were two hundred and sixty yards off, with a lip between; not one had a line to me. Let go in the rut. It holds. Dead to the elbows; I had to watch my own hand.

The read: the ground, from the hole to the bar. All my eyes. I looked up once, and it left me.

Anchor: the unbinding. Hand on it, from inside. Once.

Wind: one burst, off the stone. The lock.

Storm: one lane, up the old rut. Ten counts late.

Compression: in those ten. The right arm.

Nine. With the reading on the road, ten since Thornwater. Deployment since the Line: twenty-three.

He looked at that for a little. Then he wrote the rest beneath, as he had it.

Second nameless team. Same hand. I own a piece of the first one and I used it on the second. The account's still unpayable. It's getting longer.

The light came down the old road when it was full dark.

It was a lantern, and it was carried high, at the length of somebody's arm, as a person carries one who wishes it understood from a long way off that he is not creeping. Seln was on his feet before Cael had seen it. Lira had the bow across her knee.

"Four," said Seln, presently. "One with a spear. One who favours a leg."

They came over the brow in file, a crew's length apart, and the man in front stopped where the ruts turned, beside a thing that lay on the turf there. He held the lantern over it. Then he came on down, alone, and the three behind him stood where they were.

He was of the middle height, and heavy in the forearm, and there was a band of black leather laced on his right wrist. "You're late back," said Teague.

"We were kept."

"I saw some of it. We were on the ridge when the light went." He set the lantern down on the turf between them. "I'll say what I saw, so that you've no need to wonder what I'm carrying. "Yes."

Teague's eyes did not leave him, and Cael waited for the rest of it: how, and with what, and what a boy was who had a Wind's crack in him and a fire as well. He watched the man weigh each of those and set it down again, as he had set down a question at an inn's door two nights before.

"Then you're not on the board anymore. You're something the board doesn't have a column for."

It was the second time in three days that Cael had been told so. A one-armed man had said it of a line in a book. This man said it of him, to his face, across a lantern, with no heat in it and no fear; he might have been reading out the weight of a load.

"I've three with me, and a light," said Teague. "They'll want that rim walked before any of you sleeps. I'll have it walked."

He took up his lantern, and went back up the old road to where his three were standing.

It had been the hundred and thirteenth morning, a day and a half before, when Teague took a slip that he did not want.

He had been at the plank before the mist was off the river. The five had gone by it in the dark, two hours earlier, and he had heard the mule. Pike was setting out his book; and there was a shingle on the oak, six along from the left-hand post, which had hung there for nine days because no crew of any standing would trouble with it.

Millrace. Three stakes of the weir, gone in the last high water. To be set before the ground shuts. Four marks.

Teague drew its tack and held it out.

Pike looked at the shingle, and at him, and at the shingle again.

"That's a boy's job."

"It's on my road."

"You've no road south. You've forty marks of fence east, with my capitals on it, and you've a day's posts still to set."

"Then it'll want its capitals a day or two longer."

Pike said nothing more. He wrote the name. But he kept his one hand on the shingle for a breath after the ink was dry, and Teague knew that he had been read; and he found, somewhat to his surprise, that he did not mind it.

He had told a boy at a door that his crew would be at Millrace in two days, and it had been true when he said it only because he had decided, between one sentence and the next, to make it true. A man does not walk up to another crew and hand it the hair on his own neck.

But he could be half a day from where a certain paper pointed, with a spear and a bow and a boy, on honest business. Nobody could say that it rested on nothing, since it rested on three stakes and four marks.

They walked at noon, and slept at the fork above the mill, without a fire, a crew's length apart; and before he lay down he counted his three by their breathing, as he did every night of his life. The bow's was the short one, since that hip had not liked the ridge.

It was the boy who asked, at that fork, before the blankets were down. He had a heel of bread half way to his mouth, and he stopped it there, as he stopped eating whenever his captain was about to speak.

"Is it the five? That we're up here for?"

"It's a weir. You heard the slip said."

"I heard it. I never knew you take four marks."

Teague looked at him. He had made it a rule, nine cold terms ago, that he would not walk three people up a road for a reason that he was ashamed to give them; and the rule held on a ridge at night as it held at a plank.

"There's a paper that I hung back on a nail," he said. "There's a crew that took it down. I think that it's a bad paper, and I can't tell you what's bad in it. I said to them that if they were late, we'd come and look."

"Look for what?" said the bow. He was easing his leg out along the turf, a little at a time.

"I'll know when I see it."

"That's not a price."

"No," said Teague. "It isn't. I've none to give you. If any one of you would sooner set stakes tomorrow and go home, he can say so now, and I'll think no worse of him."

The spear said nothing, which was what he said to most things. The bow grunted, and went on easing his leg. The boy put the bread into his mouth.

They were at the weir by first light on the hundred and fourteenth, and the woman who kept the ford told him the news before he had asked for it. Five had come off the ridge the day before, at noon, with a mule; and the healer had gone up again with them, and had taken the mill's jenny, and had left word with a carter for a child at some gate to the north.

"She's not one to leave her bench for a walk," said the woman. "Thirty rounds I've counted her through this ford. She never once went up that ridge."

He set two stakes with the spear and the boy, in water to the thigh, while the bow sat on the bank and sharpened the third. He did the sum as he drove them: it was an afternoon up to that place, by the ruts, and a morning to go in and bring a case out, if it was a walk and a carry, so that they would be down at the ford again by the middle of the day.

The middle of the day came. He stood in the mill water with a maul in his hands and looked up at the notch in the ridge, and nobody came through it.

He had not said how late, and he saw that now: he had said if you're late back, as though late were a thing that would announce itself.

He gave it one hour more by the shadow of the wheel.

Then he laid the maul down on the bank, beside the third stake.

"That's not set," said the boy.

"No. It'll cost us the four marks; she'll not put her mark to two stakes of three." He was wringing out his breeches. "Get your bread. We're going up."

Not one of the three asked him why. The spear took his spear. The bow got up off the bank, on the good leg first, and slung his stave; and Teague, who had been about to tell him that he might stay with the mill and the mules, saw his face and held his tongue.

They were on the ridge at dusk, on that same day, half a mile short of where the road tips over, when he saw it.

There was a light first. It was small, and low down, where the dark ground was; a point of fire that did not flicker as a brand flickers. Before he had fairly taken it in, there was a sound that he knew as well as his own name, since he had walked eleven cold terms beside a Wind, long ago, in another crew. That crack was a Wind's.

He put up his hand, and his three stopped behind him.

Then there was a noise in the low ground that he did not know at all. It was like a squall caught in a ditch. Something pale went up the slope in a column, where the old road ran, and burst.

And then the light again, in the same place. It was held still. It was held up, by one arm, as high as that arm would go.

He stood on the ridge with the wind in his face and counted what he had. A Wind was one thing. An Ember, who could make fire stand on the air, was another, and he had worked beside two such; and whatever had gone up that ditch was a third. He had seen all three within the space of forty breaths, at one spot, and when he looked for the people who had done them he could find only one upright shape, very small, with its arm raised.

He was too old to tell himself that he had miscounted.

There were others moving. He saw them along the far edge of the low ground, against what was left of the sky: two together, going away south, and one to the west. They did not go as beaten men go; they went as people go who have practised leaving. He had seen a crew break like that only once, and he had not liked that crew.

"We'll not run in on it," he said. "Give them the time to be gone. Then we light the lantern, and we carry it where it shows."

He read the ground by that lantern as they came down, since it was the thing that he could do.

On the brow, where the ruts turned, two people had lain all day, and the frost showed him the two shapes, two yards apart, each a man's length. There was no ash of any fire, and nobody had dropped a crumb there, or a thread, or the paring of a nail. Beside the northern shape he found the round print of a stirrup pressed into the turf again and again in the one place. He counted, and there were eleven prints, and a twelfth half made.

That was a crossbow. He had expected a bow of some kind. He had not expected that every sign of its owner would stop at the height of a boot.

He said his piece to the boy at the stone, and kept it short: that he had seen a man walk out of the Quiet and declare. He did not say three, since he could not price three, and he put no question about what else there was. A captain who asks a question that he has no column for has only given himself something to carry, and he had three to carry already.

He sent the spear south-about by the ruts with the lantern, and the boy with him. They were gone the better part of two hours. They came back by the north, having walked the whole of the ruts, with a crossbow each and a third across the boy's shoulders.

"Lying down," said the spear. He was not a man of many words. "On their sides. String cut. Nothing in the lock."

"And nothing else?"

"Nothing. I looked."

The bow had the three of them across his knee before they were fairly on the grass. He turned each to the lantern, and tried each empty lock with his thumb, and shook his head over them like a man at a horse fair.

"Three makers, and not a name left on one of them." He looked up. "They're a deal better than mine."

Teague did not answer him. He was looking down the old road, to where a lamp burned beside a grey stone, and a boy sat against a bar of iron with a book on his knee.

He had a rank that he had never sent west. He had earned it on a ledge in the cold, where there was no station to see it, and had let the registry go on writing the old one; it had seemed to him then that what a man had done was worth more than what was put down about him.

So he knew a little about being something that a book had no line for. It was a very little, for he had kept back one tier, and that boy had no tier to keep back. Whatever he was, it was not written anywhere at all.

It made Teague uneasy, and he did not pretend otherwise. But six people had lain on this rim with their faces covered and their bows unmarked, and had shot a man from behind; and one boy had stood up in front of them with a light held where everybody could see it. He knew which of those two things he would sooner have on a road beside his three.

He did not sleep much. A while before the light he got up and woke them.

Nobody had asked it of him. The boy at the stone had asked him for nothing, either at an inn's door or across a lantern; he had only said noted, and yes.

But a crew that has been shot at from four sides through the whole of a day will keep looking up for a month afterward, and Teague had seen what that does to people. If there was a thing to be fetched out of that hole, they would fetch it better without having to watch the sky.

He put the spear on the southern rim, where two had stood, and sent the boy west, since the boy had the legs for it. The bow he set on the north, which was the shortest walk, and he took the brow himself.

When the sun came up over the ridge behind him, there were four on the rim, and every one had his face bare.

Cael went up to the brow when the sun was a hand above the ridge, and the man who stood there did not turn round until he was within five paces.

It was the hundred and fifteenth morning. He had slept as a stone sleeps, and woken to find that the ground came to his feet when it should, and that his right arm would bend. His left palm was wound in what remained of a roll of tape. He had counted four upright shapes on the rim before he had his boots on, one at each of the places where a hood had stood the day before, and he had been on his feet with nothing in his hands before he saw whose they were.

Cael had lain against a bar of iron the night before, shaking, and had watched a lantern go away round the ruts to look for whatever six people had left; he had thought then that it was more than a captain owed to a crew ten lines under him, and he had not known how to say so. He did not know now.

"How do I walk along a thing that I can't see?"

It took Lira the first three cords to learn the trick of it, and after that she did not put a foot wrong. Cael walked behind with the notebook, and wrote each station in a bad hand. She went with the cord's end shut in her right fist and the sling tied high against her collar-bone, a pace at a time, as a child walks along a kerb; and every few strides she tipped her head, as if she were listening, and moved her left boot a hand's breadth out or in.

"Gone," she would say, under her breath. "Back. Gone. It's like a wall that you can lean your foot on."

At each cord's end Seln knelt and cut a turf, and Karis came up along the rope, counting, with her short cord in her other hand.

The spear stood on the south, a tall man, grounded, with the butt of his weapon on the frozen turf and both hands on the shaft; and he watched a girl with one arm find an edge with her foot, sixty times over, and said nothing whatever. On the west it was the boy, sitting on his heels in the ruts with a heel of bread. He stopped chewing when Lira came abreast of him, and he had not started again when they were a hundred yards on.

They passed a good many bars of iron. Every one was old, and scaled, and stamped with the same two figures, and each stood within a boot of a turf that Seln had just cut.

It was the middle of the forenoon when Lira's fist came back to the grey stone.

"It is the same," she said. "Cord for cord, and the odd strides are the same number of strides." Her voice was not quite steady. "I said two hundred, from the ridge, by my eye, and I was twenty short of it, and a stride. It is the Fallow's round, and so it is the Fallow's radius."

"Then they're the one size," said Lira.

"To a stride. I should like somebody to tell me how that comes about by accident, five days' walk apart." She shut the book on her finger. "Nobody will. I am going down to look at a wall."

The bolt lay where it had stopped, on the thirty-first step, with its three grey feathers turned to the wall.

The steps were the grey of the floor, cut out of it and not laid. Every edge was as sharp as on the day that it was made, since no foot had ever worn one.

"Since the twentieth," said Seln, without turning round. "I was counting. The air stops there. I had it yesterday in the dark, by the feel of it on my face, and took it for my own fear."

So had Cael. He kept that to himself, and went down the last nine steps behind a light that did not flicker.

The healer came last, and it was she who said the rest of it, when all six of them stood inside the door.

"It's colder than the frost up there," said Oryn. "And it smells of nothing. A cellar smells of earth, and a well of water. I've been in sick-rooms shut up for a month that had more in them to breathe than this."

She had said at the stone that she would not sit outside a second day and listen. Four people who knew what a crossbow was were holding the rim, and she meant to be where a certain shoulder was; if anything opened, it could be carried up forty steps and two hundred yards with her walking beside it.

Cael paced the room from the door to the western wall, and then across. It was ten strides each way, as he had put it the day before, and that much of his count held. The roof did not. He had called it a foot above Brom's head; and Brom put up his left hand, and his palm lay on the grey with the elbow still bent.

"A hand," said Brom. "I'd have had my hair in it yesterday, if I'd stood up straight. I wasn't standing up straight."

None of them had been. They had seen that room once, for as long as a healer needed a lamp, with a bolt in one of them; and Cael went round it now as he would have liked to then. The roof was the underside of the floor that they had crossed, without a beam or a crack, and when he held the lantern up to it he found his own light looking back at him dully, as from still water. The floor was the same grey. There was a dust on it as thin as the bloom on a plum, which had taken their boots of yesterday along the northern wall and beside the door, and nobody's anywhere else.

The walls were cut from the floor to the roof. The work ran in courses, one above another, five to a wall, each as tall as a forearm; and in every course the fine sunk lines stood side by side in their groups, straight and hooked and crossing, as close as the words on a page.

Karis stood in the middle of the eastern wall with her lamp held up, and for some time she did not move at all.

"There is more on this one wall than I rubbed in an afternoon," she said. "There are four."

"Can you copy it?" said Brom.

"No. I have six hours of oil and a roll of paper; I can sample it, and I shall have to choose." She had not taken her eyes from the stone. "It is the same hand. I may say that now, since I can see the bars."

The healer had stopped at her stride and a half from the nearest wall. She had been round eleven stones on the Fallow thirty times and had never gone near enough to see that they were cut, and she had sat with her back to this for a whole day in the dark. She held up her two palms to it, slowly, as she held them to a patient whom she had not yet touched; and then she let them fall.

"What are they," said Oryn.

It was hardly a question. She had put it to the wall.

"Lines," Karis said.

She said it without turning round.

"I do not know that they are letters. I said so on a floor nineteen days ago, and I do not know it yet. They are lines, cut in groups, by somebody who meant something, and that is as far as I can swear." Her lamp moved along the course. "It is a great deal farther than I could swear a month ago."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Seln would let nobody near the middle of the floor until he had been round it himself.

He went on his knees, with Teague's lantern set down on the stone and pushed ahead of him a foot at a time, and he looked at the dust more than at the thing that lay in it. When he had made the whole circuit he sat back on his heels.

"One person came to this. I have his track in from the door, a little to the left of ours, and the dust has lain on it a long while. He knelt here, and here, and I cannot find where he went out." He glanced up. "That may be the dust; I say only that I can read his coming and I cannot read his going. There has been nobody since, and nothing is tied to it, and nothing is under it."

"Then we can look," said Cael.

"We can look."

It was the cord that Cael's eye went along first, since it was the only thing there that was going anywhere. It ran out over the floor toward the eastern wall, pale and thin, with a knot in it at every fifth span, and it lay as straight as a ruled line for half the width of the room. There it stopped. The rest of its length lay beside it in a coil that nobody had paid out.

Somebody had been measuring from the middle of that room to its wall, and had got half way.

"A mallet," said Brom. He was naming them as he came to them, like a man going along a bench of tools. "Iron on the head of it. A bar. And that's a book, on its face." He sounded almost injured. "Is that all? I said that a kit was a cart's worth. I said brass."

"It is a kit for one thing," said Karis. She had come away from her wall at last. "A cord to find how far, and a bar to mark where; a mallet for the bar, and a book to say that it was done. He did not come to map this country. He came to put iron on an edge."

The thing that they had come out of stood behind them all. Cael had taken it by one small lamp for the whole of what was there: a flat case as long as a man's arm, of board under tarred canvas, with a strap to go over a shoulder. Its lid was thrown right back, and nothing was left in it.

"They lie in the order that they came out," said Seln quietly. "The cord, and the mallet, and the bar; and the book last and nearest, since a man writes last. Nobody packs so. He meant to take them up again."

Karis knelt by the bar, and Cael held the lantern for her.

It was the same pattern as the two at the stone, and it was clean, since no rust had come to it in that dry cold. Under the beaten head there was the registry's stamp; and under the stamp, punched deep, were two figures, and beneath the figures a short upright stroke with a bar across its foot.

"Thirty-two," said Lira. "And it's got the mark that the newer one has."

"It was never driven," said Seln.

"No." Karis had bent until her nose was a hand from the iron, and she spoke slowly. "Look at the head. It has been beaten flat, as they all are, at the forge; but there are two bright places on it, here and here, where something has struck it since. And look at the point."

Cael looked. The bar had been drawn down to a point at its lower end, four-sided, like a great nail, and the last hair of that point was bright, and turned over on itself.

He had seen a thing like that once before, on a trestle in a barn, on the tip of a pen-knife.

Karis put out one finger and laid it on the floor beside the bar, and moved the lantern nearer. She went over the grey stone an inch at a time, for a foot in every direction, and then for another foot.

"There is not a mark," she said.

She sat back.

"He tried to drive it. Twice, by the head. It wouldn't go. Nothing goes into this."

Cael thought of a man kneeling where she knelt, with that mallet in his fist, in a room under the ground. He had struck it once, and looked. He had struck it a second time, harder. And then he had laid the mallet down beside the bar, quite neatly, and had not struck a third.

"So where is he?" said Brom.

"I do not know," said Seln.

"He left his tools. A man doesn't leave his tools."

"Nobody leaves a registry kit. It's signed out. You don't get another." Seln's mild voice had an edge in it that Cael had heard only once before, by a grey stone, the night before. "I signed for a satchel and four keys in my first posting, and I answered for every one of them for fifteen years. A surveyor answers for this. If he had walked out of that door on his own feet, he would have carried it, or he would have come back for it. And the people who sent us here knew that it was lying. They wrote abandoned on a sheet of cream paper. They left it where it was for as long as they wanted a thing in this country that somebody could be sent to fetch."

"Then he's dead," said Lira.

"Or he could not come back. I shall not choose between those, since I have no leaf that tells me."

It was Seln who turned the book over, and he did it with two fingers, as he would have handled another man's letter.

It was a field ledger, bound in limp hide, no bigger than Hesk's, with a pencil lying in its gutter. The leaves were ruled in faint blue, with a narrow column at the left hand and a wide one beside it; and the wide one was written from top to bottom, down a page and a half, in a small upright hand that used the pencil hard.

"This is not the clerk," said Seln. "This is somebody who wrote standing up, on his knee. It is his own book."

"Read it," said Karis.

She had gone back to her wall, with Lira, and had a sheet of the thin paper spread against the lowest course. She kept her face to the stone; but Cael saw that her pencil was not moving.

"There is a line at the head, set by itself, where a place is named." Seln held the leaf to the lantern for some time. "There are four signs, and after them the number that is on that bar. The number I can read; the signs are from an index, and it is not one that I ever used, or was ever shown."

"What sort of index?" said Brom.

"I don't know what this is in, and I'm not going to say."

He went on to the next line before anybody could ask him again.

"Then there are distances, measured in cords, as she measures; his cord is that one, knotted at the fives. He begins at the edge. North station to floor. East station to floor. There are eight of those, by the points of the compass and the half-points, and against every one of them he has put the same figure."

"His stations are the old irons," said Karis, to the wall. "There was a bar at each of those eight points this morning, scaled as the old one at the stone is scaled. I had a turf within a boot of every one."

"Then this is the book of whoever drove them." Seln kept his eyes on the leaf. "I put five cold terms on the old iron at the stone, and I see no cause to alter that for his book."

"The bar in his kit's got the other one's mark," said Lira. "The newer one's."

"It has. So that mark lay in this man's case five cold terms ago, and somebody set the same on a bar at our stone a good deal later. Those are two visits, and I can tell you no more of them. I said that I should not put a meaning on two strokes of a punch; I shall not put a date on them either."

"And after the distances?" said Karis.

"A line by itself. Reach, edge to centre. She would call it the radius. It is in his own figures, and he has gone over it twice with the pencil, so that it has cut the paper."

He read it out, and she wrote it down without turning her head.

"Below that he has a few lines on the floor and the stair, such as she has in her own table. I shall read them to her when she has a hand free." Seln turned the leaf. "And on the second page there is one line only."

He stopped.

It was so unlike him that all five of them looked up. He was holding the book quite still, a hand's breadth from the horn of the lantern, and his eyes were going along one line of pencil from its beginning to its end and back again.

"It is not finished," he said. "There is a line, and after it a stroke of the pencil that goes off toward the edge of the leaf, and then nothing. The rest of the book is clean."

"What's the line?" said Cael.

Seln read it as it stood.

third site confirmed on bearing —

A sheet of thin paper slid down the eastern wall and folded itself on the floor.

Karis had let go of it. She had been kneeling at the lowest course, with her left hand spread to hold the sheet and her right about to begin; and she had come up off her knees as if somebody had laid a cold hand between her shoulders.

She stood with her back to the stone, and she had gone white, and then red.

"A bearing is a line with a direction to it." It came out of her very fast, in the small exact voice. "It is a thing that a person takes with an instrument, between two places, in order to find out what else lies along it. He had two places. He had put iron on both, and he drew through them.
